1367372427.title: RNAS Culham
1367372427.content:
{{About|an airfield in Oxfordshire|HMS Hornbill II, a Royal Naval Air Station in Suffolk|Beccles Airfield}} {{Short description|Former Royal Naval Air Station in Oxfordshire, England}} {{Use dmy dates|date=January 2018}} {{Use British English|date=January 2018}} {{Infobox military installation | name = RNAS Culham
HMS ''Hornbill'' | ensign = Naval Ensign of the United Kingdom.svg | ensign_size = 90px | native_name = | part_of = | location = next to the village of [[Culham]], in [[Oxfordshire]] | nearest_town = [[Oxford]] | country = England | image = [[File:HMS_Hornbill_Ships_Badge.jpg|125px]] | image_alt = | caption = HMS ''Hornbill'' | image2 = | image2_alt = | caption2 = | type = [[Naval Air Station#Royal Navy|Royal Naval Air Station]] | coordinates = {{Coord|51|39|31|N|1|13|38|W|display=inline,title}} | gridref = | image_map = | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | pushpin_map = Oxfordshire#UK | pushpin_map_size = | pushpin_alt = | pushpin_caption = Shown within Oxfordshire | pushpin_relief = | pushpin_image = | pushpin_label = RNAS Culham | pushpin_label_position = | pushpin_mark = | pushpin_mark_size = | owner = [[British Admiralty|Admiralty]] | operator = {{Navy|UK}} | controlled_by = [[Fleet Air Arm]] | open_to_public = | site_other_label = | site_other = | site_area = | code = CM | built = {{Start date|1933}} | in_use = 1933-{{End date|1960}} | builder = | materials = | height = | length = | fate = now Culham Science Centre | condition = Disused | battles = [[World War II|Second World War]] | events = | current_commander = | past_commanders = | garrison = Fleet Air Arm | occupants = Receipt and Despatch Unit No.2
No.1 Ferry Flight
[[739 Naval Air Squadron|739 Squadron, SRPDU]]
[[1832 Naval Air Squadron|1832 RNVR (Air) Squadron]] | designations = | website = | footnotes = | IATA = | ICAO = | FAA = | TC = | LID = | GPS = | WMO = | elevation = {{Convert|190 |feet|0}} | r1_number = 06/24 | r1_length = {{Convert|1,200 |yards|0}} | r1_surface = [[Asphalt concrete]] | r2_number = 10/28 | r2_length = {{Convert|1,400 |yards|0}} | r2_surface = Asphalt concrete | r3_number = 17/35 | r3_length = {{Convert|1,200 |yards|0}} | r3_surface = Asphalt concrete | h1_number = | h1_length = | h1_surface = | airfield_other_label = | airfield_other = }} '''Royal Naval Air Station Culham''' ('''RNAS Culham''', also known as '''HMS ''Hornbill''''') was a [[Royal Navy]], [[Naval Air Station]], near [[Culham]], [[Oxfordshire]]. It opened in 1944 as an [[All-Weather Airfield]] for the [[Royal Navy]]. The [[naval air station]] was used by [[739 Naval Air Squadron|739 Photographic Trials and Development Unit]] and was later and home to [[1832 Naval Air Squadron|1832 RNVR (Air) Squadron]]. Receipt and Despatch Unit No.2 and No.1 Ferry Flight were also based here.{{cite web|title=Culham |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/FAA-Bases/Culham.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Fleet Air Arm Bases 1939 - present day |access-date=29 November 2023}} The airbase was situated around {{convert|5|miles|1}} south of the city of [[Oxford]], with the village of Culham lying {{convert|1|mile|1}} to west. The notable landmarks include the city of Oxford where through it runs [[The Isis]], which then forms a loop around the airfield to the north, west and south as it flows south east. The market town of [[Abingdon-on-Thames]] is about {{convert|2|miles|1}} to the north west. [[Didcot junction]], where a [[Cherwell Valley line|line]] running north/south, intersects the [[Great Western Main Line]], is situated {{convert|3|miles|1}} south, with [[Culham railway station]], on the north/south Oxford-Didcot line, at the south west corner of the airfield. The ground layout was typical of many bomber stations, with three [[runway]]s. However it had many [[hangar]]s, mostly sited around the field's perimeter. Initially HMS ''Hornbill'' was used to train reservists based in the Thames Valley area using several different types of aircraft including: [[Supermarine Seafire]], a navalised [[Supermarine Spitfire]] fighter aircraft, [[Hawker Sea Fury]], a single-seat fighter aircraft and [[North American T-6 Texan|North American Harvards]], an American single-engine advanced trainer aircraft. In May 1947 the Photographic Trials and Development Unit was based at HMS ''Hornbill'', and in 1951 [[1840 Naval Air Squadron]] operated from the airfield for a short time. Ab initio flight training of cadets from [[Britannia Royal Naval College]], Dartmouth, flying primary gliders, was also undertaken here in the early 1950s. == Royal Navy operational history == === Ferry Units === ==== No. 1 Ferry Squadron ==== '''No. 1 Ferry Pool''' moved from RNAS Yeovilton to RNAS Culham and immediately formed as '''No. 1 Ferry Squadron''', on 26 September 1946. The unit was allocated various aircraft:{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=325}} *[[Avro Anson]] I (August 1947 - February 1947) *[[Fairey Firefly]] F.1 (December 1946 - January 1947) *[[Airspeed Oxford]] (September 1946 - February 1947) In February 1947 the squadron was downgraded to become '''No.1 Ferry Flight''', but remained at HMS ''Hornbill''. It operated a number of different aircraft: *Avro Anson I (February - October 1947) *[[de Havilland Dominie]] (December 1947 - November 1950) *[[Fairey Firefly]] FR.4 (April 1947 - September 1948) *Fairey Firefly AS.5 (October 1949 - January 1950) *Airspeed Oxford (February - November 1947) *Supermarine Seafire F.17 (October 1947 - January 1948) No. 1 Ferry Flight disbanded at HMS ''Hornbill'' on 31 August 1950.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=326}} === Photographic Trials and Development Unit === On 1 May 1947, [[739 Naval Air Squadron]] reformed at RNAS Culham (HMS ''Hornbill'') to become the Royal Navy's Photographic Trials and Development Unit, (it had originally been intended to share the RAF's Photographic Reconnaissance resources at [[RAF Benson]], but this had become overcrowded). The squadron operated [[de Havilland Sea Mosquito]], a [[navalised aircraft|navalised]] variant of the de Havilland Mosquito, equipped as a [[torpedo bomber]] and a carrier-borne variant, and also the photo-reconnaissance version of the [[de Havilland Sea Hornet]], a twin-engine [[fighter aircraft]], until the unit finally disbanded on 12 July 1950.{{cite web |url=https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5685008e0e4c1155e1f6e9e0/t/5ce67644a4222f1ba97a07a6/1558607431478/Military+airfields+in+Oxfordshire.pdf |title=Military airfields in Oxfordshire |website=static1.squarespace.com/ |access-date=29 November 2022}}{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=46}} === Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve === '''[[Royal Naval Reserve|Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve]]''' ('''RNVR''') [[Pilot]]s and [[Air observer|Observer]]s needed to have completed between seventy-five and 125 [[Flight time|flying hours]] per year. This included non-continuous flying hours of training drills and fourteen days continuous training in [[Aerial warfare|air warfare]] and [[Aircraft ordnance|weapons]], per year. Flying was mainly done during weekends, as there was a requirement for twelve weekends on squadron duty.{{cite web|title=1832 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve Air Squadron |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/SQUADRONS/1832R_Squadron.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Royal Naval Air Squadrons 1938 - present day |access-date=29 November 2023}} The Royal Naval Reserve Air Branch was reorganised into five air divisions on 1 June 1952. HMS ''Hornbill'' was home to the Southern Air Division which was initially formed of only 1832 Naval Air Squadron. On 1 October, 1832A and 1832B RNVR fighter Squadrons were formed, and then in March 1953 these became 1836 and 1835 Naval Air Squadrons respectively. The pooled aircraft, comprising Supermarine Seafire and Hawker Sea Fury, of the Southern Air Division was divided between the three squadrons. ==== 1832 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1832 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 1 July 1947 as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron. Led by [[Lieutenant commander (Royal Navy)|Lieutenant commander]] ([[Acting rank|A]]) P Godfrey {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|OBE}} [[Royal Naval Reserve|RNVR]], the unit was one of four naval air squadrons formed in 1947 as the RNVR Air Branch, the other three were [[1830 Naval Air Squadron]] in Glasgow at [[RNAS Abbotsinch|HMS ''Sanderling'']], [[1831 Naval Air Squadron]] in [[Cheshire]] at [[RNAS Stretton (HMS Blackcap)|HMS ''Blackcap'']], and [[1833 Naval Air Squadron]] at [[RNAS Bramcote|HMS ''Gamecock'']] in [[Warwickshire]]. The squadron was initially equipped with a single North American Harvard T.2B advanced trainer aircraft and four Supermarine Seafire III fighter aircraft, although later on it received six FR.46 variants of the fighter to replace the mark IIIs. In 1951 the unit replaced its inventory with Hawker Sea Fury FB.II. On 19 July 1953, 1832 Naval Air Squadron departed for RAF Benson. ==== 1840 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1840 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 14 April 1951 as a RNVR (Air) Anti-Submarine Squadron. The [[commanding officer]] was Lieutenant Commander (A) N H Bovey {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|DSC}}, RNVR. Eight pilots and observers were detached from 1832 Naval Air Squadron and redeployed to the new squadron.{{cite web|title=1840 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve Air Squadron |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/SQUADRONS/1840R_Squadron.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Royal Naval Air Squadrons 1938 - present day |access-date=2 December 2023}} It was equipped with six Fairey Firefly FR.4, a carrier-borne fighter and anti-submarine aircraft and two North American Harvard T.2b advanced trainer aircraft.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=290}} The squadron remained at HMS ''Hornbill'' for just over two months and moved to [[RNAS Ford|RNAS Ford (HMS ''Peregrine'')]] on 30 June 1951. ==== 1832A Naval Air Squadron ==== 1832A Naval Air Squadron formed as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron on 1 October 1952. It shared the Hawker Sea Fury FB.II fighter aircraft of 1832 Naval Air Squadron. Almost six months later it was re designated 1836 Naval Air Squadron, on 23 March 1953.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} ==== 1832B Naval Air Squadron ==== 1832B Naval Air Squadron formed on 1 October 1952, as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron, sharing the Hawker Sea Fury FB.II fighter aircraft of 1832 Naval Air Squadron with 1832A RNVR Squadron. Around six months later on 23 March 1953, it was redesignated 1836 Naval Air Squadron.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} ==== 1835 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1835 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 28 March 28 1953 as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron by redesignating 1832B Naval Air Squadron. The commanding officer was Lieutenant Commander (A) A C B Ford {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|DSC}}, RNVR. It shared a common pool of aircraft with 1832 and 1836 RNVR squadrons, which were Supermarine Seafire F.17 fighter aircraft and Hawker Sea Fury fighter aircraft, FB.11 and T.20 variants, together the three squadrons formed the RNVR Southern Air Division. 1835 Naval Air Squadron moved to RAF Benson on 19 July 1953.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} ==== 1836 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1836 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 28 March 1953, as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron by redesignating 1832A Naval Air Squadron. It shared a pool of a number of Hawker Sea Fury, FB.11 and T.20 fighter aircraft, alongside some Supermarine Seafire F.17 fighter aircraft, with 1832 and 1835 RNVR Squadrons. The squadron was commanded by Lieutenant Commander (A) T O Adkin, RNVR and was a component of the RNVR Southern Air Division, alongside the other two squadrons. The division moved with its three squadrons to RAF Benson, on 19 July 1953.{{cite web|title=A history of 1836 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve Air Squadron |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/SQUADRONS/1836R_Squadron.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Royal Naval Air Squadrons 1938 - present day |access-date=3 December 2023}}{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} === Other Units === ==== Station Flight ==== [[File:De Havilland DH-89A Dominie AN1152222.jpg|thumb|A Dominie in the markings of Royal Naval Air Station Culham, an example of the type used by the Station Flight]] The Station Flight at RNAS Culham flew a number of different aircraft types, including:{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=321}} *[[Stinson Reliant]], a single-engine four- to five-seat liaison and training monoplane (March 1945) *[[de Havilland Dominie]], a short-haul biplane airliner, capable of accommodating 6–8 passengers (January - August 1959) *[[Avro Anson]] I, a British twin-engine, multi-role aircraft (January 1949 - July 1950) == Units == During the course of the operation of the airbase, the following Fleet Air Arm units were at sometime based at RNAS Culham:{{cite web|url=https://www.abct.org.uk/airfields/airfield-finder/culham-clifton-hampden/ |title=Culham (Clifton Hampden) |publisher=[[Airfields of Britain Conservation Trust]]|accessdate=17 May 2020}} * No. 1 Ferry Flight * [[739 Naval Air Squadron]] * [[812 Naval Air Squadron]] - 12/09/49 to 26/09/49, re-equipped with Fairey Firefly FR.5{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=137}} * [[1830 Naval Air Squadron]] - 12/05/53 to 15/05/53, 1830 RNVR (Air) Anti-Submarine Squadron, with Fairey Firefly AS6 * [[1832 Naval Air Squadron]] * 1832A Naval Air Squadron * 1832B Naval Air Squadron * [[1835 Naval Air Squadron]] * [[1836 Naval Air Squadron]] * [[1840 Naval Air Squadron]] == Closure == HMS ''Hornbill'' was ‘[[Ship commissioning #Decommissioning|paid off]]’ on Saturday 30 May 1953 and the airbase was put into Reserve Airfield Status. The following year it was then moved to Care and Maintenance Status, remaining so between 1954 - 59. From March 1956 it was used as an Admiralty Storage Depot.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=393}} == Post Royal Navy and current use == {{Main| Culham Centre for Fusion Energy}}The [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]] identified Culham as a site for the construction of a purpose built laboratory for plasma physics and fusion research, in the late 1950s. Construction of the Culham Laboratory (as previously known) was started in the early 1960s and the facility was officially opened in 1965. Now known as Culham Campus, the current research programme is through the [[Culham Centre for Fusion Energy]] (CCFE). The [[Joint European Torus]] (JET) nuclear fusion project is based at the site and is now (2026) in decommissioning phase.{{cite web|title=About Us - Culham Science Centre |url=https://culham.org.uk/about-us/ |website=culham.org.uk |access-date=3 December 2023}} == References == === Citations === {{Reflist}} === Bibliography === {{Refbegin}} * {{cite book |last1=Ballance |first1=Theo |last2=Howard |first2=Lee |last3=Sturtivant |first3=Ray |title=The Squadrons and Units of the Fleet Air Arm |date=2016 |publisher=Air Britain Historians Limited |isbn=978-0-85130-489-2 |language=en}} {{Refend}} == External links == * [https://culhamticketoffice.co.uk/bits/hornbill2.html Culham Ticket Office - HMS ''Hornbill''] * [https://culhamticketoffice.co.uk/imgfiles/bits/hornbill/big-aeroplane-page.jpg a page entitled ''A visit to Culham'' from an issue of ''The Aeroplane'', 12th November 1948] {{Royal Naval Air Stations}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Culham (HMS Hornbill)}} [[Category:Royal Navy air stations in England|Culham]] [[Category:Organisations based in Oxfordshire]] [[Category:Military airbases established in 1944]] [[Category:Military airbases closed in 1953]]

{{Hiero|1=pr-jtm<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gauthier |first1=Henri |title=Dictionnaire des Noms Géographiques Contenus dans les Textes Hiéroglyphiques Vol. 2 |date=1925 |page=59 |url=https://archive.org/details/Gauthier1925_2/page/n31/mode/2up}}</ref> |2=<hiero>pr:Z1-i-t:tm-im:t*niwt</hiero>| align=right|era=egypt}}

'''Pithom''' ({{langx|egy|pr-jtm}}; {{langx|hbo|פִּתֹם|Pīṯōm}}; {{langx|grc-x-koine|Ἡρώπόλις|Hērṓpólis}} or {{lang|grc|Ἡρώωνπόλις}} {{Transliteration|grc|Hērṓōnpólis}},<ref>{{cite book |editor-last1=Bard |editor-first1=Kathryn A. |editor-link1=Kathryn A. Bard |title=Encyclopedia of the Archaeology of Ancient Egypt |date=11 March 1999 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-0-203-98283-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XNdgScxtirYC |language=en}}</ref> and {{lang|grc|Πατούμος}} {{Transliteration|grc|Patoúmos}}) was an ancient city of Egypt. References in the [[Hebrew Bible]] and [[ancient Greece|ancient Greek]] and [[Roman Empire|Roman]] sources<ref>[[Strabo]] xvi. 759, 768, xvii. 803, 804; [[Arrian]], ''Exp. Alex.'' iii. 5, vii. 20; [[Josephus|Joseph.]] ''Ant. Jud.'' ii. 7. § 5; [[Pliny the Elder|Plin.]] v. 9. § 11, vi. 32. § 33; [[Pomponius Mela|Mela]], iii. 8; [[Stephanus of Byzantium|Steph. B.]] ''s. v.''; [[Ptolemy|Ptol.]] ii. 1. § 6, iv. 15. § 54</ref> exist for this city, but its exact location remains somewhat uncertain. Some scholars identified it as the later archaeological site of '''Tell el-Maskhuta''' ({{langx|ar|تل المسخوطة|translit=Tall al-Masḫuṭa}}).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Killebrew |first1=Ann E. |title=Biblical Peoples and Ethnicity: An Archaeological Study of Egyptians, Canaanite |date=October 2005 |publisher=Society of Biblical Literature |isbn=978-1-58983-097-4 |page=152 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VtAmmwapfVAC&q=Biblical+peoples+and+ethnicity:+an+archaeological |language=en}}</ref> Others identified it as the earlier archaeological site of [[Tell El Retabeh]] ({{langx|ar|تل الرتابة|translit=Tall al-Ratāba}}).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mitchell |first1=T. C. |author1-link=T. C. Mitchell |title=Biblical Archaeology: Documents for the British Museum |date=29 July 1988 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-36867-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WD92jUwjWFQC&dq=pr+itm+pitom&pg=PA40 |language=en}}</ref>

==Etymology==

The English name comes from Hebrew {{lang|he|{{script|Hebr|פיתום}}}} {{Transliteration|he|Pithom}} which was taken from the [[Egyptian language|Egyptian]] toponym ''pr-(j)tm'', "House of [[Atum]]". Atum's cult center was in [[Heliopolis (ancient Egypt)|Heliopolis]].<ref name="autogenerated1">{{citation |last=Hart |first=George |title=The Routledge Dictionary of Egyptian Gods and Goddesses |year=2005 |publisher=Psychology Press |isbn=0-415-34495-6}}.</ref>

==Biblical Pithom==

Pithom is one of the cities which, according to the [[Book of Exodus]] {{bibleverse-nb||Exodus|1:11|31}}, was built for the [[Pharaohs in the Bible#In the Book of Exodus|biblical Pharaoh]] of the oppression by the [[forced labour]] of the [[Israelites]]. The other city was [[Pi-Ramesses]]. The [[Septuagint]] adds a third, "''On'', which is [[Heliopolis (ancient Egypt)|Heliopolis]]." This full phrase is, in the Septuagint, "τήν τε Πειθὼμ καὶ Ραμεσσῆ καὶ ῎Ων, ἥ ἐστιν ῾Ηλιούπολις." These cities are called by a term rendered in the Authorized Version "treasure cities" and in the Revised Version "store cities" ({{langx|he|מסכְּנוֹת֙|miskǝnoṯ}}). The Septuagint renders it {{lang|grc|πόλεις ὀχυραί}} "strong [or "fortified"] cities." The same term is used for certain cities of [[King Solomon]] in [[Books of Kings|I Kings]] 9:19 (comp. also [[Books of Chronicles|II Chronicles]] 16:4).

==Graeco-Roman Heroöpolis==
[[File:Canal of the Pharaohs Map-en.svg|thumb|Approximate location of Canal of the Pharaohs]]
Heroöpolis was a large city east of the [[Nile Delta]], situated near the mouth of the [[Canal of the Pharaohs|Royal Canal]] which connected the [[Nile]] with the [[Red Sea]]. Although not immediately upon the coast, but nearly due north of the [[Bitter Lakes]], Heroöpolis was of sufficient importance, as a trading station, to confer its name upon the arm of the Red Sea<ref>{{lang|grc|Ἡρωοπολίτης κόλπος}}, Ptol. v. 17. § 1, [[Latin]]: ''Heroopoliticus Sinus''</ref> which runs up the Egyptian mainland as far as [[Arsinoe (Gulf of Suez)|Arsinoë]] (near modern [[Suez]])—the modern [[Gulf of Suez]].<ref>Theophrast. ''Hist. Plant.'' iii. 8.</ref> It was the capital of the 8th [[nome (Egypt)|nome]] of [[Lower Egypt]].

==Location==
Early on, the location of Pithom—just like the locations of other similar sites, such as [[Tanis, Egypt|Tanis]]—had been the subject of much conjecture and debate.

The 10th-century Jewish scholar [[Saadia Gaon]] identified Pithom's location in his Judeo-Arabic translation of the Hebrew Bible as the [[Faiyum]], {{convert|100|km|0|abbr=off}} southwest of [[Cairo]].<ref>Saadia Gaon, ''Tafsir'' (Judeo-Arabic translation of the Pentateuch), Exodus 1:11;
 ''Rabbi Saadia Gaon's Commentaries on the Torah'' (ed. [[Yosef Qafih]]), [[Mossad Harav Kook]]: Jerusalem 1984, p. 63 (Exodus 1:11) (Hebrew)</ref>

[[Édouard Naville]] and [[Flinders Petrie]] were looking for Pithom along the [[Wadi Tumilat]], an arable strip of land serving as the ancient transit route between Egypt and Canaan across the Sinai—the biblical 'Way of [[Shur (Bible)|Shur]]'.<ref name="Block">[https://books.google.com/books?id=EFYp8I3icisC&pg=PA113 ''Israel: Ancient Kingdom Or Late Invention?'']  Daniel Isaac Block, ed. B&H Publishing Group, 2008. p. 113 {{ISBN|0805446796}}</ref>

===Tell El Retaba===
{{main|Tell er-Retaba}}
Eight miles west of Tell El Maskhuta is the site of Tell El Retabeh. This is approximately the midpoint of Wadi Tumilat. The earliest find known from the site is the jasper weight of king [[Nebkaure Khety]] ([[First Intermediate Period of Egypt]]), but such an object might have been brought from elsewhere. Naville identified all these locations as being in the region of [[Sukkot (place)|Tjeku]] (Sukkot), the 8th Lower Egypt [[nome (Egypt)|nome]].

Excavations at the Tell El Retabeh have shown that the site was first settled during the [[Second Intermediate Period of Egypt]]. Following the expulsion of the [[Hyksos]] during the reign of [[Ahmose I]], a short-lived Egyptian settlement followed but ended in the middle of the 18th Dynasty. At the beginning of the [[19th Dynasty of Egypt]], a newer settlement was established, and [[Ramesses II]] built new fortifications, a Temple of Atum and many other structures. The site was inhabited also under the 20th Dynasty, the Third Intermediate Period (11th–7th century BC) and the Late Period (7th–4th century BC).<ref name="PoSlovak">{{Cite web|title=Tell el-Retaba|url=https://pcma.uw.edu.pl/en/2019/01/12/tell-el-retaba-2/|access-date=2020-07-28|website=pcma.uw.edu.pl}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Formation of an Empire. Results of the Season 2017 in Tell el-Retaba |journal=Ägypten und Levante |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1553/aeundl29s15 |last1=Hudec |first1=Jozef |volume=29 |pages=15–52 |last2=Hulková |first2=Lucia |doi=10.1553/aeundl29s15 |year=2020 |issn=1015-5104 |last3=Dubcová |first3=Veronika |last4=Wodzińska |first4=Anna}}</ref>

Some scholars, such as [[Manfred Bietak]] and [[Kenneth Kitchen]], have argued that this was the ancient Pithom.<ref name="Block" /> This opinion goes back to the 19th century, when [[Alan Gardiner]] first identified Pithom with the site of Tell El Retaba, and this was later accepted by [[William F. Albright]],<ref>{{cite book | last = Bromiley | first = Geoffrey W. | title = International Standard Bible Encyclopedia: K-P | publisher = Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Co | year = 1994 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=Zkla5Gl_66oC&pg=PA876 | isbn = 978-0-8028-3783-7| page = 876 }}</ref> and Kenneth Kitchen.<ref>{{cite book | last = Kitchen | first = Kenneth A. | author-link = Kenneth Kitchen  | title = Ramesside Inscriptions, Ramesside Inscriptions, Notes and Comments Volume II: Ramesses II, Royal Inscriptions | publisher =  Wiley-Blackwell | year = 1999 | url =  https://books.google.com/books?id=8b6GI3DaJJwC&q=naville+pithom+Tjeku+kenneth+kitchen&pg=PA266  | isbn = 978-0-631-18435-5| page = 270 }}</ref> Although [[John Van Seters|John van Seters]] and [[Neil Asher Silberman]] argue that Tell El Retaba was unoccupied during the period when we find monuments relating to a town called Pithom,<ref name="Seters">Seters, John Van, "The Geography of the Exodus", in Silberman, Neil Ash (editor), ''The Land That I Will Show You: Essays in History and Archaeology of the Ancient Near East in Honor of J. Maxwell Miller'', Sheffield Academic Press, 1997, p. 261-262, {{ISBN|978-1850756507}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=YzQe_4Waz34C&dq=Per-Atum+Toronto+excavations&pg=PA261]</ref> this claim has been disputed by [[James K. Hoffmeier]] and [[Gary Rendsburg]] based on recent findings at the site.<ref name="HoRe">{{cite journal |title=Pithom and Rameses (Exodus 1:11): Historical, Archaeological, and Linguistic Issues (Part I) |journal=Journal of Ancient Egyptian Interconnections |url=https://www.academia.edu/97588266 |last1=Hoffmeier |first1=James K. |date=March 2022 |issue=1 |volume=33 |pages=1–19 |last2=Rendsburg |first2=Gary A. |issn=1944-2815}}</ref>

The joint [[Poland|Polish]]-[[Slovakia|Slovak]] expedition has carried out a systematic research at Tell El Retaba since 2007.<ref>[http://aigyptos.sk/en/tel-el-retabi Aigyptos Foundation] Slovak Egyptological team</ref> It is conducted with the cooperation of several institutions: Institute of Archaeology [[University of Warsaw]], the [[Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology University of Warsaw]], the [[Slovak Academy of Sciences]] and the Aigyptos Foundation.<ref name="PoSlovak" />

More recent analyses have demonstrated that the designation for the temple of Atum, ''pr-itm'', can be found in inscriptions at both sites—both at Tell El Retaba and at Tell El Maskhuta. This seems to demonstrate that the name 'Pithom' was used originally for the earlier site, Tell El Retaba, before it was abandoned. When the newer city of Tel El Maskhuta was built, the same name was applied to it as well, as the temple of Atum was moved to El Maskhuta. Thus, in effect, 'Pithom' was moved to a new location, a phenomenon that is attested for some other cities as well, such as [[Migdol]].<ref>James K. Hoffmeier, [https://books.google.com/books?id=SMZnDgFxiTUC&pg=PA64 ''Ancient Israel in Sinai: The Evidence for the Authenticity of the Wilderness Tradition.''] Oxford University Press, 2005, p. 64, {{ISBN|0198035403}}</ref>

===Wadi Tumilat Project – Tell El Maskhuta===
In the spring of 1883, Naville believed he had identified Pithom as the archaeological site [[Tell el-Maschuta|Tell El Maskhuta]]. The site of Pithom, as identified by Naville, is at the eastern edge of Wadi Tumilat, southwest of [[Ismailia]]. Petrie agreed with this identification. John S. Holladay Jr., a more recent investigator of the site, also supports this opinion. Alternatively, the recent Italian excavators have suggested identifying the site as the ancient city of Tjeku (Biblical [[Sukkot (place)|Sukkot]]).<ref name="Italian">{{cite book |title=Proceedings of the XI International Congress of Egyptologists, Florence, Italy 23-30 August 2015 |last1=Capriotti Vittozzi |first1=Giuseppina |publisher=Archaeopress Publishing Ltd |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-78491-601-5 |last2=Angelini |first2=Andrea |editor-last=Rosati |editor-first=Gloria |page=82 |chapter=The Tell el-Maskhuta Project |editor-last2=Guidotti |editor-first2=M. Cristina |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TIbwswEACAAJ&pg=PA82}}</ref>

Here was found a group of granite statues representing [[Ramesses II]], two inscriptions naming ''Pr-Itm'' (Temple of Atum), storehouses and bricks made without straw. Recent excavations have also uncovered a significant [[New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom]] tomb at the site.<ref name="Italian" /> The excavations carried on by Naville for the [[Egypt Exploration Society|Egypt Exploration Fund]] uncovered a city wall, a ruined temple, and the remains of a series of brick buildings with very thick walls and consisting of rectangular chambers of various sizes, opening only at the top and without any entrances to one another.

Modern excavations at Tel El Maskhuta were carried out by the [[University of Toronto]] 'Wadi Tumilat Project' under the direction of John S. Holladay Jr. They worked over five seasons between 1978 and 1985. These excavations have shown that the history of Tel El Maskhuta is quite complex. There was a Middle Bronze IIB settlement there (18th–17th centuries BC), associated with the [[Hyksos]], followed by a long break until the late 7th century BC, when there was rebuilding.<ref>Holladay, John S. Jr., "Tell el-Maskhuta: preliminary report on the Wadi Tumilat Project, 1978-1979", ARCE Reports 6, Cities of the Delta 3, Undena, 1982.{{ISBN|0890030847}}</ref>

This construction at the end of the 7th century may have been carried out by Pharaoh [[Necho II]], possibly as part of his uncompleted canal building project from the Nile to the Gulf of Suez.<ref name="Seters" /><ref>{{cite book |editor-last=V. Philips Long |title=Israel's Past in Present Research: Essays on Ancient Israelite Historiography |year=2000|publisher=Eisenbrauns|isbn=978-1-57506-028-6|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZJjgv3PmvkIC&q=Pithom+7th&pg=PA398|author=Neils Peter Lemche|chapter=Is It Still Possible to Write a History of Ancient Israel? |page=398}}</ref>

The '''Okarito kiwi''' ('''''Apteryx rowi'''''), also known as '''Rowi''' or '''Okarito brown kiwi''', is a member of the [[Kiwi (bird)|kiwi]] family [[Apterygidae]], described as [[Bird species new to science|new to science]] in 2003.<ref name=tennyson/> The species is part of the [[brown kiwi]] complex, and is [[morphology (biology)|morphologically]] very similar to other members of that complex. It is found in a restricted area of the [[Ōkārito]] forest on the [[West Coast, New Zealand|West Coast]] of [[New Zealand]]'s [[South Island]],<ref name="Clements"/> and has a population of only about 600 birds.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.odt.co.nz/regions/west-coast/rare-rowi-kiwi-be-released-westland|title=Rare rowi kiwi to be released in Westland|last=Mills|first=Laura|date=2018-12-13|website=[[Otago Daily Times]] |language=en|access-date=2019-10-26}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The Okarito kiwi is a [[Monotypic taxon|monotypic]] species, i.e. there are no recognised [[subspecies]].<ref name="Clements" /> The genus name ''[[Apteryx]]'' stems from the Greek "without wings".<ref name=gotch/> Originally assumed to be the same species as the [[Southern brown kiwi]] ''A. australis'', DNA testing shows that the possible split off from this species was 8.2 million years ago, and the split from their closest relatives, the Northern Island brown kiwi ''[[A. mantelli]]'' was around 6.2 million years ago.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brewer |first1=David |title=Birds New to Science: Fifty Years of Avian Discovery |date=2018 |publisher=Christopher Helm |location=London |isbn=978-1-4729-0628-1 |page=22 |language=en}}</ref> This bird is a [[ratite]] and has similarities to the others ([[emu]], [[ostrich]], [[Rhea (bird)|rhea]], [[cassowary]]). Its [[sternum]] has no keel, its wings are minimal, and it has no [[preen gland]]. Its [[palate]] is also distinctive, and its feathers have no [[barbule]]s or aftershaft.  Other features that are similar to only the other [[Kiwi (bird)|kiwi]] is a weak [[gizzard]] and no tail, only a [[pygostyle]].<ref name="Davies"/>

The taxonomic status of the Okarito Forest population of kiwi has been debated since the 1950s, first by Brian Reid and Colin Roderick of the New Zealand Wildlife Service, who claimed the population was distinct from the kiwi found in [[Fiordland]]. The presence of a distinct kiwi led to the southern Okarito Forest becoming a protected area in the 1970s, and later being integrated into [[Westland Tai Poutini National Park]].<ref name=tennyson/> Recognition of the Okarito kiwi being a separate taxon slowly gained recognition since the early 1990s. Indications that the population was a distinct species included DNA evidence undertaken by [[Allan J. Baker]] in 1995 showing great variation in the genetics of kiwi populations,<ref name=tennyson/><ref>{{cite Q|Q28776040}}</ref> and the discovery of ''[[Apterygon okarito]]'', a louse that exclusively uses the Okarito kiwi as a host.<ref name=tennyson/><ref>{{cite Q|Q54594669}}</ref> The species was first formally described in 2003.<ref name=tennyson/>

A 2016 study conducted phylogenetic and population genetic analyses of the genus ''Apteryx''. A Bayesian phylogeny using 1,710 base pairs of mtDNA for 203 individuals (including [[Holocene]]-aged fossil kiwi) showed that all five recognized species of kiwi are reciprocally monophyletic. The phylogeny also showed extensive differentiation between extant populations within ''A. australis'' and ''A. mantelli'' as well as fossil populations in ''A. australis'', ''A. owenii'' and ''A. rowi''. The researchers generated the following species tree of the five recognized species of kiwi in two clades (spotted and brown) with all divergence events having occurred within the last 8 million years.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Weir | first1=Jason T. | last2=Haddrath | first2=Oliver | last3=Robertson | first3=Hugh A. | last4=Colbourne | first4=Rogan M. | last5=Baker | first5=Allan J. | title=Explosive ice age diversification of kiwi | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | date=2016 | volume=113 | issue=38 | pages=E5580-7 | doi=10.1073/pnas.1603795113 | doi-access=free | pmid=27573837 | pmc=5035888 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Ramstad |first1=Kristina M. |last2=Dunning |first2=Luke T. |title=Population Genomics: Wildlife |chapter=Population Genomics Advances and Opportunities in Conservation of Kiwi (Apteryx spp.) |date=2020 |pages=493–521 |doi=10.1007/13836_2019_71 |isbn=978-3-030-63488-9 }}</ref>

== Description ==
This species is a medium-sized kiwi measuring around {{Convert|55|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length. It is [[sexually dimorphic]], with females being larger than males and having longer beaks. The weight of the male ranges from {{Convert|1.57 to 2.25|kg|lb|abbr=on}}, and the female weighs {{Convert|1.95–3.97|kg|lb|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fjeldså |first=Jon |last2=Sharpe |first2=Christopher J. |date=2020 |title=Okarito Brown Kiwi (Apteryx rowi), version 1.0 |url=https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/okbkiw1/cur/introduction |journal=Birds of the World |language=en |doi=10.2173/bow.okbkiw1.01 |issn=2771-3105|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Range and habitat==
The Okarito brown kiwi lives in the Okarito forest on the West Coast of New Zealand's South Island.<ref name="Clements" /><ref name="DOC"/>

On 29 June 2010, three breeding pairs were released onto [[Blumine Island]] as part of a breeding programme.<ref name="Stuff.co.nz_3869779">{{cite news |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/3869779/Kiwi-released-on-Blumine-Island |title=Kiwi released on Blumine Island |date=30 June 2010 |work=[[The Marlborough Express]] |access-date=1 November 2011}}</ref> In 2012, twenty rowi were released on [[Mana Island (New Zealand)|Mana Island]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of Mana Island {{!}} Friends of Mana Island |url=https://manaisland.org.nz/mana-island-2/history/ |access-date=2025-03-20 |language=en-NZ}}</ref> A new population was established in the Omoeroa Ranges near [[Fox Glacier / Te Moeka o Tuawe|Fox Glacier]] in late 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Naish|first=Joanne|date=2 September 2021|title=New chick a sign of hope for rarest kiwi|page=9|work=[[The Press]]}}</ref> In 2021 signs of rowi were detected in Ballyhooly Bush, remnant [[Prumnopitys taxifolia|mataī]] forest on the Lower Whataroa River flats, 24 km from Ōkārito forest.<ref>{{Cite news |date=25 August 2021 |title=Rare kiwi found at Whataroa |page=1 |work=[[Greymouth Star]] }}</ref>

==Reproduction==
The female can lay up to three [[Egg (biology)|eggs]], each in a different [[bird nest|nest]]. Both the male and the female incubate the eggs. The egg is very large, as it weighs 20% of the female's weight (as in all kiwi). The eggs incubate for 75–85 days.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sales |first1=James |date=2005 |title=The endangered kiwi: A review |journal=Folia Zoologica |volume=54 |number=1–2 |pages=1–20 |url=https://phthiraptera.myspecies.info/content/endangered-kiwi-review}}</ref> Most pairs are monogamous throughout their lives.<ref name="DOC"/>

==Status and conservation==
The Okarito kiwi is currently classified as [[Vulnerable species|Vulnerable]] by the [[IUCN]] due to habitat loss and predation by introduced stoats.<ref name="iucn status 18 November 2021" /> Conservation efforts such as Operation Nest Egg and the stoat control regime have been partially successful in restoring the rowi population. However, the rowi is still in a fragile stage of existence. [[Predation]], mainly from imported animals such as [[stoats]], is still the biggest threat to the rowi. The South Okarito Forest was designated a kiwi sanctuary in 2000.<ref name="DOC"/>

The [[West Coast Wildlife Centre]] in Franz Josef village operates a conservation programme as part of Operation Nest Egg.  Eggs at risk of predation are removed, the chicks hatched in captivity, raised in a natural predator-free environment until old enough to fend for themselves, and then returned to the wild. The operation opened in 2010 and has been responsible for raising the wild population of rowi from just 165 ageing adults in the 1990s to 600 {{as of|2019|lc=y}}.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Waterworth|first=Kerrie|date=9 February 2018|title=Rescuing rowi|page=8|work=[[Greymouth Star]]}}</ref> Surveys have ensured that there is no noticeable difference in behaviour between such birds and rowi growing up fully in the wild. The Wildlife Centre is the only place in New Zealand where one can see rowi in a nocturnal walkthrough area.<ref>{{cite news|publisher=[[The Press]]|date=20 July 2012|first1=Anna |last1=Turner|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/7318181/Influx-of-kiwi-eggs-forces-centre-expansion|title=Influx of kiwi eggs forces centre expansion|access-date=19 March 2015}}</ref>

The '''North Island brown kiwi''' ('''''Apteryx mantelli''''') is a [[Nocturnal animal|nocturnal]] [[flightless bird]] and species of [[Kiwi (bird)|kiwi]] that is widespread in the northern two-thirds of the [[North Island]] of [[New Zealand]]. Its population was estimated in 2015 to be 26,600 of which mature individuals numbered between 10,000 and 19,999.<ref name=bli2>{{cite web |title=North Island Brown Kiwi |url=https://datazone.birdlife.org/species/factsheet/north-island-brown-kiwi-apteryx-mantelli |access-date=30 October 2026 |work=BirdLife}}</ref> It is the most common kiwi species. The eggs laid by the North Island brown kiwi are among the largest eggs relative to its body size.<ref>{{cite book|title=Guinness World Records |year=2013|page=50|edition=Hardcover |isbn=978-1-904994-87-9 |last1=Records |first1=Guinness World |publisher=Guinness World Records }}</ref>

==Description==
It is a large brown kiwi, possessing spiky, streaked feathers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=North Island brown kiwi {{!}} Kiwi-nui {{!}} New Zealand Birds Online |url=https://www.nzbirdsonline.org.nz/species/north-island-brown-kiwi |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=www.nzbirdsonline.org.nz |language=en}}</ref> North Island brown kiwi display size-based [[sexual dimorphism]], where the females are observably larger than the males.<ref name=":0" /> The males weigh between {{Convert|1.44–3.06|kg|lb|abbr=on}} and females weigh between {{Convert|2.06–3.85|kg|lb|abbr=on}}. The long [[Bill (anatomy)|bill]] measures {{Convert|13–20.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=del Hoyo |first=Josep |last2=Collar |first2=Nigel |last3=Garcia |first3=Ernest |last4=Sharpe |first4=Christopher J. |date=2020 |title=North Island Brown Kiwi (Apteryx mantelli), version 1.0 |url=https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/nibkiw1/cur/introduction |journal=Birds of the World |language=en |doi=10.2173/bow.nibkiw1.01 |issn=2771-3105|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[File:Apteryx mantelli (AM LB8581-1).jpg|thumb|left|Museum specimen of a rare white (albino) ''A. mantelli'']]
In 2004, an injured bird was found with streaked white around the head and identified by [[Massey University]].<ref>{{Cite press release |url=http://masseynews.massey.ac.nz/2004/Press_Releases/11_09_04.html |title=Massey News Article – do ya think I'm sexy? |access-date=26 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070218222833/http://masseynews.massey.ac.nz/2004/Press_Releases/11_09_04.html |archive-date=18 February 2007 }}</ref> The white feathering was likely due to a rarely seen genetic variation sometimes described as a [[Albinism|partial albino]]. Few documented cases exist with only a painting of one found in [[Ōtorohanga]] in the 18th century and a specimen in the [[Canterbury Museum, Christchurch|Canterbury Museum]]. The injured bird recovered and was introduced into a breeding programme.

==Ecology==
===Range===
Various isolated and framented populations of North Island brown kiwi are found on [[North Island]] and adjacent islands of New Zealand. It is most abundant in [[Northland Peninsula|Northland]] and is also sparsely distributed in the [[Coromandel Peninsula]], [[Bay of Plenty]], [[Gisborne District|Gisborne]] to the northern [[Ruahine Range]] and from [[Tongariro]] to [[Taranaki]]. Stable populations are also found on [[Little Barrier Island]], [[Kawau]] and [[Ponui Island]]. The species has also been successfully introduced to three pest-free offshore islands of [[Motukawanui]], [[Motuora]] and [[Motutapu]] since 1991. Translocated populations also exist on various mainland sites.<ref name=bli2/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Brown kiwi |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-animals/birds/birds-a-z/kiwi/brown-kiwi/ |website=www.doc.govt.nz |publisher=Department of Conservation |access-date=2 June 2025}}</ref> The population has likely declined by at least 90% since 1900 and continues to decline at the rate of 2.5% per annum in mainland populations due to predators, however, this is balanced by population increases in regions with absent to low number of predators. The extent of occurrence range is {{convert|157000|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}, with a population of around 26,600 estimated in 2015, which was down from an estimated populations of 35,000 in 1996.<ref name=bli2/> A hybrid population of 2,000 is also found on Ponui Island.<ref name="Mlee">{{cite web|author=Mike Lee|url=https://www.mikelee.co.nz/ponui-kiwi-for-waiheke/|title=Letter to the editor Gulf News|date=5 February 2024}}</ref> Estimates suggest that the population of North Island brown kiwi has suffered from a reduction of 30-49% across three generations (26 years).<ref name=bli2/>

===Habitat===
Historically, prior to [[History of New Zealand#Polynesian settlement and development of Māori culture|human colonisation]], New Zealand's native forests covered terrestrial land and provided the assumed primary habitat for all kiwi species,<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara. |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1995 |title=Habitat Use and Selectivity by the Brown Kiwi (Apteryx australis mantelli) in a Patchy Environment |journal=The Auk |volume=112 |issue=3 |pages=680–689 |jstor=4088683 |issn=0004-8038}}</ref> which thrived in this ecosystem.

In modern day New Zealand, North Island brown kiwi appear to generally prefer densely vegetated lowland and coastal New Zealand native forest (subtropical and [[temperate forests]]) as their population densities are highest in these habitats.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan J. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel. |date=2011 |title=The secret life of wild brown kiwi: studying behaviour of a cryptic species by direct observation |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=209–219 |jstor=24060731 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref><ref name=":16">Butler, D.; McLennan, J. (n.d.). ''[https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/tsrp02.pdf Kiwi Recovery Plan]''. Department of Conservation.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jamieson |first1=Sarah E. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel |last3=Jensen |first3=Thomas |last4=Morrison |first4=Kyle W. |last5=Durrant |first5=Barbara. |date=2016 |title=Roosting Preferences of North Island Brown Kiwis (apteryx Mantelli) |journal=The Wilson Journal of Ornithology |volume=128 |issue=4 |pages=857–866 |doi=10.1676/15-064.1 |jstor=26429952 |issn=1559-4491}}</ref> However, due to widespread [[Forestry in New Zealand|deforestation and destruction]] of these native forests post colonisation, the availability and abundance of these preferred habitats has significantly decreased.<ref>Miller, P.; Pierce, Ray. (1995). "[https://www.birdsnz.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Notornis_42_3_203.pdf Distribution and decline of the North Island brown kiwi (Apteryx australis mantelli) in Northland]". ''Notornis''. '''42'''.</ref> Although the characteristics of North Island brown kiwi, such as a low reproductive rate and longevity, suggest this species is accustomed to a stable environment, the North Island brown kiwi has been shown to be adaptive to an array of habitat types outside of its historical, ideal habitats.<ref name=":15" /> It can also be found utilising exotic [[pine forests]], overgrown pasture, sand dunes, [[shrublands]], scrub, regenerating forests and forest remnants.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":16" /><ref name=":17" /> This variety in potential habitat usage has been suggested to be possible by the North Island brown kiwi selectively utilising small patches of favourable or ideal habitats amongst other habitat type patches.<ref name=":15" /> North Island brown kiwi appear to thrive in exotic forests similarly to native forests. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the population densities, body weights and productivity of North Island brown kiwi in exotic forests is comparable to those within New Zealand's native forests.<ref name=":16" />

Although there is an acknowledged favourable habitat, the current primary driver of habitat usage in the North Island brown kiwi appears to be food and shelter site availability with reproduction also being a factor.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":17" /> Not in relation to favourable habitat availability within a given territory.<ref name=":15" /> For example, nesting sites of the North Island brown kiwi in a territory containing patches of different habitat types typically were found within or 25m near secondary succession vegetation and/or native vegetation. Kiwi chicks shortly after hatching can only walk short distances and therefore require adequate nearby habitats, which are selected for by nesting parental North Island brown kiwi.<ref name=":15" />

===Threats===
The major threat to North Island brown kiwi comes from predators, such as dogs, cats, [[stoat]] (''[[Mustela erminea]]'') and [[ferret]] (''[[Mustela furo]]''). A single predator can significantly impact a population within a time period, such as when a single dog killed around 500 birds in a span of six weeks. Over 70 incidents of predations by dogs were recorded in Northland  between 1990 and 1995. The smaller male of the species is at a greater risk of predation by ferrets. Juvenile kiwi of weights above 800g become too large for stoats.<ref name=bli2/> A study in 1996 found that 94% of chicks died before reaching breeding age in areas where mammalian pest control was not carried out.<ref name=":17"/>

Deforestation and clearance of habitats is also a major threat. However, due to ongoing conservation efforts, the rate of loss of native habitat has decreased rapidly and is thus not considered a major factor in population reductions. Avian diseases and novel [[pathogens]] brought on by introduced populations of other [[ratites]] to New Zealand are also deemed a threat.<ref name=bli2/> 

==Behaviour==
===Foraging===
[[File:Apteryx mantelli 111225377.gif|thumb|Foraging at night]]
Kiwi species, such as the North Island brown kiwi, have been found to allocate the majority of their time to foraging, as compared to other behaviours such as vigilance, walking, socialising etc.<ref name=":0" /> Their diet primarily consists of invertebrate species, including spiders and worms, which make up 85–95% of their intake, with plant material comprising the remainder.

Over evolutionary history, the visual organs of ''[[Apteryx]]'' species have been greatly diminished, leading to an overall reduction in their visual field. In fact, ''Apteryx'' has the smallest visual field reported of any bird species that rely on non-visual cues for foraging purposes.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Martin |first1=Graham R. |last2=Wilson |first2=Kerry-Jayne. |last3=Wild |first3=J. Martin. |last4=Parsons |first4=Stuart. |last5=Kubke |first5=M. Fabiana. |last6=Corfield |first6=Jeremy. |date=2007 |title=Kiwi Forego Vision in the Guidance of Their Nocturnal Activities |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=2 |issue=2 |article-number=e198 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0000198 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=1805817 |pmid=17332846|bibcode=2007PLoSO...2..198M }}</ref> It has been proposed that this adaptation arose due to their nocturnal, forest-floor foraging behaviour, where low light conditions render visual perception less critical. Under these conditions, a reduction in reliance of visual cues may increase overall fitness by lowering metabolic costs associated with maintaining visual functions and extracting visual information.<ref name=":1" /> This suggestion is further supported by the behaviour of other nocturnal, forest floor foraging species that similarly are unable to or do not rely on visual cues for foraging, suggesting [[convergent evolution]] across various orders, families and species.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan J. |last2=Corfield |first2=Jeremy R. |last3=Iwaniuk |first3=Andrew N. |last4=Castro |first4=Isabel |last5=Alley |first5=Maurice R. |last6=Birkhead |first6=Tim R. |last7=Parsons |first7=Stuart. |date=2013 |title=The Anatomy of the bill Tip of Kiwi and Associated Somatosensory Regions of the Brain: Comparisons with Shorebirds |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=8 |issue=11 |article-number=e80036 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0080036 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=3828210 |pmid=24244601|bibcode=2013PLoSO...880036C }}</ref>

[[File:Kiwi skull (cropped).jpg|thumb|Skull of a North Island brown kiwi. The beak is long, narrow and slightly curved downwards]]
Given the reduction in their visual senses, ''Apteryx'' species, including the North Island brown kiwi are required to utilise their additional senses, particularly remote touch and smell to find prey.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Remote touch foraging is facilitated by the bill-tip sensory organ found at the end of kiwi species' long, narrow and slightly down curved beaks.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel. |last3=Alley |first3=Maurice. |date=2007 |title=A new prey-detection mechanism for kiwi ( Apteryx spp.) suggests convergent evolution between paleognathous and neognathous birds |journal=Journal of Anatomy |language=en |volume=211 |issue=4 |pages=493–502 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-7580.2007.00786.x |issn=0021-8782 |pmc=2375824 |pmid=17711422}}</ref> The bill-tip organ consists of [[mechanoreceptors]], such as [[Corpuscles of Herbst|Herbst corpuscles]] and terminal cell receptors, found within sensory pits in the bone of the beak tip.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> These mechanoreceptors are sensitive to the vibrations and pressure gradients soil dwelling invertebrates make underground, allowing kiwi to detect their prey without visual or auditory cues.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan J. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel. |last3=Potter |first3=Murray A. |date=2009 |title=The relative importance of olfaction and remote touch in prey detection by North Island brown kiwis |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0003347209003236 |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=78 |issue=4 |pages=899–905 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2009.07.015 |issn=0003-3472|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The North Island brown kiwi's most common form of foraging has been observed to be tapping and probing the ground substrate with their beaks.<ref name=":0" /> This form of foraging is thought to allow for either smell or tactile sensing of prey, with the North Island brown kiwi capable of switching between these sensory modalities depending on the available stimuli.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

===Courtship and reproduction===
[[File:Bul02Bird326a.jpg|thumb|Illustration of chick]]
The North Island brown kiwi has been found to primarily engage in monogamous, long term pairings regardless of the sex ratio within a population.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara. |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1991 |title=Social Organization of North Island Brown Kiwi: Long-term Pairs and Three Types of Male Spacing Behaviour |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1439-0310.1991.tb00292.x |journal=Ethology |language=en |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=47–62 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0310.1991.tb00292.x |bibcode=1991Ethol..89...47T |issn=0179-1613|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1999 |title=The Mating System and Stability of Pairs in Kiwi Apteryx spp. |journal=Journal of Avian Biology |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=143–151 |doi=10.2307/3677123 |jstor=3677123 |issn=0908-8857}}</ref> During courtship and the breeding period, individuals can be observed softly grunting while exhibiting bill to bill raised stretching behavioural displays, thought to reinforce established bonds between pairs and has been observed to occasionally occur before copulation.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Jolly |first=J.N. |date=1989 |title=A field study of the breeding biology of the little spotted kiwi ( Apteryx owenii ) with emphasis on the causes of nest failures |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03036758.1989.10421846 |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand |language=en |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=433–448 |doi=10.1080/03036758.1989.10421846 |bibcode=1989JRSNZ..19..433J |issn=0303-6758|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Additionally, prior to copulation, North Island brown kiwi pairs have also been observed to engage in mutual chasing, leaping, loud screeches and snorting.<ref name=":8">{{Citation |last1=Reid |first1=Brian |chapter=The Kiwi |date=1975 |title=Biogeography and Ecology in New Zealand |pages=301–330 |editor-last=Kuschel |editor-first=G. |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-010-1941-5_7 |access-date=2024-10-15 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-010-1941-5_7 |isbn=978-94-010-1941-5 |last2=Williams |first2=G.R.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Once a partnership has formed, the pair prepares their nest for the breeding season within their territory, a process that spans around a 2-month period.<ref name=":8" /> This preparation includes burrowing and lining the nests walls and floors with plant material such as fern fronds. Nest sites are typically located underground, within rock crevices or hollowed areas of tree trunks and roots.<ref name=":8" />

After the nest is prepared, the female within the pair contributes her sole parental effort by laying significantly energetically expensive, large eggs.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> Female North Island brown kiwi can lay up to five eggs in a single clutch and up to seven eggs during a breeding season (multiple clutches), though a complete brood that can be properly incubated contains two eggs, which is the average amount of eggs produced by a female in a single clutch.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=McLennan |first=J.A. |date=1988 |title=Breeding of North Island Brown Kiwi, Apteryx Australis Mantelli, in Hawke's Bay, New Zealand |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=11 |pages=89–97 |jstor=24052821 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last=Colbourne |first=Rogan. |date=2002 |title=Incubation behaviour and egg physiology of kiwi (Apteryx spp.) in natural habitats |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=129–138 |jstor=24055315 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref> Eggs are {{Convert|12.5 x 7.8|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length and width and weigh {{Convert|430|g|lb|abbr=on}}.<ref>Dickison, Mike. (2007). The Allometry of Giant Flightless Birds. Table 4.2</ref> Egg laying has been recorded in every month between June and November in a high-density population.<ref name=bli2/> Once the eggs are laid, the male within a pair solely provides incubation, starting from one to seven days post hatch and between 74 and 84 days in total.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":10" /> During incubation, male North Island brown kiwi develop a brood patch, where feathers are shed from the lower abdomen, which has been assumed to facilitate more direct contact for enhanced heat transfer, as observed in other kiwi species.<ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McLennan |first1=J.A. |last2=McCann |first2=A.J. |date=1991 |title="Incubation Temperatures of Great Spotted Kiwi, Apteryx haastii" |url=https://newzealandecology.org/nzje/1907.pdf |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=163–166}}</ref> The eggs are also regularly turned during incubation.<ref name=":10" />

When males leave their nest for foraging, they often conceal the nest's entrance using surrounding plant material, dirt and plant litter. This has been proposed as an anti-predator mechanism against the New Zealand native [[weka]] bird species. It has also been proposed that this could be a technique utilised to control the amount of humidity within a nest.<ref name=":10" /> Generally, incubating males typically leave the nest to forage for roughly a five-hour period, half of the time spent by non-incubating individuals, suggesting a reduction in foraging time due to parental duties.<ref name=":9" />

Once a chick hatches, it consumes the remaining shell and egg contents as these are highly nutritious. After hatching, chicks do not receive further parental care as they are born precocious fully-feathered and with near full senses and mobility.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":11">Bain, I, A. (2018). [https://ir.canterbury.ac.nz/server/api/core/bitstreams/70b0fafb-a558-4897-b472-81c604d1f72d/content Egg-size variation in North Island brown kiwi (Apteryx mantelli): influences and consequences] [Masters Thesis, University of Canterbury]. UC Research Repository.</ref> Chicks generally leave the nest within ten days of hatching and remain in their parent's territory, foraging and nesting independently, until they are large enough to establish their own territory.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":11" /> Research has indicated that more chicks hatch in reused nests than in previously unused burrows.<ref name=bli2/>

===Vocalisations===
[[File:Kiwi Female North Island brown kiwi song.ogg|thumb|Female song]]
Kiwi species possess unique vocalisations that, like those of other bird species, are proposed to serve in a variety of different social functions.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Corfield |first1=Jeremy. |last2=Gillman |first2=Len. |last3=Parsons |first3=Stuart. |date=2008 |title=Vocalizations of the North Island Brown Kiwi (''Apteryx mantelli'') |url=https://academic.oup.com/auk/article/125/2/326/5148223 |journal=The Auk |volume=125 |issue=2 |pages=326–335 |doi=10.1525/auk.2008.06234 |issn=0004-8038}}</ref> The most common distinctive sound produced by the North Island brown kiwi is termed the "whistle call", which is performed solo or in a duet. Mates exclusively perform duets as a form of pair communication.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara. |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1992 |title=Spatial organization of the North Island Brown Kiwi Apteryx australis mantelli: sex, pairing status and territoriality |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1474-919X.1992.tb07222.x |journal=Ibis |language=en |volume=134 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1111/j.1474-919X.1992.tb07222.x |issn=0019-1019|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Generally, the vocalisations of the North Island brown kiwi are believed to play roles in territory defence, social communication and courtship purposes.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13" /> It has been observed that call rates tend to increase during the breeding period and decrease during the incubation period.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":14">Colbourne, R.; Digby, A. (2016). ''[https://www.doc.govt.nz/documents/science-and-technical/drds348entire.pdf Call rate behaviour of brown kiwi (Apteryx mantelli) and great spotted kiwi (A. haastii) in relation to temporal and environmental parameters]'': DOC Research and Development Series 348. Department of Conservation.</ref> North Island brown kiwi vocalisation is suited for short-range calls to close-by individuals and territory neighbours.<ref name=":12" />

There are notable differences between the two sexes' vocalisations. Male North Island brown kiwi calls produce high-pitched (≤36) multi-harmonic notes, whereas females typically emit low-frequency notes.<ref name=":12" /> These differences are attributed to differences in the structure and size of their [[Syrinx (bird anatomy)|vocal organs]].<ref name=":12" /> Additionally, males have been observed to have a significantly higher call rate compared to females.<ref name=":14" />

==Taxonomy==
The North Island brown kiwi, or brown kiwi at the time, was first described as ''Apteryx australis'' by [[Abraham Dee Bartlett]], in 1813, based on a specimen from [[Dusky Sound]], [[South Island]], New Zealand.<ref name="Davies">{{cite book|author=Davies, S.J.J.F. |year=2003|chapter=Kiwis|editor=Hutchins, Michael|title=Grzimek's Animal Life Encyclopedia|volume=8 |edition=2nd|location=Farmington Hills, MI|publisher=Gale Group|pages=89–92|isbn=0-7876-5784-0}}</ref> This is a monotypic species.<ref name="Clements">{{field guide birds of the world|Apteryx mantelli}}</ref>

The brown kiwi (then ''Apteryx australis'') was originally thought to additionally include the [[rowi]] (Okarito kiwi) and the [[tokoeka]] species. However, through genetic testing in 1994, it was determined that the tokoeka was a separate, distinct taxon.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baker |first1=A.J. |last2=Daugherty |first2=C.H. |last3=Colbourne |first3=R. |last4=McLennan |first4=J.L. |date=1995 |title=Flightless brown kiwis of New Zealand possess extremely subdivided population structure and cryptic species like small mammals. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=92 |issue=18 |pages=8254–8258 |doi=10.1073/pnas.92.18.8254 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=41135 |pmid=7667277|bibcode=1995PNAS...92.8254B }}</ref> Once the tokoeka was separated into its own species, it was given the name ''Apteryx australis,'' eventually leading to the official binomial name of ''Apteryx mantelli'' to describe the North Island brown kiwi.<ref name=":18" /> In 2003, more comprehensive genetic tests were performed and it was definitively determined that rowi was also a separate species<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last1=Burbidge |first1=Maryann L. |last2=Colbourne |first2=Rogan M. |last3=Robertson |first3=Hugh A. |last4=Baker |first4=Allan J. |date=2003 |title=Molecular and other biological evidence supports the recognition of at least three species of brown kiwi |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1023386506067 |journal=Conservation Genetics |language=en |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=167–177 |doi=10.1023/A:1023386506067 |bibcode=2003ConG....4..167B |issn=1572-9737|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and was later given the binomial name ''Apteryx rowi.''<ref>Tennyson A.J.D.; Palma R.L.; Robertson H.A.; Worthy T.H.; Gill B.J. (2003). A new species of kiwi (Aves, Apterygiformes) from Okarito. N Z Rec Auckland Mus.40: 55–64</ref> The genome of ''Apteryx mantelli'' was sequenced in 2015.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Le Duc|first1=Diana|last2=Renaud|first2=Gabriel|last3=Krishnan|first3=Arunkumar|last4=Almén|first4=Markus Sällman|last5=Huynen|first5=Leon|last6=Prohaska|first6=Sonja J.|last7=Ongyerth|first7=Matthias|last8=Bitarello|first8=Bárbara D.|last9=Schiöth|first9=Helgi B.|last10=Hofreiter|first10=Michael|last11=Stadler|first11=Peter F.|date=2015-07-23|title=Kiwi genome provides insights into evolution of a nocturnal lifestyle|journal=Genome Biology|volume=16|issue=1|page=147|doi=10.1186/s13059-015-0711-4|s2cid=3156484 |issn=1465-6906|doi-access=free|pmid=26201466 |pmc=4511969 |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0028-1FE4-8|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

A 2016 study conducted phylogenetic and population genetic analyses of the genus ''Apteryx''. A Bayesian phylogeny using 1,710 base pairs of mtDNA for 203 individuals (including [[Holocene]]-aged fossil kiwi) showed that all five recognized species of kiwi are reciprocally monophyletic. The phylogeny also showed extensive differentiation between extant populations within ''A. australis'' and ''A. mantelli'' as well as fossil populations in ''A. australis'', ''A. owenii'' and ''A. rowi''. The researchers generated the following species tree of the five recognized species of kiwi in two clades (spotted and brown) with all divergence events having occurred within the last 8 million years.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Weir | first1=Jason T. | last2=Haddrath | first2=Oliver | last3=Robertson | first3=Hugh A. | last4=Colbourne | first4=Rogan M. | last5=Baker | first5=Allan J. | title=Explosive ice age diversification of kiwi | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | date=2016 | volume=113 | issue=38 | pages=E5580-7 | doi=10.1073/pnas.1603795113 | doi-access=free | pmid=27573837 | pmc=5035888 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Ramstad |first1=Kristina M. |last2=Dunning |first2=Luke T. |title=Population Genomics: Wildlife |chapter=Population Genomics Advances and Opportunities in Conservation of Kiwi (Apteryx spp.) |date=2020 |pages=493–521 |doi=10.1007/13836_2019_71 |isbn=978-3-030-63488-9 }}</ref>

==Conservation==
[[File:Paora 2458.jpg|thumb|"[[Paora (kiwi)|Paora]]", the first north island brown kiwi born in U.S]]
The North Island brown kiwi was first assessed to be [[Endangered species|Endangered]] by the [[IUCN Red List]] in 2014, it was later assessed to be [[Vulnerable species|Vulnerable]] in 2017.<ref name="iucn status 18 November 2021" /><ref name=bli2/> In 1996, there were around 35,000 North Island brown kiwi. In 2006, there were 20,000.<ref name=":17">{{cite journal |last1=Sales |first1=James. |date=2005 |title=The endangered kiwi: a review |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/242117254 |journal=Folia Zool |volume=54 |issue=1 |page=20 }}</ref>

Nationwide studies show that on average only 5% of kiwi chicks survive to adulthood. However, in areas under active pest management, survival rates for North Island brown kiwi can be far higher. For example, prior to a joint [[1080 usage in New Zealand|1080 poison operation]] undertaken by [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]] and the [[Animal Health Board (New Zealand)|Animal Health Board]] in [[Tongariro|Tongariro forest]] in 2006, 32 kiwi chicks were radio-tagged, of which 18 survived to adulthood. Due to ongoing pest control, the adult kiwi population at Tongariro has almost doubled since 1998.{{citation needed|date=November 2017}} In 2006, kiwi were released into [[Remutaka Forest Park]] by the Remutaka Conservation Trusts. As of 2024, the population has reached 300 individuals in the park and surrounding areas, extending to [[Upper Hutt]] and [[Whitemans Valley]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/522282/watch-kiwi-spreading-from-remutaka-ranges-to-upper-hutt |title=Watch: Kiwi spreading from Remutaka Ranges to Upper Hutt |date=16 July 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] }}</ref>

{{excerpt|Paora (kiwi)|only=paragraph|hat=no}}

In 2022, eleven North Island brown kiwi were released on the south coast of [[Wellington]] after a 100 year absence.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-22 |title=Brown kiwi released on Wellington's southwest coast |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/afternoons/audio/2018868095/brown-kiwi-released-on-wellington-s-southwest-coast |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}}</ref> Fifty more kiwi were released into the hills of Wellington in May 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-09 |title=Fifty kiwi set to be released into the hills of Wellington |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/489547/fifty-kiwi-set-to-be-released-into-the-hills-of-wellington |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}}</ref>

The series follows four or five couples as they compete against each other to renovate and style houses/apartments and sell them at [[auction]] for the highest price. The original series first ran for two consecutive seasons in 2003 and 2004, and was originally hosted by [[Jamie Durie]]. The Nine Network revived ''The Block'' after a six-year absence, with a third season commenced airing on 22 September 2010,{{Cite news| title = The Block| publisher = TV-Tonight.com.au | date = 10 September 2010| url =http://www.tvtonight.com.au/2010/09/the-block.html| access-date = 10 September 2010 }}{{Cite news| title = Airdate: The Block| work = Nine Network Pres Release| publisher = TV-Tonight.com.au | date = 9 September 2010| url = http://www.tvtonight.com.au/2010/09/airdate-the-block.html| access-date = 9 September 2010 }} this time hosted by television personality and builder [[Scott Cam]].{{Cite news | title = The Block returns to Nine | work = The Spy Report | publisher = Media Spy | date = 21 March 2010 | url = http://www.mediaspy.org/report/2010/03/21/the-block-returns-to-nine/ | access-date = 13 June 2010 }} [[Shelley Craft]] joined as co-host from the fourth season. ''The Block'' has a large number of commercial sponsors and prominently features brand sponsorships regularly throughout episodes.{{cite news|url=https://www.news.com.au/finance/business/media/brands-such-as-mitre-10-the-good-guys-suzuki-and-iselect-were-the-real-winners-of-the-block-fans-v-faves/news-story/681ccb6b94898f7f00404c45e9999169|title=Brands such as Mitre 10, The Good Guys, Suzuki and iSelect were the real winners of The Block: Fans v Faves|date=11 April 2014|access-date=7 August 2017|work=news.com.au|first=Wenlei|last=Ma}} == Format == The original format of the series featured four couples with a prior relationship renovating a derelict apartment block in the [[Sydney]] suburb of [[Bondi, New South Wales|Bondi]], with each couple renovating a separate apartment over a period of 12 weeks and with a budget of [[Australian dollar|A$]]40,000. The apartments were then sold at [[auction]], with each couple keeping any profit made above a set reserve price and the couple with the highest profit winning a A$100,000 prize. The current format is relatively the same except the series usually features five couples, it is mainly based in [[Melbourne]] suburbs and the budget is $100,000+.{{cite news|last=Warneke|first=Ross|title=The Block's a winner or I'm out to pasture|newspaper=The Age|date=5 June 2003|location=Melbourne|page=6 (Green Guide)}} The first season was filmed at [[Bondi, New South Wales|Bondi]] and the second at [[Manly, New South Wales|Manly]]. The third season again took place in Sydney, in the suburb of [[Vaucluse, New South Wales|Vaucluse]].{{Cite news | title = The Block returns to Sydney | work = The Spy Report | publisher = Media Spy | date = 13 June 2010 | url = http://www.mediaspy.org/report/2010/06/13/the-block-returns-to-sydney/ | access-date = 13 June 2010 }} Moving to [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]], the fourth season was filmed in the [[Melbourne]] suburb of [[Richmond, Victoria|Richmond]], Victoria on Cameron Street. Breaking with tradition, season four was filmed in four side-by-side houses as opposed to an apartment block of four. Season four saw television personality [[Shelley Craft]] join Scott Cam in hosting the show.{{citation needed|date=June 2025}} Season five began airing in April 2012. As with season four, season five has retained the four separate houses format, as opposed to four apartments in a single apartment block as in earlier seasons. Season five is again set in Melbourne, on Dorcas Street, and is set in four adjacent multi-storey town houses. Season six returned to Sydney, in Bondi, for the tenth anniversary. The program has remained in Melbourne since season seven.{{citation needed|date=June 2025}} The first three seasons of ''The Block'' aired once weekly for 13, 26 and 9 weeks respectively.[http://catchup.ninemsn.com.au/section.aspx?sectionid=75933§ionname=theblock&subsectionid=6763878&subsectionname=1 The Block | TV Shows Online | ninemsn Video]. Catchup.ninemsn.com.au.[http://catchup.ninemsn.com.au/section.aspx?sectionid=75933§ionname=theblock&subsectionid=204363&subsectionname=2 The Block | TV Shows Online | ninemsn Video]. Catchup.ninemsn.com.au.[http://catchup.ninemsn.com.au/section.aspx?sectionid=75933§ionname=theblock&subsectionid=7801690&subsectionname=3 The Block | TV Shows Online | ninemsn Video]. Catchup.ninemsn.com.au. Since season four, the program has aired across multiple nights per week.[http://catchup.ninemsn.com.au/section.aspx?sectionid=75933§ionname=theblock&subsectionid=7801691&subsectionname=4 The Block | TV Shows Online | ninemsn Video]. In Season 8, they returned to the show as a team. *{{note|3|3}} This amount of money is split between the two contestants in the team. ==Season synopsis== === Season 1 === [[File:Jamie Durie in September 2012.jpg|thumb|[[Jamie Durie]] hosted the first two seasons of the show.]] {{main|The Block season 1}} The first season of ''The Block'' began airing on 1 June 2003 on the [[Nine Network]], replacing ''[[Backyard Blitz]]'' and ''Location Location'' in the network's flagship time slot{{cite news|last=Melloy|first=Neil|title=Reality is a queer thing|newspaper=The Courier Mail|date=24 May 2003|location=Brisbane|page=27}} of Sunday at 6:30 to 7:30 pm ([[Australian Eastern Standard Time|AEST]]). The season was presented by ''Backyard Blitz'' host [[Jamie Durie]] and filmed in [[Bondi, New South Wales|Bondi]], [[New South Wales]], with the majority of filming being completed prior to the series airing for editing purposes. Selected from approximately 2,000 applicants, the four couples in the season were: * '''Adam Thorn''' (aged 30) and '''Fiona Mills''' (27), a married couple from [[Banksia, New South Wales|Banksia]]. A data analyst and former sales representative, the couple had renovated three properties prior to competing on ''The Block''.{{cite news|last=Wells|first=Rachel|title=Everyone a winner as buyers vie for chip off the Block|newspaper=The Age|date=18 August 2003|author2=Jenkins, Melissa|location=Melbourne|page=3}}{{cite news|title=They've been around the Block – now they'll chase their dream|newspaper=The Advertiser|date=23 August 2003|location=Adelaide|page=5}} They renovated the first ground-floor apartment (flat number one) and were widely considered the "show favourites" throughout the course of the season. Their apartment—which was the last to be auctioned—sold for $751,000 earning them the highest profit of $156,000 as well as the winning prize of $100,000. Mills appeared on the cover of ''[[Ralph (magazine)|Ralph]]'' while the season was airing in July 2003.{{cite news|title=Fiona tries another type of stripping|newspaper=The Advertiser|editor1-last=Williams|editor1-first=Nadine|editor2-last=Hurt|editor2-first=Jessica|date=28 July 2003|page=20}} * '''Warren Sonin''' (37) and '''Gavin Atkins''' (35), a [[sales management|sales manager]] and [[public relations]] manager from [[Elizabeth Bay, New South Wales|Elizabeth Bay]], New South Wales. They are the first male same-sex couple to compete on ''The Block''.{{cite news|last1=Sutton|first1=Candace|title=Gay TV tut-tutting straight from past – Radio chip at new Block guarantees top ratings|work=[[The Sun-Herald]]|publisher=[[Fairfax Media]]|date=8 June 2003|location=Sydney|page=46}}{{cite news|last1=Jinman|first1=Richard|title=Doing their block down at Bondi|work=[[The Age]]|publisher=[[Fairfax Media]]|date=5 June 2003|location=Melbourne|page=19 (Green Guide)}} * '''Paul''' and '''Kylie Ingram''' * '''Phil Rankine''' and '''[[Amity Dry]]''' The auction profits had a combined result of ${{val|fmt=commas|{{#expr:156000+75000+ 60000+152000}}}}. {|class="wikitable" style="text-align: center; font-size: 9pt; line-height:16px; width:70%" | !Flat !
