1383163455.title: RNAS Culham
1383163455.content:
{{About|an airfield in Oxfordshire|HMS Hornbill II, a Royal Naval Air Station in Suffolk|Beccles Airfield}} {{Short description|Former Royal Naval Air Station in Oxfordshire, England}} {{Use dmy dates|date=January 2018}} {{Use British English|date=January 2018}} {{Infobox military installation | name = RNAS Culham
HMS ''Hornbill'' | ensign = Naval Ensign of the United Kingdom.svg | ensign_size = 90px | native_name = | part_of = | location = next to the village of [[Culham]], in [[Oxfordshire]] | nearest_town = [[Oxford]] | country = England | image = [[File:HMS_Hornbill_Ships_Badge.jpg|125px]] | image_alt = | caption = HMS ''Hornbill'' | image2 = | image2_alt = | caption2 = | type = [[Naval Air Station#Royal Navy|Royal Naval Air Station]] | coordinates = {{Coord|51|39|31|N|1|13|38|W|display=inline,title}} | gridref = | image_map = | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | pushpin_map = Oxfordshire#UK | pushpin_map_size = | pushpin_alt = | pushpin_caption = Shown within Oxfordshire | pushpin_relief = | pushpin_image = | pushpin_label = RNAS Culham | pushpin_label_position = | pushpin_mark = | pushpin_mark_size = | owner = [[British Admiralty|Admiralty]] | operator = {{Navy|UK}} | controlled_by = [[Fleet Air Arm]] | open_to_public = | site_other_label = | site_other = | site_area = | code = CM | built = {{Start date|1933}} | in_use = 1933-{{End date|1960}} | builder = | materials = | height = | length = | fate = now Culham Science Centre | condition = Disused | battles = [[World War II|Second World War]] | events = | current_commander = | past_commanders = | garrison = Fleet Air Arm | occupants = Receipt and Despatch Unit No.2
No.1 Ferry Flight
[[739 Naval Air Squadron|739 Squadron, SRPDU]]
[[1832 Naval Air Squadron|1832 RNVR (Air) Squadron]] | designations = | website = | footnotes = | IATA = | ICAO = | FAA = | TC = | LID = | GPS = | WMO = | elevation = {{Convert|190 |feet|0}} | r1_number = 06/24 | r1_length = {{Convert|1,200 |yards|0}} | r1_surface = [[Asphalt concrete]] | r2_number = 10/28 | r2_length = {{Convert|1,400 |yards|0}} | r2_surface = Asphalt concrete | r3_number = 17/35 | r3_length = {{Convert|1,200 |yards|0}} | r3_surface = Asphalt concrete | h1_number = | h1_length = | h1_surface = | airfield_other_label = | airfield_other = }} '''Royal Naval Air Station Culham''', commonly referred to as '''RNAS Culham'''; (commissioned '''HMS ''Hornbill''''') was a [[Royal Navy]], [[Naval Air Station]], near [[Culham]], [[Oxfordshire]]. It opened in 1944 as an [[All-Weather Airfield]] for the [[Royal Navy]]. The [[naval air station]] was used by [[739 Naval Air Squadron|739 Photographic Trials and Development Unit]] and was later and home to [[1832 Naval Air Squadron|1832 RNVR (Air) Squadron]]. Receipt and Despatch Unit No.2 and No.1 Ferry Flight were also based here.{{cite web|title=Culham |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/FAA-Bases/Culham.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Fleet Air Arm Bases 1939 - present day |access-date=29 November 2023}} The airbase was situated around {{convert|5|miles|1}} south of the city of [[Oxford]], with the village of Culham lying {{convert|1|mile|1}} to west. The notable landmarks include the city of Oxford where through it runs [[The Isis]], which then forms a loop around the airfield to the north, west and south as it flows south east. The market town of [[Abingdon-on-Thames]] is about {{convert|2|miles|1}} to the north west. [[Didcot junction]], where a [[Cherwell Valley line|line]] running north/south, intersects the [[Great Western Main Line]], is situated {{convert|3|miles|1}} south, with [[Culham railway station]], on the north/south Oxford-Didcot line, at the south west corner of the airfield. The ground layout was typical of many bomber stations, with three [[runway]]s. However it had many [[hangar]]s, mostly sited around the field's perimeter. Initially HMS ''Hornbill'' was used to train reservists based in the Thames Valley area using several different types of aircraft including: [[Supermarine Seafire]], a navalised [[Supermarine Spitfire]] fighter aircraft, [[Hawker Sea Fury]], a single-seat fighter aircraft and [[North American T-6 Texan|North American Harvards]], an American single-engine advanced trainer aircraft. In May 1947 the Photographic Trials and Development Unit was based at HMS ''Hornbill'', and in 1951 [[1840 Naval Air Squadron]] operated from the airfield for a short time. Ab initio flight training of cadets from [[Britannia Royal Naval College]], Dartmouth, flying primary gliders, was also undertaken here in the early 1950s. == Royal Navy operational history == === Ferry Units === ==== No. 1 Ferry Squadron ==== '''No. 1 Ferry Pool''' moved from RNAS Yeovilton to RNAS Culham and immediately formed as '''No. 1 Ferry Squadron''', on 26 September 1946. The unit was allocated various aircraft:{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=325}} *[[Avro Anson]] I (August 1947 - February 1947) *[[Fairey Firefly]] F.1 (December 1946 - January 1947) *[[Airspeed Oxford]] (September 1946 - February 1947) In February 1947 the squadron was downgraded to become '''No.1 Ferry Flight''', but remained at HMS ''Hornbill''. It operated a number of different aircraft: *Avro Anson I (February - October 1947) *[[de Havilland Dominie]] (December 1947 - November 1950) *[[Fairey Firefly]] FR.4 (April 1947 - September 1948) *Fairey Firefly AS.5 (October 1949 - January 1950) *Airspeed Oxford (February - November 1947) *Supermarine Seafire F.17 (October 1947 - January 1948) No. 1 Ferry Flight disbanded at HMS ''Hornbill'' on 31 August 1950.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=326}} === Photographic Trials and Development Unit === On 1 May 1947, [[739 Naval Air Squadron]] reformed at RNAS Culham (HMS ''Hornbill'') to become the Royal Navy's Photographic Trials and Development Unit, (it had originally been intended to share the RAF's Photographic Reconnaissance resources at [[RAF Benson]], but this had become overcrowded). The squadron operated [[de Havilland Sea Mosquito]], a [[navalised aircraft|navalised]] variant of the de Havilland Mosquito, equipped as a [[torpedo bomber]] and a carrier-borne variant, and also the photo-reconnaissance version of the [[de Havilland Sea Hornet]], a twin-engine [[fighter aircraft]], until the unit finally disbanded on 12 July 1950.{{cite web |url=https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5685008e0e4c1155e1f6e9e0/t/5ce67644a4222f1ba97a07a6/1558607431478/Military+airfields+in+Oxfordshire.pdf |title=Military airfields in Oxfordshire |website=static1.squarespace.com/ |access-date=29 November 2022}}{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=46}} === Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve === '''[[Royal Naval Reserve|Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve]]''' ('''RNVR''') [[Pilot]]s and [[Air observer|Observer]]s needed to have completed between seventy-five and 125 [[Flight time|flying hours]] per year. This included non-continuous flying hours of training drills and fourteen days continuous training in [[Aerial warfare|air warfare]] and [[Aircraft ordnance|weapons]], per year. Flying was mainly done during weekends, as there was a requirement for twelve weekends on squadron duty.{{cite web|title=1832 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve Air Squadron |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/SQUADRONS/1832R_Squadron.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Royal Naval Air Squadrons 1938 - present day |access-date=29 November 2023}} The Royal Naval Reserve Air Branch was reorganised into five air divisions on 1 June 1952. HMS ''Hornbill'' was home to the Southern Air Division which was initially formed of only 1832 Naval Air Squadron. On 1 October, 1832A and 1832B RNVR fighter Squadrons were formed, and then in March 1953 these became 1836 and 1835 Naval Air Squadrons respectively. The pooled aircraft, comprising Supermarine Seafire and Hawker Sea Fury, of the Southern Air Division was divided between the three squadrons. ==== 1832 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1832 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 1 July 1947 as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron. Led by [[Lieutenant commander (Royal Navy)|Lieutenant commander]] ([[Acting rank|A]]) P Godfrey {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|OBE}} [[Royal Naval Reserve|RNVR]], the unit was one of four naval air squadrons formed in 1947 as the RNVR Air Branch, the other three were [[1830 Naval Air Squadron]] in Glasgow at [[RNAS Abbotsinch|HMS ''Sanderling'']], [[1831 Naval Air Squadron]] in [[Cheshire]] at [[RNAS Stretton (HMS Blackcap)|HMS ''Blackcap'']], and [[1833 Naval Air Squadron]] at [[RNAS Bramcote|HMS ''Gamecock'']] in [[Warwickshire]]. The squadron was initially equipped with a single North American Harvard T.2B advanced trainer aircraft and four Supermarine Seafire III fighter aircraft, although later on it received six FR.46 variants of the fighter to replace the mark IIIs. In 1951 the unit replaced its inventory with Hawker Sea Fury FB.II. On 19 July 1953, 1832 Naval Air Squadron departed for RAF Benson. ==== 1840 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1840 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 14 April 1951 as a RNVR (Air) Anti-Submarine Squadron. The [[commanding officer]] was Lieutenant Commander (A) N H Bovey {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|DSC}}, RNVR. Eight pilots and observers were detached from 1832 Naval Air Squadron and redeployed to the new squadron.{{cite web|title=1840 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve Air Squadron |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/SQUADRONS/1840R_Squadron.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Royal Naval Air Squadrons 1938 - present day |access-date=2 December 2023}} It was equipped with six Fairey Firefly FR.4, a carrier-borne fighter and anti-submarine aircraft and two North American Harvard T.2b advanced trainer aircraft.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=290}} The squadron remained at HMS ''Hornbill'' for just over two months and moved to [[RNAS Ford|RNAS Ford (HMS ''Peregrine'')]] on 30 June 1951. ==== 1832A Naval Air Squadron ==== 1832A Naval Air Squadron formed as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron on 1 October 1952. It shared the Hawker Sea Fury FB.II fighter aircraft of 1832 Naval Air Squadron. Almost six months later it was re designated 1836 Naval Air Squadron, on 23 March 1953.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} ==== 1832B Naval Air Squadron ==== 1832B Naval Air Squadron formed on 1 October 1952, as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron, sharing the Hawker Sea Fury FB.II fighter aircraft of 1832 Naval Air Squadron with 1832A RNVR Squadron. Around six months later on 23 March 1953, it was redesignated 1836 Naval Air Squadron.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} ==== 1835 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1835 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 28 March 28 1953 as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron by redesignating 1832B Naval Air Squadron. The commanding officer was Lieutenant Commander (A) A C B Ford {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|DSC}}, RNVR. It shared a common pool of aircraft with 1832 and 1836 RNVR squadrons, which were Supermarine Seafire F.17 fighter aircraft and Hawker Sea Fury fighter aircraft, FB.11 and T.20 variants, together the three squadrons formed the RNVR Southern Air Division. 1835 Naval Air Squadron moved to RAF Benson on 19 July 1953.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} ==== 1836 Naval Air Squadron ==== [[1836 Naval Air Squadron]] re-formed at RNAS Culham on 28 March 1953, as a RNVR (Air) Fighter Squadron by redesignating 1832A Naval Air Squadron. It shared a pool of a number of Hawker Sea Fury, FB.11 and T.20 fighter aircraft, alongside some Supermarine Seafire F.17 fighter aircraft, with 1832 and 1835 RNVR Squadrons. The squadron was commanded by Lieutenant Commander (A) T O Adkin, RNVR and was a component of the RNVR Southern Air Division, alongside the other two squadrons. The division moved with its three squadrons to RAF Benson, on 19 July 1953.{{cite web|title=A history of 1836 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve Air Squadron |url=https://www.royalnavyresearcharchive.org.uk/SQUADRONS/1836R_Squadron.htm |work=Royal Navy Research Archive - Royal Naval Air Squadrons 1938 - present day |access-date=3 December 2023}}{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=288}} === Other Units === ==== Station Flight ==== [[File:De Havilland DH-89A Dominie AN1152222.jpg|thumb|A Dominie in the markings of Royal Naval Air Station Culham, an example of the type used by the Station Flight]] The Station Flight at RNAS Culham flew a number of different aircraft types, including:{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=321}} *[[Stinson Reliant]], a single-engine four- to five-seat liaison and training monoplane (March 1945) *[[de Havilland Dominie]], a short-haul biplane airliner, capable of accommodating 6–8 passengers (January - August 1959) *[[Avro Anson]] I, a British twin-engine, multi-role aircraft (January 1949 - July 1950) == Units == During the course of the operation of the airbase, the following Fleet Air Arm units were at sometime based at RNAS Culham:{{cite web|url=https://www.abct.org.uk/airfields/airfield-finder/culham-clifton-hampden/ |title=Culham (Clifton Hampden) |publisher=[[Airfields of Britain Conservation Trust]]|accessdate=17 May 2020}} * No. 1 Ferry Flight * [[739 Naval Air Squadron]] * [[812 Naval Air Squadron]] - 12/09/49 to 26/09/49, re-equipped with Fairey Firefly FR.5{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=137}} * [[1830 Naval Air Squadron]] - 12/05/53 to 15/05/53, 1830 RNVR (Air) Anti-Submarine Squadron, with Fairey Firefly AS6 * [[1832 Naval Air Squadron]] * 1832A Naval Air Squadron * 1832B Naval Air Squadron * [[1835 Naval Air Squadron]] * [[1836 Naval Air Squadron]] * [[1840 Naval Air Squadron]] == Closure == HMS ''Hornbill'' was ‘[[Ship commissioning #Decommissioning|paid off]]’ on Saturday 30 May 1953 and the airbase was put into Reserve Airfield Status. The following year it was then moved to Care and Maintenance Status, remaining so between 1954 - 59. From March 1956 it was used as an Admiralty Storage Depot.{{sfn|Ballance|Howard|Sturtivant|2016|p=393}} == Post Royal Navy and current use == {{Main| Culham Centre for Fusion Energy}}The [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]] identified Culham as a site for the construction of a purpose built laboratory for plasma physics and fusion research, in the late 1950s. Construction of the Culham Laboratory (as previously known) was started in the early 1960s and the facility was officially opened in 1965. Now known as Culham Campus, the current research programme is through the [[Culham Centre for Fusion Energy]] (CCFE). The [[Joint European Torus]] (JET) nuclear fusion project is based at the site and is now (2026) in decommissioning phase.{{cite web|title=About Us - Culham Science Centre |url=https://culham.org.uk/about-us/ |website=culham.org.uk |access-date=3 December 2023}} == References == === Citations === {{Reflist}} === Bibliography === {{Refbegin}} * {{cite book |last1=Ballance |first1=Theo |last2=Howard |first2=Lee |last3=Sturtivant |first3=Ray |title=The Squadrons and Units of the Fleet Air Arm |date=2016 |publisher=Air Britain Historians Limited |isbn=978-0-85130-489-2 |language=en}} {{Refend}} == External links == * [https://culhamticketoffice.co.uk/bits/hornbill2.html Culham Ticket Office - HMS ''Hornbill''] * [https://culhamticketoffice.co.uk/imgfiles/bits/hornbill/big-aeroplane-page.jpg a page entitled ''A visit to Culham'' from an issue of ''The Aeroplane'', 12th November 1948] {{Royal Naval Air Stations}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Culham (HMS Hornbill)}} [[Category:Royal Navy air stations in England|Culham]] [[Category:Organisations based in Oxfordshire]] [[Category:Military airbases established in 1944]] [[Category:Military airbases closed in 1953]]

The '''North Island brown kiwi''' ('''''Apteryx mantelli''''') is a [[Nocturnal animal|nocturnal]] [[flightless bird]] and species of [[Kiwi (bird)|kiwi]] that is widespread in the northern two-thirds of the [[North Island]] of [[New Zealand]]. Its population was estimated in 2015 to be 26,600 of which mature individuals numbered between 10,000 and 19,999.<ref name=bli2>{{cite web |title=North Island Brown Kiwi |url=https://datazone.birdlife.org/species/factsheet/north-island-brown-kiwi-apteryx-mantelli |access-date=30 October 2026 |work=BirdLife}}</ref> It is the most common kiwi species. The eggs laid by the North Island brown kiwi are among the largest eggs relative to its body size.<ref>{{cite book|title=Guinness World Records |year=2013|page=50|edition=Hardcover |isbn=978-1-904994-87-9 |last1=Records |first1=Guinness World |publisher=Guinness World Records }}</ref>

==Description==
It is a large brown kiwi, possessing spiky, streaked feathers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=North Island brown kiwi {{!}} Kiwi-nui {{!}} New Zealand Birds Online |url=https://www.nzbirdsonline.org.nz/species/north-island-brown-kiwi |access-date=2026-06-29 |website=www.nzbirdsonline.org.nz |language=en}}</ref> North Island brown kiwi display size-based [[sexual dimorphism]], where the females are observably larger than the males.<ref name=":0" /> The males weigh between {{Convert|1.44–3.06|kg|lb|abbr=on}} and females weigh between {{Convert|2.06–3.85|kg|lb|abbr=on}}. The long [[Bill (anatomy)|bill]] measures {{Convert|13–20.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=del Hoyo |first=Josep |last2=Collar |first2=Nigel |last3=Garcia |first3=Ernest |last4=Sharpe |first4=Christopher J. |date=2020 |title=North Island Brown Kiwi (Apteryx mantelli), version 1.0 |url=https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/nibkiw1/cur/introduction |journal=Birds of the World |language=en |doi=10.2173/bow.nibkiw1.01 |issn=2771-3105|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[File:Apteryx mantelli (AM LB8581-1).jpg|thumb|left|Museum specimen of a rare white (albino) ''A. mantelli'']]
In 2004, an injured bird was found with streaked white around the head and identified by [[Massey University]].<ref>{{Cite press release |url=http://masseynews.massey.ac.nz/2004/Press_Releases/11_09_04.html |title=Massey News Article – do ya think I'm sexy? |access-date=26 September 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070218222833/http://masseynews.massey.ac.nz/2004/Press_Releases/11_09_04.html |archive-date=18 February 2007 }}</ref> The white feathering was likely due to a rarely seen genetic variation sometimes described as a [[Albinism|partial albino]]. Few documented cases exist with only a painting of one found in [[Ōtorohanga]] in the 18th century and a specimen in the [[Canterbury Museum, Christchurch|Canterbury Museum]]. The injured bird recovered and was introduced into a breeding programme.

==Ecology==
===Range===
Various isolated and framented populations of North Island brown kiwi are found on [[North Island]] and adjacent islands of New Zealand. It is most abundant in [[Northland Peninsula|Northland]] and is also sparsely distributed in the [[Coromandel Peninsula]], [[Bay of Plenty]], [[Gisborne District|Gisborne]] to the northern [[Ruahine Range]] and from [[Tongariro]] to [[Taranaki]]. Stable populations are also found on [[Little Barrier Island]], [[Kawau]] and [[Ponui Island]]. The species has also been successfully introduced to three pest-free offshore islands of [[Motukawanui]], [[Motuora]] and [[Motutapu]] since 1991. Translocated populations also exist on various mainland sites.<ref name=bli2/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Brown kiwi |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-animals/birds/birds-a-z/kiwi/brown-kiwi/ |website=www.doc.govt.nz |publisher=Department of Conservation |access-date=2 June 2025}}</ref> The population has likely declined by at least 90% since 1900 and continues to decline at the rate of 2.5% per annum in mainland populations due to predators, however, this is balanced by population increases in regions with absent to low number of predators. The extent of occurrence range is {{convert|157000|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}, with a population of around 26,600 estimated in 2015, which was down from an estimated populations of 35,000 in 1996.<ref name=bli2/> A hybrid population of 2,000 is also found on Ponui Island.<ref name="Mlee">{{cite web|author=Mike Lee|url=https://www.mikelee.co.nz/ponui-kiwi-for-waiheke/|title=Letter to the editor Gulf News|date=5 February 2024}}</ref> Estimates suggest that the population of North Island brown kiwi has suffered from a reduction of 30-49% across three generations (26 years).<ref name=bli2/>

===Habitat===
Historically, prior to [[History of New Zealand#Polynesian settlement and development of Māori culture|human colonisation]], New Zealand's native forests covered terrestrial land and provided the assumed primary habitat for all kiwi species,<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara. |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1995 |title=Habitat Use and Selectivity by the Brown Kiwi (Apteryx australis mantelli) in a Patchy Environment |journal=The Auk |volume=112 |issue=3 |pages=680–689 |jstor=4088683 |issn=0004-8038}}</ref> which thrived in this ecosystem.

In modern day New Zealand, North Island brown kiwi appear to generally prefer densely vegetated lowland and coastal New Zealand native forest (subtropical and [[temperate forests]]) as their population densities are highest in these habitats.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan J. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel. |date=2011 |title=The secret life of wild brown kiwi: studying behaviour of a cryptic species by direct observation |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=209–219 |jstor=24060731 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref><ref name=":16">Butler, D.; McLennan, J. (n.d.). ''[https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/tsrp02.pdf Kiwi Recovery Plan]''. Department of Conservation.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jamieson |first1=Sarah E. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel |last3=Jensen |first3=Thomas |last4=Morrison |first4=Kyle W. |last5=Durrant |first5=Barbara. |date=2016 |title=Roosting Preferences of North Island Brown Kiwis (apteryx Mantelli) |journal=The Wilson Journal of Ornithology |volume=128 |issue=4 |pages=857–866 |doi=10.1676/15-064.1 |jstor=26429952 |issn=1559-4491}}</ref> However, due to widespread [[Forestry in New Zealand|deforestation and destruction]] of these native forests post colonisation, the availability and abundance of these preferred habitats has significantly decreased.<ref>Miller, P.; Pierce, Ray. (1995). "[https://www.birdsnz.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Notornis_42_3_203.pdf Distribution and decline of the North Island brown kiwi (Apteryx australis mantelli) in Northland]". ''Notornis''. '''42'''.</ref> Although the characteristics of North Island brown kiwi, such as a low reproductive rate and longevity, suggest this species is accustomed to a stable environment, the North Island brown kiwi has been shown to be adaptive to an array of habitat types outside of its historical, ideal habitats.<ref name=":15" /> It can also be found utilising exotic [[pine forests]], overgrown pasture, sand dunes, [[shrublands]], scrub, regenerating forests and forest remnants.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":16" /><ref name=":17" /> This variety in potential habitat usage has been suggested to be possible by the North Island brown kiwi selectively utilising small patches of favourable or ideal habitats amongst other habitat type patches.<ref name=":15" /> North Island brown kiwi appear to thrive in exotic forests similarly to native forests. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the population densities, body weights and productivity of North Island brown kiwi in exotic forests is comparable to those within New Zealand's native forests.<ref name=":16" />

Although there is an acknowledged favourable habitat, the current primary driver of habitat usage in the North Island brown kiwi appears to be food and shelter site availability with reproduction also being a factor.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":17" /> Not in relation to favourable habitat availability within a given territory.<ref name=":15" /> For example, nesting sites of the North Island brown kiwi in a territory containing patches of different habitat types typically were found within or 25m near secondary succession vegetation and/or native vegetation. Kiwi chicks shortly after hatching can only walk short distances and therefore require adequate nearby habitats, which are selected for by nesting parental North Island brown kiwi.<ref name=":15" />

===Threats===
The major threat to North Island brown kiwi comes from predators, such as dogs, cats, [[stoat]] (''[[Mustela erminea]]'') and [[ferret]] (''[[Mustela furo]]''). A single predator can significantly impact a population within a time period, such as when a single dog killed around 500 birds in a span of six weeks. Over 70 incidents of predations by dogs were recorded in Northland  between 1990 and 1995. The smaller male of the species is at a greater risk of predation by ferrets. Juvenile kiwi of weights above 800g become too large for stoats.<ref name=bli2/> A study in 1996 found that 94% of chicks died before reaching breeding age in areas where mammalian pest control was not carried out.<ref name=":17"/>

Deforestation and clearance of habitats is also a major threat. However, due to ongoing conservation efforts, the rate of loss of native habitat has decreased rapidly and is thus not considered a major factor in population reductions. Avian diseases and novel [[pathogens]] brought on by introduced populations of other [[ratites]] to New Zealand are also deemed a threat.<ref name=bli2/> 

==Behaviour==
===Foraging===
[[File:Apteryx mantelli 111225377.gif|thumb|Foraging at night]]
Kiwi species, such as the North Island brown kiwi, have been found to allocate the majority of their time to foraging, as compared to other behaviours such as vigilance, walking, socialising etc.<ref name=":0" /> Their diet primarily consists of invertebrate species, including spiders and worms, which make up 85–95% of their intake, with plant material comprising the remainder.

Over evolutionary history, the visual organs of ''[[Apteryx]]'' species have been greatly diminished, leading to an overall reduction in their visual field. In fact, ''Apteryx'' has the smallest visual field reported of any bird species that rely on non-visual cues for foraging purposes.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Martin |first1=Graham R. |last2=Wilson |first2=Kerry-Jayne. |last3=Wild |first3=J. Martin. |last4=Parsons |first4=Stuart. |last5=Kubke |first5=M. Fabiana. |last6=Corfield |first6=Jeremy. |date=2007 |title=Kiwi Forego Vision in the Guidance of Their Nocturnal Activities |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=2 |issue=2 |article-number=e198 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0000198 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=1805817 |pmid=17332846|bibcode=2007PLoSO...2..198M }}</ref> It has been proposed that this adaptation arose due to their nocturnal, forest-floor foraging behaviour, where low light conditions render visual perception less critical. Under these conditions, a reduction in reliance of visual cues may increase overall fitness by lowering metabolic costs associated with maintaining visual functions and extracting visual information.<ref name=":1" /> This suggestion is further supported by the behaviour of other nocturnal, forest floor foraging species that similarly are unable to or do not rely on visual cues for foraging, suggesting [[convergent evolution]] across various orders, families and species.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan J. |last2=Corfield |first2=Jeremy R. |last3=Iwaniuk |first3=Andrew N. |last4=Castro |first4=Isabel |last5=Alley |first5=Maurice R. |last6=Birkhead |first6=Tim R. |last7=Parsons |first7=Stuart. |date=2013 |title=The Anatomy of the bill Tip of Kiwi and Associated Somatosensory Regions of the Brain: Comparisons with Shorebirds |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=8 |issue=11 |article-number=e80036 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0080036 |doi-access=free |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=3828210 |pmid=24244601|bibcode=2013PLoSO...880036C }}</ref>

[[File:Kiwi skull (cropped).jpg|thumb|Skull of a North Island brown kiwi. The beak is long, narrow and slightly curved downwards]]
Given the reduction in their visual senses, ''Apteryx'' species, including the North Island brown kiwi are required to utilise their additional senses, particularly remote touch and smell to find prey.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Remote touch foraging is facilitated by the bill-tip sensory organ found at the end of kiwi species' long, narrow and slightly down curved beaks.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel. |last3=Alley |first3=Maurice. |date=2007 |title=A new prey-detection mechanism for kiwi ( Apteryx spp.) suggests convergent evolution between paleognathous and neognathous birds |journal=Journal of Anatomy |language=en |volume=211 |issue=4 |pages=493–502 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-7580.2007.00786.x |issn=0021-8782 |pmc=2375824 |pmid=17711422}}</ref> The bill-tip organ consists of [[mechanoreceptors]], such as [[Corpuscles of Herbst|Herbst corpuscles]] and terminal cell receptors, found within sensory pits in the bone of the beak tip.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> These mechanoreceptors are sensitive to the vibrations and pressure gradients soil dwelling invertebrates make underground, allowing kiwi to detect their prey without visual or auditory cues.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Cunningham |first1=Susan J. |last2=Castro |first2=Isabel. |last3=Potter |first3=Murray A. |date=2009 |title=The relative importance of olfaction and remote touch in prey detection by North Island brown kiwis |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0003347209003236 |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=78 |issue=4 |pages=899–905 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2009.07.015 |issn=0003-3472|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The North Island brown kiwi's most common form of foraging has been observed to be tapping and probing the ground substrate with their beaks.<ref name=":0" /> This form of foraging is thought to allow for either smell or tactile sensing of prey, with the North Island brown kiwi capable of switching between these sensory modalities depending on the available stimuli.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

===Courtship and reproduction===
[[File:Bul02Bird326a.jpg|thumb|Illustration of chick]]
The North Island brown kiwi has been found to primarily engage in monogamous, long term pairings regardless of the sex ratio within a population.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara. |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1991 |title=Social Organization of North Island Brown Kiwi: Long-term Pairs and Three Types of Male Spacing Behaviour |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1439-0310.1991.tb00292.x |journal=Ethology |language=en |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=47–62 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0310.1991.tb00292.x |bibcode=1991Ethol..89...47T |issn=0179-1613|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1999 |title=The Mating System and Stability of Pairs in Kiwi Apteryx spp. |journal=Journal of Avian Biology |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=143–151 |doi=10.2307/3677123 |jstor=3677123 |issn=0908-8857}}</ref> During courtship and the breeding period, individuals can be observed softly grunting while exhibiting bill to bill raised stretching behavioural displays, thought to reinforce established bonds between pairs and has been observed to occasionally occur before copulation.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Jolly |first=J.N. |date=1989 |title=A field study of the breeding biology of the little spotted kiwi ( Apteryx owenii ) with emphasis on the causes of nest failures |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03036758.1989.10421846 |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of New Zealand |language=en |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=433–448 |doi=10.1080/03036758.1989.10421846 |bibcode=1989JRSNZ..19..433J |issn=0303-6758|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Additionally, prior to copulation, North Island brown kiwi pairs have also been observed to engage in mutual chasing, leaping, loud screeches and snorting.<ref name=":8">{{Citation |last1=Reid |first1=Brian |chapter=The Kiwi |date=1975 |title=Biogeography and Ecology in New Zealand |pages=301–330 |editor-last=Kuschel |editor-first=G. |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-010-1941-5_7 |access-date=2024-10-15 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-010-1941-5_7 |isbn=978-94-010-1941-5 |last2=Williams |first2=G.R.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Once a partnership has formed, the pair prepares their nest for the breeding season within their territory, a process that spans around a 2-month period.<ref name=":8" /> This preparation includes burrowing and lining the nests walls and floors with plant material such as fern fronds. Nest sites are typically located underground, within rock crevices or hollowed areas of tree trunks and roots.<ref name=":8" />

After the nest is prepared, the female within the pair contributes her sole parental effort by laying significantly energetically expensive, large eggs.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> Female North Island brown kiwi can lay up to five eggs in a single clutch and up to seven eggs during a breeding season (multiple clutches), though a complete brood that can be properly incubated contains two eggs, which is the average amount of eggs produced by a female in a single clutch.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=McLennan |first=J.A. |date=1988 |title=Breeding of North Island Brown Kiwi, Apteryx Australis Mantelli, in Hawke's Bay, New Zealand |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=11 |pages=89–97 |jstor=24052821 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last=Colbourne |first=Rogan. |date=2002 |title=Incubation behaviour and egg physiology of kiwi (Apteryx spp.) in natural habitats |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=129–138 |jstor=24055315 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref> Eggs are {{Convert|12.5 x 7.8|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length and width and weigh {{Convert|430|g|lb|abbr=on}}.<ref>Dickison, Mike. (2007). The Allometry of Giant Flightless Birds. Table 4.2</ref> Egg laying has been recorded in every month between June and November in a high-density population.<ref name=bli2/> Once the eggs are laid, the male within a pair solely provides incubation, starting from one to seven days post hatch and between 74 and 84 days in total.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":10" /> During incubation, male North Island brown kiwi develop a brood patch, where feathers are shed from the lower abdomen, which has been assumed to facilitate more direct contact for enhanced heat transfer, as observed in other kiwi species.<ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McLennan |first1=J.A. |last2=McCann |first2=A.J. |date=1991 |title="Incubation Temperatures of Great Spotted Kiwi, Apteryx haastii" |url=https://newzealandecology.org/nzje/1907.pdf |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=163–166}}</ref> The eggs are also regularly turned during incubation.<ref name=":10" />

When males leave their nest for foraging, they often conceal the nest's entrance using surrounding plant material, dirt and plant litter. This has been proposed as an anti-predator mechanism against the New Zealand native [[weka]] bird species. It has also been proposed that this could be a technique utilised to control the amount of humidity within a nest.<ref name=":10" /> Generally, incubating males typically leave the nest to forage for roughly a five-hour period, half of the time spent by non-incubating individuals, suggesting a reduction in foraging time due to parental duties.<ref name=":9" />

Once a chick hatches, it consumes the remaining shell and egg contents as these are highly nutritious. After hatching, chicks do not receive further parental care as they are born precocious fully-feathered and with near full senses and mobility.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":11">Bain, I, A. (2018). [https://ir.canterbury.ac.nz/server/api/core/bitstreams/70b0fafb-a558-4897-b472-81c604d1f72d/content Egg-size variation in North Island brown kiwi (Apteryx mantelli): influences and consequences] [Masters Thesis, University of Canterbury]. UC Research Repository.</ref> Chicks generally leave the nest within ten days of hatching and remain in their parent's territory, foraging and nesting independently, until they are large enough to establish their own territory.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":11" /> Research has indicated that more chicks hatch in reused nests than in previously unused burrows.<ref name=bli2/>

===Vocalisations===
[[File:Kiwi Female North Island brown kiwi song.ogg|thumb|Female song]]
Kiwi species possess unique vocalisations that, like those of other bird species, are proposed to serve in a variety of different social functions.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Corfield |first1=Jeremy. |last2=Gillman |first2=Len. |last3=Parsons |first3=Stuart. |date=2008 |title=Vocalizations of the North Island Brown Kiwi (''Apteryx mantelli'') |url=https://academic.oup.com/auk/article/125/2/326/5148223 |journal=The Auk |volume=125 |issue=2 |pages=326–335 |doi=10.1525/auk.2008.06234 |issn=0004-8038}}</ref> The most common distinctive sound produced by the North Island brown kiwi is termed the "whistle call", which is performed solo or in a duet. Mates exclusively perform duets as a form of pair communication.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Taborsky |first1=Barbara. |last2=Taborsky |first2=Michael. |date=1992 |title=Spatial organization of the North Island Brown Kiwi Apteryx australis mantelli: sex, pairing status and territoriality |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1474-919X.1992.tb07222.x |journal=Ibis |language=en |volume=134 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1111/j.1474-919X.1992.tb07222.x |issn=0019-1019|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Generally, the vocalisations of the North Island brown kiwi are believed to play roles in territory defence, social communication and courtship purposes.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13" /> It has been observed that call rates tend to increase during the breeding period and decrease during the incubation period.<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":14">Colbourne, R.; Digby, A. (2016). ''[https://www.doc.govt.nz/documents/science-and-technical/drds348entire.pdf Call rate behaviour of brown kiwi (Apteryx mantelli) and great spotted kiwi (A. haastii) in relation to temporal and environmental parameters]'': DOC Research and Development Series 348. Department of Conservation.</ref> North Island brown kiwi vocalisation is suited for short-range calls to close-by individuals and territory neighbours.<ref name=":12" />

There are notable differences between the two sexes' vocalisations. Male North Island brown kiwi calls produce high-pitched (≤36) multi-harmonic notes, whereas females typically emit low-frequency notes.<ref name=":12" /> These differences are attributed to differences in the structure and size of their [[Syrinx (bird anatomy)|vocal organs]].<ref name=":12" /> Additionally, males have been observed to have a significantly higher call rate compared to females.<ref name=":14" />

==Taxonomy==
The North Island brown kiwi, or brown kiwi at the time, was first described as ''Apteryx australis'' by [[Abraham Dee Bartlett]], in 1813, based on a specimen from [[Dusky Sound]], [[South Island]], New Zealand.<ref name="Davies">{{cite book|author=Davies, S.J.J.F. |year=2003|chapter=Kiwis|editor=Hutchins, Michael|title=Grzimek's Animal Life Encyclopedia|volume=8 |edition=2nd|location=Farmington Hills, MI|publisher=Gale Group|pages=89–92|isbn=0-7876-5784-0}}</ref> This is a monotypic species.<ref name="Clements">{{field guide birds of the world|Apteryx mantelli}}</ref>

The brown kiwi (then ''Apteryx australis'') was originally thought to additionally include the [[rowi]] (Okarito kiwi) and the [[tokoeka]] species. However, through genetic testing in 1994, it was determined that the tokoeka was a separate, distinct taxon.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baker |first1=A.J. |last2=Daugherty |first2=C.H. |last3=Colbourne |first3=R. |last4=McLennan |first4=J.L. |date=1995 |title=Flightless brown kiwis of New Zealand possess extremely subdivided population structure and cryptic species like small mammals. |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=92 |issue=18 |pages=8254–8258 |doi=10.1073/pnas.92.18.8254 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=41135 |pmid=7667277|bibcode=1995PNAS...92.8254B }}</ref> Once the tokoeka was separated into its own species, it was given the name ''Apteryx australis,'' eventually leading to the official binomial name of ''Apteryx mantelli'' to describe the North Island brown kiwi.<ref name=":18" /> In 2003, more comprehensive genetic tests were performed and it was definitively determined that rowi was also a separate species<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last1=Burbidge |first1=Maryann L. |last2=Colbourne |first2=Rogan M. |last3=Robertson |first3=Hugh A. |last4=Baker |first4=Allan J. |date=2003 |title=Molecular and other biological evidence supports the recognition of at least three species of brown kiwi |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1023386506067 |journal=Conservation Genetics |language=en |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=167–177 |doi=10.1023/A:1023386506067 |bibcode=2003ConG....4..167B |issn=1572-9737|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and was later given the binomial name ''Apteryx rowi.''<ref>Tennyson A.J.D.; Palma R.L.; Robertson H.A.; Worthy T.H.; Gill B.J. (2003). A new species of kiwi (Aves, Apterygiformes) from Okarito. N Z Rec Auckland Mus.40: 55–64</ref> The genome of ''Apteryx mantelli'' was sequenced in 2015.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Le Duc|first1=Diana|last2=Renaud|first2=Gabriel|last3=Krishnan|first3=Arunkumar|last4=Almén|first4=Markus Sällman|last5=Huynen|first5=Leon|last6=Prohaska|first6=Sonja J.|last7=Ongyerth|first7=Matthias|last8=Bitarello|first8=Bárbara D.|last9=Schiöth|first9=Helgi B.|last10=Hofreiter|first10=Michael|last11=Stadler|first11=Peter F.|date=2015-07-23|title=Kiwi genome provides insights into evolution of a nocturnal lifestyle|journal=Genome Biology|volume=16|issue=1|page=147|doi=10.1186/s13059-015-0711-4|s2cid=3156484 |issn=1465-6906|doi-access=free|pmid=26201466 |pmc=4511969 |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0028-1FE4-8|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

A 2016 study conducted phylogenetic and population genetic analyses of the genus ''Apteryx''. A Bayesian phylogeny using 1,710 base pairs of [[mtDNA]] for 203 individuals (including [[Holocene]]-aged fossil kiwi) showed that all five recognized species of kiwi are reciprocally monophyletic. The phylogeny also showed extensive differentiation between extant populations within ''A. australis'' and ''A. mantelli'' as well as fossil populations in ''A. australis'', ''A. owenii'' and ''A. rowi''. ==Conservation==
[[File:Paora 2458.jpg|thumb|"[[Paora (kiwi)|Paora]]", the first north island brown kiwi born in U.S]]
The North Island brown kiwi was first assessed to be [[Endangered species|Endangered]] by the [[IUCN Red List]] in 2014, it was later assessed to be [[Vulnerable species|Vulnerable]] in 2017.<ref name="iucn status 18 November 2021" /><ref name=bli2/> In 1996, there were around 35,000 North Island brown kiwi. In 2006, there were 20,000.<ref name=":17">{{cite journal |last1=Sales |first1=James. |date=2005 |title=The endangered kiwi: a review |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/242117254 |journal=Folia Zool |volume=54 |issue=1 |page=20 }}</ref>

Nationwide studies show that on average only 5% of kiwi chicks survive to adulthood. However, in areas under active pest management, survival rates for North Island brown kiwi can be far higher. For example, prior to a joint [[1080 usage in New Zealand|1080 poison operation]] undertaken by [[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]] and the [[Animal Health Board (New Zealand)|Animal Health Board]] in [[Tongariro|Tongariro forest]] in 2006, 32 kiwi chicks were radio-tagged, of which 18 survived to adulthood. Due to ongoing pest control, the adult kiwi population at Tongariro has almost doubled since 1998.{{citation needed|date=November 2017}} In 2006, kiwi were released into [[Remutaka Forest Park]] by the Remutaka Conservation Trusts. As of 2024, the population has reached 300 individuals in the park and surrounding areas, extending to [[Upper Hutt]] and [[Whitemans Valley]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/522282/watch-kiwi-spreading-from-remutaka-ranges-to-upper-hutt |title=Watch: Kiwi spreading from Remutaka Ranges to Upper Hutt |date=16 July 2024 |work=[[RNZ]] }}</ref>

{{excerpt|Paora (kiwi)|only=paragraph|hat=no}}

In 2022, eleven North Island brown kiwi were released on the south coast of [[Wellington]] after a 100 year absence.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-22 |title=Brown kiwi released on Wellington's southwest coast |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/afternoons/audio/2018868095/brown-kiwi-released-on-wellington-s-southwest-coast |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}}</ref> Fifty more kiwi were released into the hills of Wellington in May 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-09 |title=Fifty kiwi set to be released into the hills of Wellington |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/489547/fifty-kiwi-set-to-be-released-into-the-hills-of-wellington |access-date=2023-05-08 |website=[[RNZ]] |language=en-nz}}</ref>

'''Antoin Sevruguin''' ({{langx|fa|آنتوان سورگین}}; 1851–1933),<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Melikian |first=Souren |author-link=Souren Melikian |last2= |first2= |others=International Herald Tribune |date=2000-03-11 |title=Opening a Window on a Lost Past |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/03/11/style/IHT-opening-a-window-on-a-lost-past.html |access-date=2022-10-17 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Navab |first=Aphrodite Désirée |date=2002 |title=To Be or Not to Be an Orientalist?: The Ambivalent Art of Antoin Sevruguin |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4311439 |journal=Iranian Studies |volume=35 |issue=1/3 |pages=113–144 |issn=0021-0862}}</ref> known as '''Antoin Khan''' ([[Persian language|Persian]]: آنتوان خان) was an Iranian [[photographer]] of [[Armenian people|Armenian]]-[[Georgian people|Georgian]] descent, in Iran during the [[Qajar Iran|Qajar]] and [[Pahlavi Iran|Pahlavi]] eras.

==Early life==
Born into a [[Russian Empire|Russian]] family of [[Armenian people|Armenian]]-[[Georgian people|Georgian]] origin in the [[Embassy of Russia in Tehran|Russian embassy]] of [[Tehran]], [[Iran]]: Antoin Sevruguin was one of the many children of Vasily Sevryugin and a Georgian "Ms. Ashin".<ref name=":0" /> Vasily Sevryugin (or Vassil de Sevruguin) was a Russian diplomat to Tehran.<ref name=":0" /> Achin had raised her children in [[Tbilisi]], Georgia because she was denied her husband's pension. After Vassil died in a horse riding accident Antoin gave up the art form of painting and took up photography to support his family. His brothers Kolia and Emanuel helped him set up a studio in Tehran on Ala al-dawla Street (today [[Ferdowsi Street|Ferdowsi St.]]).

== Career ==

=== Practice and themes ===
Because Sevruguin travelled Persia and took pictures of the country, his travels record the Iran as it was in his time. Sevruguins pictures show Tehran as a small city. They show monuments, bridges and landscapes which have changed since then.

==== Royalty, nobility, and cultural figures ====
[[Image:Antoin Sevruguin.svg|thumb|'''Antoin Sevruguin''' signature]]
Many of Antoin's photographs were taken from 1870 to 1930. Because Sevruguin spoke [[Persian language|Persian]] as well as other languages, he was capable of communicating with different social strata and tribes from his country Iran. His photos of the royal court, the [[Qajar harem]], mosques, and other religious monuments were compared to those of other Western photographers in Iran. [[Naser al-Din Shah Qajar]] (r. 1846–1896) took a special interest in photography, and many royal buildings and events were portrayed by Sevruguin.

==== Ethnographical photography ====
Some of Sevruguin's portraitures fed preexisting stereotypes of Easterners but had commercial value, and today, they are proven to be historical records of regional dress. Photographic studios in the nineteenth century advertised a type of picture known in French as "types". These were portraits of typical ethnic groups and their occupation. They informed the European viewer, unfamiliar with [[Persian culture]], about the looks of regional dress, handcraft, [[Religion in Iran|religion]], and professions. Photographing regional costumes was an accepted method of ethnological research in the nineteenth century. Many European ethnological museums bought Sevruguin portraiture to complement their scientific collection. Museums collected pictures of merchants in the bazaar, members of a [[Pahlevani and zoorkhaneh rituals|Zurkhana]] (a wrestling arena), [[dervish]]es, gatherings of crowds to see the [[ta'ziyeh]] (Iranian dramatic presentation depicting the Passion of [[Shiite]] Imams), people engaged in Shiite rituals, and more. Sevruguin's portraits were also spread as postcards with the text: 'Types persans' ([[French language|French]] for Persian types). Sevruguin was a photographer who had no boundaries in portraying people of all social classes and ethnic backgrounds. He portrayed members of the Iranian royal family as well as beggars, fellow countrymen of Iran or Westerners, farmers working fields, rug weavers at work, army officers, religious officials, [[Zoroastrians]], [[Iranian Armenians|Armenians]], [[Lurs]], [[Iranian Georgians|Georgians]], [[Kurds]], Shasavan, [[Assyrian people|Assyrians]], and [[Gilaks|Gilak]].

=== Sevruguin's Studio ===
Many Westerners who lived in Iran and travelers who visited the country brought back photographs from Antoin Sevruguin, often mentioning him in their travelogues of the time. Sevruguin's photographic studio, located on Avenue Ala al-Dawla, was one among several photographic studios on that street. Local residents could have their pictures taken in his studio, often posing in front of a painted backdrop. Most photographs were captured as glass negatives and printed as albumen prints. These prints frequently featured a logo with Sevruguin's name on one side. However, many 19th-century tourists found his name challenging to spell in Western languages, leading to various misspellings such as Sevraguine, Sevrugin, Sevriogin, Segruvian, and Serunian. Phonetically, his name was spelled "Sevr-joe-gien."

=== Vandalism ===
In 1908 the world was denied the rich collection of Sevruguin's images when [[Persian Cossack Brigade|Cossacks]] of [[Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar]] (r. 1907–1909) inadvertently bombed his store in suppression of Zahiru’d-Dawla, the [[Iranian constitutional revolution|constitutionalist]] Governor of [[Rasht]]. His house along with the whole street was burned.

Up to that point, Antoin had over 7000 photographs. Only 2000 were salvaged. As the photographs depicted numerous figures associated with the former Qajar regime and showed "conditions far removed from his own notions of a modern westernized nation", [[Reza Shah Pahlavi]] (r. 1925–1941) confiscated the remaining images.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |last=Navab |first=Aphrodite Désirée |date=July 20, 2003 |title=Sevruguin, Antoin |url=http://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/sevruguin-antoin-1 |website=[[Encyclopaedia Iranica]] |publisher=}}</ref>

==Legacy==
After his death from a kidney infection, Sevruguin's images resurfaced. He was survived by seven children from his marriage to Louise Gourgenian. 

In 1951–1952, an American historian of Iranian Islamic architecture, Myron Bement Smith, learned that 692 plates on glass by Sevrugian were up for sale at the [[American Presbyterian Mission]] in Tehran.<ref name=":0" /> Smith bought the images for USD 200, and when he died, his widow Katharine Smith donated the photo plates archive to the Smithsonian Institution.<ref name=":0" /> Only 696 of Sevruguin's negatives survive today.<ref name=":1" />

The small exhibit curated by [[Massumeh Farhad]], "Antoin Sevruguin and the Persian Image" (2001) was held at the [[Harvard Art Museums|Sackler Museum]] of Harvard University.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rexer |first=Lyle |date=2001-05-13 |title=Art/Architecture; A Persian Pioneer In a Western Art |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/05/13/arts/art-architecture-a-persian-pioneer-in-a-western-art.html |access-date=2022-10-17 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> The [[Runa Islam]] exhibition "Projects 95: Runa Islam" (2011) at the [[Museum of Modern Art]] (MoMA) featured the work "Emergence" (2011), that had been derived from one of Sevruguin's images.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rosenberg |first=Karen |date=2011-08-18 |title=The Magic of Movies, Born From a Single Snapshot |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/19/arts/design/projects-95-runa-islam-at-moma-review.html |access-date=2022-10-17 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

'''Mom Rajawongse Pridiyathorn Devakula''' ({{langx|th|หม่อมราชวงศ์ปรีดิยาธร เทวกุล}}; {{RTGS|Mom Ratchawong Pridiyathon Thewakun}}; {{IPA|th|prīːdìjāːtʰɔːn tʰē:wâkūn|}}; born 15 July 1947) is a Thai economist. He was the Governor of the [[Bank of Thailand]] from 2001 to 2006. Following the [[2006 Thai coup d'état]] he served as minister of finance and deputy prime minister in the [[Thailand 2006 interim civilian government|interim civilian government]] led by Prime Minister [[Surayud Chulanont]].<ref>''The Nation''. 9 October 2006. [https://web.archive.org/web/20061023071324/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/09/headlines/headlines_30015730.php Surayud Cabinet appointed by royal command].</ref> Following the [[2014 Thai coup d'état]] he was appointed a deputy prime minister in the first military appointed cabinet<ref>''Bangkok Post''. 31 August 2014  [http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/local/429745/prayuth-1-cabinet-endorsed Prayuth 1 cabinet endorsed]</ref> under General [[Prayut Chan-o-cha]]. Two days earlier he had resigned from his position as chairman of the board of Post Publishing PLC, the publisher of the ''[[Bangkok Post]]'', Thailand's leading English-language newspaper.<ref>''Bangkok Post''. 29 August 2014  [http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/politics/429272/pridiyathorn-quits-as-post-chairman Pridiyathorn quits as Post's chairman]</ref>

==Early life and education==
Pridiyathorn is a son of Prince [[Priditheppong Devakula]]. He is therefore a grandson of Prince [[Devawongse Varopakarn]], and a great-grandson of King [[Mongkut|Rama IV.]] (Mongkut). Reflecting his distant royal descent, Thai media refer to him as ''Mom Ui'' ({{langx|th|หม่อมอุ๋ย}}; "Lord Ui"), using his nickname, "Ui".<ref>{{cite web | script-title=th:"ดร.โกร่ง" พ้นเก้าอี้ ปธ.แบงก์ชาติ สะพัด "ทนง-หม่อมอุ๋ย" ตัวเต็งคนใหม่ | url = http://www.manager.co.th/iBizChannel/ViewNews.aspx?NewsID=9560000085950 | work = Manager | date = 2013-07-14 | accessdate = 2013-07-14| language = Thai }}</ref>

Pridiyathorn was educated at [[Saint Gabriel's College, Bangkok]] from year 1 to 12. During his childhood, Pridiyathorn rarely came second in school exams. He was nearly always first in his studies. {{Citation needed|date=May 2014}} He studied economics at [[Thammasat University]], graduating with a bachelor's degree, and at the [[Wharton School]] of the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he earned an [[MBA]] in 1970.<ref name="Wharton">{{Citation |url=http://www.wharton.upenn.edu/125anniversaryissue/devakula.html |title=A Trusted Leader for Turbulent Times, Pridiyathorn Devakula, WG'70 |work=125 Influential People and Ideas |publisher=The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140528161054/http://www.wharton.upenn.edu:80/125anniversaryissue/devakula.html |archivedate=2014-05-28 }}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1971 to 1990 he worked for the [[Thai Farmers Bank]], becoming senior executive vice president. In 1990 he became official spokesman for Prime Minister [[Chatichai Choonhavan]]. In the governments of [[Anand Panyarachun]] and [[Suchinda Kraprayoon]] (1991–92) he was deputy minister of commerce. He was appointed a member of the [[National Assembly of Thailand|Thai Senate]] from 1992 to 1993. In 1993 he became president of the [[Export-Import Bank of Thailand]]. Pridiyathorn served as the Chairman of the NIST International School Foundation, the governing body of [[NIST International School]], from 2009 to 2017.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nist.ac.th/about-nist-international-school-bangkok-thailand/governance/ |title = NIST International School - Our Governance}}</ref>

=== Bank of Thailand Governor ===
In May 2001 he was appointed Governor of the [[Bank of Thailand]], the nation's central bank. He is also a director of the Civil Service Commission and of the [[Thammasat University]] Council. Pridiyathorn repeatedly criticised Prime Minister [[Thaksin Shinawatra]] who took office in 2001. Pridiyathorn disagreed with Thaksin's spending policy, which he saw as a cause of inflation.<ref name="Wharton"/>

In 2004, the state-owned [[Krung Thai Bank]] (KTB) shocked Thailand's financial world by reclassifying approximately 40 billion baht as problem loans. Pridiyathorn threatened to fire KTB chief executive officer [[Viroj Nualkhair]] if he did not resign. Viroj was a former financial advisor to media proprietor [[Sondhi Limthongkul]], having helped him make the initial public offering of one of his first companies.<ref>[http://www.nationmultimedia.com/search/page.arcview.php?clid=6&id=58371 ''The Nation'', "New party, old friends aid Sondhi", 11 April 2002] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312004752/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/search/page.arcview.php?clid=6&id=58371 |date=12 March 2007 }}</ref>  As Krung Thai Bank head, Viroj had forgiven 1.6 billion baht of Sondhi's debts and arranged for further rounds of forgiveness. Using all his media outlets, Sondhi attacked Pridiyathorn and defended Viroj. Viroj was eventually forced to leave Krung Thai Bank. Sondhi's public criticism of Thaksin started to increase, eventually leading to the establishment of the [[People's Alliance for Democracy]].<ref>''The Nation'', [http://www.nationmultimedia.com/specials/sondhi/nov30.php The good old days] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081211192222/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/specials/sondhi/nov30.php |date=2008-12-11 }}, 30 November 2005</ref>

===Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance===
[[File:Pridiyathorn Fulbright talk.JPG|thumb|Mom Rajawongse Pridiyathorn at Fulbright Seminar II in 2009]]
Two days after the coup which deposed Prime Minister [[Thaksin Shinawatra]], the Bangkok newspaper ''[[The Nation (Thailand)|The Nation]]'' reported that business leaders had asked the junta ([[Council for Democratic Reform under Constitutional Monarchy]]) to appoint Pridiyathorn as an interim prime minister. He was notably endorsed by [[Chatri Sophonpanich]], chairman of [[Bangkok Bank]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/09/22/business/business_30014294.php |title=Business chiefs want Pridiyathorn as prime minister |access-date=2006-09-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605051954/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/09/22/business/business_30014294.php |archive-date=2011-06-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Eventually, the junta chose retired general [[Surayud Chulanont]] as interim prime minister, but he in turn named Pridiyathorn to his cabinet as minister of finance, a move that business leaders saw as positive.<ref>Business reporters. 10 October 2006. [https://web.archive.org/web/20061115150316/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/10/business/business_30015771.php Executives upbeat on new line-up], ''The Nation''.</ref> He was succeeded as governor of the Bank of Thailand by [[Tarisa Watanagase]], the first woman to head the BOT.<ref>Srisukkasem, Anoma. October 18, 2006. [https://web.archive.org/web/20061028031317/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/18/headlines/headlines_30016476.php Tarisa becomes BOT's first female chief], ''The Nation''.</ref>

Pridiyathorn's policies as minister of finance included:
* Fiscal deficits.  A [[budget deficit]] of 147 billion [[baht]] for fiscal year 2007. This was the first budget deficit since 2003.<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/11/15/headlines/headlines_30018962.php Massive loss from Thaksin projects] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061115022430/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/11/15/headlines/headlines_30018962.php |date=2006-11-15 }}, 16 November 2006</ref>  Fiscal deficits were also expected for 2008.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/k1e1p8p0m7vjh Deficit to continue into fiscal 2008], 17 February 2007</ref>
* Suvarnabhumi City.  Pridiyathorn opposed the establishment of a new province, dubbed [[Nakhon Suvarnabhumi Province|Suvarnabhumi City]], around the newly constructed [[Suvarnabhumi Airport]].  The plan to establish a new province had been proposed by the deposed government of [[Thaksin Shinawatra]].  "There are a lot of retention ponds in the area and water experts said they serve as waterways, allowing floods to flow to the sea.  If there are buildings, they will obstruct water from flowing out, and cause the inner city to flood.  If the Department of Town and Country Planning proposes to build a community in the area, I'll oppose it," said Pridiyathorn.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=113924 Pridiyathorn opposes 'Suvarnabhumi City'], 1 November 2006</ref>
* [[Capital control]]s. Pridiyathorn instituted capital controls to attempt to reverse a strengthening of the [[baht]], but reversed the measure after the Thai stock market crashed, destroying US$20 billion of market value in one day.  Pridiyathorn later noted that "This was not a mistake.  Measures always have side effects. Once we knew the side effects, we quickly fixed it.... Just one day of stocks falling is not considered much damage."<ref>''New York Times'', [https://www.nytimes.com/2006/12/20/business/20baht.html After Thai Stocks Plunge, a Policy Shift Is Revised], 20 December 2006</ref>  He came under harsh criticism.  Bratin Sanyal, head of Asian equity investments at [[ING Group|ING]] in Hong Kong noted, "The one thing worse than an incompetent central bank is an incompetent central bank that flip-flops."  Catherine Tan, head of Asia Emerging Markets at Forecast in Singapore, noted, "They are proving themselves to be very unprofessional. Their actions are very irresponsible. They have totally lost credibility... I don't see foreigners returning to Thailand any time in the near future. Markets now have no confidence in the government."<ref>''USA Today'', [https://www.usatoday.com/money/markets/world/2006-12-20-thai-rebound_x.htm Thailand's stock market bounces back, but financial analysts rip leaders], 20 December 2006</ref>  The [[Export-Import Bank of Thailand]] also criticized the capital controls.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/p1x4k5n1r5ire Exim Bank raps central bank policy], 28 March 2007</ref>
* Limiting foreign companies investing in List I and II businesses (including media, telecoms, and aviation) from holding more than 50 percent of shares.  List III businesses (including retailers and hotels) were exempted from the new restrictions.  Investors holding more than 50 percent would be forced to lower their stakes within a year.  Investors holding more than 50 percent of voting rights would be forced to lower their voting stakes within a year.  Finance Minister Pridiyathorn noted, "If they [foreign investors] had seen the details [of the foreign investment law], I am sure that they would be happy."<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/09/headlines/headlines_30023662.php Thailand to limit foreign stake in firms to 50 per cent] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070111063405/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/09/headlines/headlines_30023662.php |date=2007-01-11 }}, 9 January 2007</ref><ref>''Bloomberg'', [https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601087&sid=apnV.j9kiuXc&refer=home Thailand Tightens Overseas Investment Rules, Caps], 9 January 2007</ref>  He later backtracked, and said that the changes would largely be limited to the telecom industry.  The proposed changes in the investment rules—which were approved in principle by the cabinet and still needing approval by the National Legislative Assembly that was appointed after the coup—don't appear as sweeping as many investors had feared. Retailers, insurers, banks and brokers are specifically exempted from the proposed changes to the investment law. That effectively leaves hypermarket operators such as Tesco PLC of Britain and Carrefour SA of France, both of which have large chains in Thailand, off the hook.<ref>''The Wall Street Journal Asia'', [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB116832831193071216 Thailand Tightens Rules On Foreign Investment], 10 January 2007</ref>
*Corruption investigations into Thaksin Shinawatra.  Pridiyathorn sparked controversy in his dealings with [[Jaruvan Maintaka]] of the junta-appointed Assets Examination Committee.  Jaruvan accused Thaksin's wife of inappropriately buying a plot of land from the [[Financial Institutions Development Fund]] (FIDF) while Pridiyathorn was FIDF Chairman.  Pridiyathorn asserted that the purchase was legal and refused to file charges, claiming that the FIDF was not a damaged party.  Jaruvan then claimed that Pridiyathorn violated the law by sitting on the boards of more than three state enterprises.  Pridiyathorn countered by claiming that Jaruvan was trying to destroy his reputation.<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/politics/politics_30028159.php Departure not totally unexpected, given recent controversies] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930031021/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/politics/politics_30028159.php |date=2007-09-30 }}, 1 March 2007</ref>
*Monetary policy.  Pridiyathorn took the unusual step of urging the [[Bank of Thailand]] to cut interest rates by half a percentage point, rather than 25 [[basis point]]s as expected by most analysts.  Bank of Thailand is independent of the Ministry of Finance, and did not heed Pridiyathorn's call.  He resigned the next day.<ref>''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070302110301/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/02/28/business/business_30028061.php Ministry calls for big cut by BOT], 28 February 2007</ref><ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/d1q1n9r2p8wxi Central bank lowers key rate], 28 February 2007</ref>

Pridiyathorn resigned on 28 February 2007. As a reason for his resignation he cited Premier Surayud's decision to appoint Pridiyathorn's rival, former Thaksin-government Finance Minister [[Somkid Jatusripitak]], as a "[[self-sufficiency economy]]" special envoy. Somkid resigned from his position after less than a week. Another reason given was the Minister to the Office of the Prime Minister [[Thirapat Serirangsan]]'s alleged preference for certain private media interests.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/y1e1s8e9b3afb Pridiyathorn resigns as deputy prime minister and finance minister], 28 February 2007</ref> Several analysts speculated that he was referring to the preferential treatment the junta gave to leading anti-Thaksin critic [[Sondhi Limthongkul]], who was also a long-time critic of Pridiyathorn.<ref>''IHT'', [http://pages.citebite.com/p1m1l9u8i3tph Thai minister resigns amid cabinet disarray], 28 February 2007</ref><ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/topstories/topstories.php?id=117117 Pridiyathorn resigns as deputy PM, finance minister], 28 February 2007</ref>

His resignation shocked the political world as well as the business community. "The reasons he gave were quite strange," noted Pornsilp Patcharinpanakul, deputy secretary-general of Board of Trade.<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/business/business_30028169.php Concern over stability of govt] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070303001103/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/business/business_30028169.php |date=2007-03-03 }}, 1 March 2007</ref> Pridiyathorn was replaced by [[Chalongphob Sussangkarn]]. [[CDRM|Junta]] leader General [[Saprang Kalayanamitr]] was also implicated in Pridiyathorn's resignation.  The ''Bangkok Post'' reported that Pridiyathorn resigned in protest after a CNS member lobbied him to sell shares of IRPC (formerly known as Thai Petrochemical Industry or TPI) back to a former shareholder. Saprang's brother, Chienchuan, was a key financial advisor to [[Prachai Liaophairat]], the estranged founder of TPI.<ref name="Chienchuang">''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070929135359/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/03/23/business/business_20003369.php Ethanol rises to Bt23 per litre], 23 March 2006</ref><ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/i1h2c7l2m8onq Goings on at Channel 9], 8 March 2007</ref>

===Economic advisor to the 2014 junta===
Pridiyathorn was an outspoken critic of [[Yingluck Shinawatra]]'s government, especially its scheme assuring a  [[price floor|fixed minimum]] rice price to farmers.<ref>{{Cite news |author=Surasak Tumcharoen |title=News Analysis: Post-election crisis could prolong political uncertainty in Thailand |agency=Xinhua |date=14 February 2014 |url=http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/world/2014-02/14/c_133116457.htm |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141119164508/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/world/2014-02/14/c_133116457.htm |archivedate=19 November 2014 }}</ref> In November 2013 he estimated the costs of the programme at 425 billion baht.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Supunnabul Suwannakij |author2=Suttinee Yuvejattana |title=Thailand Spurns IMF's Call to Rethink Rice-Purchase Program |publisher=Bloomberg |date=13 November 2013 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-11-13/thailand-spurns-imf-call-to-rethink-state-rice-buying-program.html}}</ref> In February 2014 he called Yingluck's economic policies a failure and asked her to step down.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Pridiyathorn calls Yingluck a failed government |publisher=Thai PBS |date=6 February 2014 |url=http://englishnews.thaipbs.or.th/pridiyathorn-calls-yingluck-failed-government/ |access-date=27 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113000831/http://englishnews.thaipbs.or.th/pridiyathorn-calls-yingluck-failed-government/ |archive-date=13 November 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Instead, he called for the appointment of a "neutral", unelected government.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.bangkokpost.com/learning/learning-from-news/393739/pm-should-quit-says-pridiyathorn |title=Pridiyathorn calls on PM to quit |newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=7 February 2014}}</ref>

After the [[2014 Thai coup d'état|22 May 2014 coup d'état]], the junta—which calls itself [[National Council for Peace and Order]]—appointed Somkid a member of its "advisory board" in charge of economic issues.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Prawit, Somkid, Pridiyathorn named advisers |newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=27 May 2014 |url=http://bangkokpost.com/news/local/412074/prawit-somkid-pridiyathorn-named-advisers |archive-url=https://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20140804175415/http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/local/412074/prawit%2Dsomkid%2Dpridiyathorn%2Dnamed%2Dadvisers |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 4, 2014 }}</ref>

On 31 August Pridiyathorn was appointed a deputy prime minister in the first military-appointed cabinet under General [[Prayut Chan-o-cha]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/local/429745/prayuth-1-cabinet-endorsed |title=Prayuth 1 cabinet endorsed |newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=31 August 2014}}</ref>

==Wealth==
Disclosures to the National Counter Corruption Commission revealed that 30 days after leaving his cabinet position in March 2007, Pridiyathorn had 730 million baht in assets, a slight drop from 754 million baht when he took office in October 2006. His wife, Praphaphan, had a net worth of 283 million baht, while his daughter Pudjeep had seven million baht.<ref>''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070503130321/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/29/index.php Pridiyathorn tops latest NCCC], 29 April 2007</ref>

In October 2014 the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) published the declared wealth of all ministers in the cabinet.  Pridiyathorn was the wealthiest with assets of 1.38 billion baht.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/politics/440647/nacc-releases-list-of-cabinet-ministers-declared-assets-and-liabilities Pridiyathorn is richest cabinet minister], 31 October 2014</ref>
