'''Mom Rajawongse Pridiyathorn Devakula''' ({{langx|th|หม่อมราชวงศ์ปรีดิยาธร เทวกุล}}; {{RTGS|Mom Ratchawong Pridiyathon Thewakun}}; {{IPA|th|prīːdìjāːtʰɔːn tʰē:wâkūn|}}; born 15 July 1947) is a Thai economist. He was the Governor of the [[Bank of Thailand]] from 2001 to 2006. Following the [[2006 Thai coup d'état]] he served as minister of finance and deputy prime minister in the [[Thailand 2006 interim civilian government|interim civilian government]] led by Prime Minister [[Surayud Chulanont]].<ref>''The Nation''. 9 October 2006. [https://web.archive.org/web/20061023071324/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/09/headlines/headlines_30015730.php Surayud Cabinet appointed by royal command].</ref> Following the [[2014 Thai coup d'état]] he was appointed a deputy prime minister in the first military appointed cabinet<ref>''Bangkok Post''. 31 August 2014  [http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/local/429745/prayuth-1-cabinet-endorsed Prayuth 1 cabinet endorsed]</ref> under General [[Prayut Chan-o-cha]]. Two days earlier he had resigned from his position as chairman of the board of Post Publishing PLC, the publisher of the ''[[Bangkok Post]]'', Thailand's leading English-language newspaper.<ref>''Bangkok Post''. 29 August 2014  [http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/politics/429272/pridiyathorn-quits-as-post-chairman Pridiyathorn quits as Post's chairman]</ref>

==Early life and education==
Pridiyathorn is a son of Prince [[Priditheppong Devakula]]. He is therefore a grandson of Prince [[Devawongse Varopakarn]], and a great-grandson of King [[Mongkut|Rama IV.]] (Mongkut). Reflecting his distant royal descent, Thai media refer to him as ''Mom Ui'' ({{langx|th|หม่อมอุ๋ย}}; "Lord Ui"), using his nickname, "Ui".<ref>{{cite web | script-title=th:"ดร.โกร่ง" พ้นเก้าอี้ ปธ.แบงก์ชาติ สะพัด "ทนง-หม่อมอุ๋ย" ตัวเต็งคนใหม่ | url = http://www.manager.co.th/iBizChannel/ViewNews.aspx?NewsID=9560000085950 | work = Manager | date = 2013-07-14 | accessdate = 2013-07-14| language = Thai }}</ref>

Pridiyathorn was educated at [[Saint Gabriel's College (Thailand)|Saint Gabriel's College]] from year 1 to 12. During his childhood, Pridiyathorn rarely came second in school exams. He was nearly always first in his studies. {{Citation needed|date=May 2014}} He studied economics at [[Thammasat University]], graduating with a bachelor's degree, and at the [[Wharton School]] of the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he earned an [[MBA]] in 1970.<ref name="Wharton">{{Citation |url=http://www.wharton.upenn.edu/125anniversaryissue/devakula.html |title=A Trusted Leader for Turbulent Times, Pridiyathorn Devakula, WG'70 |work=125 Influential People and Ideas |publisher=The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140528161054/http://www.wharton.upenn.edu:80/125anniversaryissue/devakula.html |archivedate=2014-05-28 }}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1971 to 1990 he worked for the [[Thai Farmers Bank]], becoming senior executive vice president. In 1990 he became official spokesman for Prime Minister [[Chatichai Choonhavan]]. In the governments of [[Anand Panyarachun]] and [[Suchinda Kraprayoon]] (1991–92) he was deputy minister of commerce. He was appointed a member of the [[National Assembly of Thailand|Thai Senate]] from 1992 to 1993. In 1993 he became president of the [[Export-Import Bank of Thailand]]. Pridiyathorn served as the Chairman of the NIST International School Foundation, the governing body of [[NIST International School]], from 2009 to 2017.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nist.ac.th/about-nist-international-school-bangkok-thailand/governance/ |title = NIST International School - Our Governance}}</ref>

=== Bank of Thailand Governor ===
In May 2001 he was appointed Governor of the [[Bank of Thailand]], the nation's central bank. He is also a director of the Civil Service Commission and of the [[Thammasat University]] Council. Pridiyathorn repeatedly criticised Prime Minister [[Thaksin Shinawatra]] who took office in 2001. Pridiyathorn disagreed with Thaksin's spending policy, which he saw as a cause of inflation.<ref name="Wharton"/>

In 2004, the state-owned [[Krung Thai Bank]] (KTB) shocked Thailand's financial world by reclassifying approximately 40 billion baht as problem loans. Pridiyathorn threatened to fire KTB chief executive officer [[Viroj Nualkhair]] if he did not resign. Viroj was a former financial advisor to media proprietor [[Sondhi Limthongkul]], having helped him make the initial public offering of one of his first companies.<ref>[http://www.nationmultimedia.com/search/page.arcview.php?clid=6&id=58371 ''The Nation'', "New party, old friends aid Sondhi", 11 April 2002] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312004752/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/search/page.arcview.php?clid=6&id=58371 |date=12 March 2007 }}</ref>  As Krung Thai Bank head, Viroj had forgiven 1.6 billion baht of Sondhi's debts and arranged for further rounds of forgiveness. Using all his media outlets, Sondhi attacked Pridiyathorn and defended Viroj. Viroj was eventually forced to leave Krung Thai Bank. Sondhi's public criticism of Thaksin started to increase, eventually leading to the establishment of the [[People's Alliance for Democracy]].<ref>''The Nation'', [http://www.nationmultimedia.com/specials/sondhi/nov30.php The good old days] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081211192222/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/specials/sondhi/nov30.php |date=2008-12-11 }}, 30 November 2005</ref>

===Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance===
[[File:Pridiyathorn Fulbright talk.JPG|thumb|Mom Rajawongse Pridiyathorn at Fulbright Seminar II in 2009]]
Two days after the coup which deposed Prime Minister [[Thaksin Shinawatra]], the Bangkok newspaper ''[[The Nation (Thailand)|The Nation]]'' reported that business leaders had asked the junta ([[Council for Democratic Reform under Constitutional Monarchy]]) to appoint Pridiyathorn as an interim prime minister. He was notably endorsed by [[Chatri Sophonpanich]], chairman of [[Bangkok Bank]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/09/22/business/business_30014294.php |title=Business chiefs want Pridiyathorn as prime minister |access-date=2006-09-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605051954/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/09/22/business/business_30014294.php |archive-date=2011-06-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Eventually, the junta chose retired general [[Surayud Chulanont]] as interim prime minister, but he in turn named Pridiyathorn to his cabinet as minister of finance, a move that business leaders saw as positive.<ref>Business reporters. 10 October 2006. [https://web.archive.org/web/20061115150316/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/10/business/business_30015771.php Executives upbeat on new line-up], ''The Nation''.</ref> He was succeeded as governor of the Bank of Thailand by [[Tarisa Watanagase]], the first woman to head the BOT.<ref>Srisukkasem, Anoma. October 18, 2006. [https://web.archive.org/web/20061028031317/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/18/headlines/headlines_30016476.php Tarisa becomes BOT's first female chief], ''The Nation''.</ref>

Pridiyathorn's policies as minister of finance included:
* Fiscal deficits.  A [[budget deficit]] of 147 billion [[baht]] for fiscal year 2007. This was the first budget deficit since 2003.<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/11/15/headlines/headlines_30018962.php Massive loss from Thaksin projects] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061115022430/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/11/15/headlines/headlines_30018962.php |date=2006-11-15 }}, 16 November 2006</ref>  Fiscal deficits were also expected for 2008.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/k1e1p8p0m7vjh Deficit to continue into fiscal 2008], 17 February 2007</ref>
* Suvarnabhumi City.  Pridiyathorn opposed the establishment of a new province, dubbed [[Nakhon Suvarnabhumi Province|Suvarnabhumi City]], around the newly constructed [[Suvarnabhumi Airport]].  The plan to establish a new province had been proposed by the deposed government of [[Thaksin Shinawatra]].  "There are a lot of retention ponds in the area and water experts said they serve as waterways, allowing floods to flow to the sea.  If there are buildings, they will obstruct water from flowing out, and cause the inner city to flood.  If the Department of Town and Country Planning proposes to build a community in the area, I'll oppose it," said Pridiyathorn.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=113924 Pridiyathorn opposes 'Suvarnabhumi City'], 1 November 2006</ref>
* [[Capital control]]s. Pridiyathorn instituted capital controls to attempt to reverse a strengthening of the [[baht]], but reversed the measure after the Thai stock market crashed, destroying US$20 billion of market value in one day.  Pridiyathorn later noted that "This was not a mistake.  Measures always have side effects. Once we knew the side effects, we quickly fixed it.... Just one day of stocks falling is not considered much damage."<ref>''New York Times'', [https://www.nytimes.com/2006/12/20/business/20baht.html After Thai Stocks Plunge, a Policy Shift Is Revised], 20 December 2006</ref>  He came under harsh criticism.  Bratin Sanyal, head of Asian equity investments at [[ING Group|ING]] in Hong Kong noted, "The one thing worse than an incompetent central bank is an incompetent central bank that flip-flops."  Catherine Tan, head of Asia Emerging Markets at Forecast in Singapore, noted, "They are proving themselves to be very unprofessional. Their actions are very irresponsible. They have totally lost credibility... I don't see foreigners returning to Thailand any time in the near future. Markets now have no confidence in the government."<ref>''USA Today'', [https://www.usatoday.com/money/markets/world/2006-12-20-thai-rebound_x.htm Thailand's stock market bounces back, but financial analysts rip leaders], 20 December 2006</ref>  The [[Export-Import Bank of Thailand]] also criticized the capital controls.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/p1x4k5n1r5ire Exim Bank raps central bank policy], 28 March 2007</ref>
* Limiting foreign companies investing in List I and II businesses (including media, telecoms, and aviation) from holding more than 50 percent of shares.  List III businesses (including retailers and hotels) were exempted from the new restrictions.  Investors holding more than 50 percent would be forced to lower their stakes within a year.  Investors holding more than 50 percent of voting rights would be forced to lower their voting stakes within a year.  Finance Minister Pridiyathorn noted, "If they [foreign investors] had seen the details [of the foreign investment law], I am sure that they would be happy."<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/09/headlines/headlines_30023662.php Thailand to limit foreign stake in firms to 50 per cent] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070111063405/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/09/headlines/headlines_30023662.php |date=2007-01-11 }}, 9 January 2007</ref><ref>''Bloomberg'', [https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601087&sid=apnV.j9kiuXc&refer=home Thailand Tightens Overseas Investment Rules, Caps], 9 January 2007</ref>  He later backtracked, and said that the changes would largely be limited to the telecom industry.  The proposed changes in the investment rules—which were approved in principle by the cabinet and still needing approval by the National Legislative Assembly that was appointed after the coup—don't appear as sweeping as many investors had feared. Retailers, insurers, banks and brokers are specifically exempted from the proposed changes to the investment law. That effectively leaves hypermarket operators such as Tesco PLC of Britain and Carrefour SA of France, both of which have large chains in Thailand, off the hook.<ref>''The Wall Street Journal Asia'', [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB116832831193071216 Thailand Tightens Rules On Foreign Investment], 10 January 2007</ref>
*Corruption investigations into Thaksin Shinawatra.  Pridiyathorn sparked controversy in his dealings with [[Jaruvan Maintaka]] of the junta-appointed Assets Examination Committee.  Jaruvan accused Thaksin's wife of inappropriately buying a plot of land from the [[Financial Institutions Development Fund]] (FIDF) while Pridiyathorn was FIDF Chairman.  Pridiyathorn asserted that the purchase was legal and refused to file charges, claiming that the FIDF was not a damaged party.  Jaruvan then claimed that Pridiyathorn violated the law by sitting on the boards of more than three state enterprises.  Pridiyathorn countered by claiming that Jaruvan was trying to destroy his reputation.<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/politics/politics_30028159.php Departure not totally unexpected, given recent controversies] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930031021/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/politics/politics_30028159.php |date=2007-09-30 }}, 1 March 2007</ref>
*Monetary policy.  Pridiyathorn took the unusual step of urging the [[Bank of Thailand]] to cut interest rates by half a percentage point, rather than 25 [[basis point]]s as expected by most analysts.  Bank of Thailand is independent of the Ministry of Finance, and did not heed Pridiyathorn's call.  He resigned the next day.<ref>''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070302110301/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/02/28/business/business_30028061.php Ministry calls for big cut by BOT], 28 February 2007</ref><ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/d1q1n9r2p8wxi Central bank lowers key rate], 28 February 2007</ref>

Pridiyathorn resigned on 28 February 2007. As a reason for his resignation he cited Premier Surayud's decision to appoint Pridiyathorn's rival, former Thaksin-government Finance Minister [[Somkid Jatusripitak]], as a "[[self-sufficiency economy]]" special envoy. Somkid resigned from his position after less than a week. Another reason given was the Minister to the Office of the Prime Minister [[Thirapat Serirangsan]]'s alleged preference for certain private media interests.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/y1e1s8e9b3afb Pridiyathorn resigns as deputy prime minister and finance minister], 28 February 2007</ref> Several analysts speculated that he was referring to the preferential treatment the junta gave to leading anti-Thaksin critic [[Sondhi Limthongkul]], who was also a long-time critic of Pridiyathorn.<ref>''IHT'', [http://pages.citebite.com/p1m1l9u8i3tph Thai minister resigns amid cabinet disarray], 28 February 2007</ref><ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/topstories/topstories.php?id=117117 Pridiyathorn resigns as deputy PM, finance minister], 28 February 2007</ref>

His resignation shocked the political world as well as the business community. "The reasons he gave were quite strange," noted Pornsilp Patcharinpanakul, deputy secretary-general of Board of Trade.<ref>''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/business/business_30028169.php Concern over stability of govt] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070303001103/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/business/business_30028169.php |date=2007-03-03 }}, 1 March 2007</ref> Pridiyathorn was replaced by [[Chalongphob Sussangkarn]]. [[CDRM|Junta]] leader General [[Saprang Kalayanamitr]] was also implicated in Pridiyathorn's resignation.  The ''Bangkok Post'' reported that Pridiyathorn resigned in protest after a CNS member lobbied him to sell shares of IRPC (formerly known as Thai Petrochemical Industry or TPI) back to a former shareholder. Saprang's brother, Chienchuan, was a key financial advisor to [[Prachai Liaophairat]], the estranged founder of TPI.<ref name="Chienchuang">''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070929135359/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/03/23/business/business_20003369.php Ethanol rises to Bt23 per litre], 23 March 2006</ref><ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/i1h2c7l2m8onq Goings on at Channel 9], 8 March 2007</ref>

===Economic advisor to the 2014 junta===
Pridiyathorn was an outspoken critic of [[Yingluck Shinawatra]]'s government, especially its scheme assuring a  [[price floor|fixed minimum]] rice price to farmers.<ref>{{Cite news |author=Surasak Tumcharoen |title=News Analysis: Post-election crisis could prolong political uncertainty in Thailand |agency=Xinhua |date=14 February 2014 |url=http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/world/2014-02/14/c_133116457.htm |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141119164508/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/world/2014-02/14/c_133116457.htm |archivedate=19 November 2014 }}</ref> In November 2013 he estimated the costs of the programme at 425 billion baht.<ref>{{Cite news |author1=Supunnabul Suwannakij |author2=Suttinee Yuvejattana |title=Thailand Spurns IMF's Call to Rethink Rice-Purchase Program |publisher=Bloomberg |date=13 November 2013 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-11-13/thailand-spurns-imf-call-to-rethink-state-rice-buying-program.html}}</ref> In February 2014 he called Yingluck's economic policies a failure and asked her to step down.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Pridiyathorn calls Yingluck a failed government |publisher=Thai PBS |date=6 February 2014 |url=http://englishnews.thaipbs.or.th/pridiyathorn-calls-yingluck-failed-government/ |access-date=27 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113000831/http://englishnews.thaipbs.or.th/pridiyathorn-calls-yingluck-failed-government/ |archive-date=13 November 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Instead, he called for the appointment of a "neutral", unelected government.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.bangkokpost.com/learning/learning-from-news/393739/pm-should-quit-says-pridiyathorn |title=Pridiyathorn calls on PM to quit |newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=7 February 2014}}</ref>

After the [[2014 Thai coup d'état|22 May 2014 coup d'état]], the junta—which calls itself [[National Council for Peace and Order]]—appointed Somkid a member of its "advisory board" in charge of economic issues.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Prawit, Somkid, Pridiyathorn named advisers |newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=27 May 2014 |url=http://bangkokpost.com/news/local/412074/prawit-somkid-pridiyathorn-named-advisers |archive-url=https://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20140804175415/http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/local/412074/prawit%2Dsomkid%2Dpridiyathorn%2Dnamed%2Dadvisers |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 4, 2014 }}</ref>

On 31 August Pridiyathorn was appointed a deputy prime minister in the first military-appointed cabinet under General [[Prayut Chan-o-cha]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/local/429745/prayuth-1-cabinet-endorsed |title=Prayuth 1 cabinet endorsed |newspaper=Bangkok Post |date=31 August 2014}}</ref>

==Wealth==
Disclosures to the National Counter Corruption Commission revealed that 30 days after leaving his cabinet position in March 2007, Pridiyathorn had 730 million baht in assets, a slight drop from 754 million baht when he took office in October 2006. His wife, Praphaphan, had a net worth of 283 million baht, while his daughter Pudjeep had seven million baht.<ref>''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070503130321/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/29/index.php Pridiyathorn tops latest NCCC], 29 April 2007</ref>

In October 2014 the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) published the declared wealth of all ministers in the cabinet.  Pridiyathorn was the wealthiest with assets of 1.38 billion baht.<ref>''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/news/politics/440647/nacc-releases-list-of-cabinet-ministers-declared-assets-and-liabilities Pridiyathorn is richest cabinet minister], 31 October 2014</ref>

Chitravadee Chulanont | children = 3 | father = [[Phayom Chulanont]] | education = [[Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy]]
[[National Defence College of Thailand]] | profession = [[Soldier]] | rank = {{ubl|[[General]]|[[Admiral]]|[[Air Chief Marshal]]}} | allegiance = Thailand | branch = [[Royal Thai Army]] | commands = {{ubil|[[List of Commanders of the Royal Thai Armed Forces Headquarters|Supreme Commander]]|[[List of Commanders of the Royal Thai Army|Commander-in-Chief: Army]]|Commanding General of the [[Royal Thai Army Special Warfare Command|Army Special Warfare]]}} | service_years = 1965–2003 | battles = * '''[[Cold War]]''' * [[Communist insurgency in Thailand]] * [[Black May (1992)|Black May]] * '''[[1999 East Timorese crisis]]''' ** [[International Force East Timor]] * '''[[2003 Phnom Penh riots|Operation Pochentong 1]]''' * '''[[Thaksin Shinawatra#The War on Drugs|War on Drugs]]''' | mawards = * [[Order of Rama|Rama Medal]] * Freemen Safeguarding Medal (First Class) * Border Service Medal * Chakra Mala Medal * Darjah Kepahlawanan Angkatan Tentera * [[Darjah Utama Bakti Cemerlang (Tentera)]] * [[Pingat Jasa Gemilang (Tentera)]] * [[Legion of Merit|Legion of Merit Commander]] * Bintang Kartika Eka Paksi Utama * [[Order of National Security Merit|Tongil Medal]] | signature = ลายเซ็นสุรยุทธ์ จุลานนท์ ภาษาอังกฤษ.png | height = {{height|m=1.65|precision=0}} | caption = Surayud in 2007 | honorific_suffix = [[Order of Chula Chom Klao|PCh]] [[Order of the White Elephant|MPCh]] [[Order of the Crown of Thailand|MVM]] [[Order of Rama|RM]] }} '''Surayud Chulanont''' ({{langx|th|สุรยุทธ์ จุลานนท์}}, {{RTGS|Surayut Chulanon}}, {{IPA|th|sù.rá.jút t͡ɕù.laː.non|IPA}}; born 28 August 1943) is a Thai former politician and military officer who was the 24th [[prime minister of Thailand]] and head of Thailand's [[Thailand 2006 interim civilian government|interim government]] between 2006 and 2008. He is a former supreme commander of the [[Royal Thai Army]] and is currently [[Privy Council (Thailand)|Privy Councilor]] to [[King Vajiralongkorn]]. Surayud came from a military family, but his father defected from the Royal Thai Army to the [[Communist Party of Thailand]] when Surayud was a boy. Surayud joined the Thai Army and rose to power as an aide to General [[Prem Tinsulanonda]]. He commanded troops during [[Black May (1992)|Bloody May]], the violent 1992 crackdown on anti-government protesters, but he denied giving his men the order to shoot protesters. He was promoted to army commander during the government of [[Chuan Leekpai]] and was promoted to supreme commander in 2003, under the government of [[Thaksin Shinawatra]]. Upon his retirement from the army, he was appointed by King [[Bhumibol Adulyadej]] to the [[Privy Council of Thailand]]. Surayud and Privy Council President Prem Tinsulanonda played a key role in the promotion of General [[Sonthi Boonratklin]] to the position of army commander. Sonthi overthrew the government of Thaksin in a [[2006 Thailand coup|coup on 19 September 2006]] and implored Surayud to be the head of interim government. Surayud's government was controversial. There was a significant worsening in perceived levels of corruption during his government.Transparency International, [http://www.transparency.org/news_room/latest_news/press_releases/2007/2007_09_26_cpi_2007_en 2007 Corruption Perceptions Index] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011001633/http://www.transparency.org/news_room/latest_news/press_releases/2007/2007_09_26_cpi_2007_en |date=11 October 2007 }} Surayud's Deputy Finance Minister, Sommai Pasee, was sentenced to jail for abuse of power.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/12/13/headlines/headlines_30058996.php Convicted deputy finance minister resigns] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215182513/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/12/13/headlines/headlines_30058996.php |date=15 December 2007 }}, 13 December 2007 Surayud raised the military budget by 35% and was accused of economic mismanagement, rampant human rights abuses, and [[Flip-flop (politics)|flip-flopping]] on numerous policies. [[Article 19]] ranked Thailand as falling behind [[Cambodia]] and [[Indonesia]] in terms of [[freedom of expression]].''The Nation'', [http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/10/16/national/national_30052593.php Defamation law decried] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071018130354/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/10/16/national/national_30052593.php |date=18 October 2007 }}, 16 October 2007 Thailand's economic growth rate slowed to the lowest level in five years and was ranked the lowest in the region.''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/topstories/topstories.php?id=123625 Thailand's economic growth lowest in region, World Bank says]''Xinhua'', [http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/2007-11/15/content_7081430.htm World Bank urges Thailand to enhance economy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081211012732/http://news.xinhuanet.com/english/2007-11/15/content_7081430.htm |date=11 December 2008 }}, 15 November 2007 However, Surayud was praised for apologising for atrocities committed by the Thai military fighting the [[South Thailand insurgency]], although the apology was accompanied by a sharp escalation in violence. He has been accused of [[forest reserve]] encroachment (a charge that was not investigated since the [[statute of limitations]] had run out by two years) and of illegally acquiring [[train carriage]]s for display in his forest home. == Family and education == Surayud came from a long line of military leaders. His maternal grandfather was Phraya [[Sri Sitthi Songkhram]] (Din Tharab), a royalist leader during the failed [[Boworadej]] Rebellion. Surayud's father was Lt. Colonel [[Phayom Chulanont]], a Royal Thai Army military officer who, as "Comrade Too Khamtan" ({{langx|th|สหายตู้คำตัน, [[Royal Thai General System of Transcription|RTGS]]: sahai tu khamtan}}), became a member of the Central Committee [[Communist Party of Thailand]] and Chief of Staff of the People's Liberation Army of Thailand.''The Nation'', [http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/01/12/Special_Report/data/Special_Report_19636134.html Comrades-In-Arms: Their war gone by] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312141000/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/01/12/Special_Report/data/Special_Report_19636134.html |date=12 March 2007 }}, 12 January 2006 Surayud completed his early education at [[Saint Gabriel's College, Bangkok]] and [[Suankularb Wittayalai School]] in Bangkok. He graduated from the inaugural class of [[Armed Forces Preparatory Academy (Thailand)|Armed Forces Preparatory Academy]]. As a boy, Surayud's [[Phayom Chulanont|father]] left his family to go underground to join the [[Communist Party of Thailand|Communists]]. Phayom explained his defection by citing corruption in the army and its inability to defend the powerless.''Time'' Magazine, [https://web.archive.org/web/20030422123830/http://www.time.com/time/asia/2003/heroes/surayud_chulanont.html Surayud Chulanont: A soldier who answered to the people], 28 April 2003 His father's defection to the Communists had a large impact on Surayud. Surayud's son, Non, noted that, "My father always told me that we must help each other redeem the tarnished family name of Chulanont so that Thais can look up to it."{{in lang|th}} ''Matichon Weekly'', "จาก 'ปู่พโยม' ถึง 'พ่ิอสุรยุทธ์' 'จุลานนท์' ในสายตา 'ร.อ.นนท์' 'นายกฯสุรยุทธ์' และการปฏิวัติ ในสายตาลูกทหาร" ("From 'Grandfather Phayom' to 'Father Surayud', 'Chulanont' in the Eyes of 'Captain Non', 'Premier Surayud' and Rebellion in the Eyes of the Son of a Soldier"), 15–21 December 2006 Surayud entered [[Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy]] (CRMA) and graduated from Class 12. Surayud was conferred honorary doctor of philosophy degrees in: 1. Communication Arts in 1995 by Wongchavalidkul University, Thailand. 2. Liberal Arts (Rural Planning and Development) in 2000 by Maejo University, Thailand. 3. Liberal Arts (Political Science) in 2004 by Prince of Songkla University, Thailand. 4. Engineering in April 2007 by [[Tokai University]], Japan. 5. Social Development in December 2008 by Huachiew University, Thailand.{{Citation needed|date=August 2020}} Surayud currently serves as a chancellor of the council of [[King Mongkut's Institute of Technology Ladkrabang]] (KMITL) and Phetchaburi Rajabhat University. == Military career == Early in his army career, Surayud served in several army divisions including a light artillery unit and a paratrooper unit. He conducted operations against the [[Communist Party of Thailand]] (CPT) while his father was a leader of the CPT. From 1972 to 1978, he was an instructor at the Special Warfare School. He was an aide to General [[Prem Tinsulanonda]] when Prem was appointed army commander and later [[Prime Minister of Thailand]]. Surayud was appointed Commander of the Special Warfare Command in 1992, where he was the commanding officer of [[Sonthi Boonratklin]].[http://www.rta.mi.th/command/command31.htm {{in lang|th}} Surayud Chulanont's official resume from the Royal Thai Army website] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011221204003/http://www.rta.mi.th/command/command31.htm |date=21 December 2001 }} During [[Black May (1992)|Bloody May]], the violent crackdown 1992 on anti-government protesters, Surayud's men were seen at areas near the Royal Hotel, where protesters were seen being searched for weapons and later dragged into the hotel. He later claimed that he never gave orders for his soldiers to shoot.IHT, [http://www.iht.com/articles/2006/10/01/news/thai.php Thai junta shores up role in politics], 1 October 2006 According to a later interview, "It convinced me that the army should never be involved in politics." Days later he told a national television audience that he deplored the loss of life and that he had not given any orders to shoot. In 1994, he was appointed commander of the 2nd Army Region. Surayud was promoted to army commander in late-1998. At the time, his promotion was controversial, as Surayud had been politically "shelved" at a staff position. To secure his vision of a politics-free army, Surayud appointed several of his classmates from Class 12 of the [[Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy|CRMA]] to key positions. Among these were Lt Gen [[Sompong Maivichit]], who he made head of army-controlled Channel 5 television station, replacing Gen [[Pang Malakul na Ayudhya]], and Lt Gen [[Boonrod Somtap]], who he promoted to a key subordinate position to replace Gen [[Charn Boonprasert]].''The Nation'', [http://www.burmalibrary.org/reg.burma/archives/199902/msg00391.html Editorial & Opinion: Surayuth guns for reforms], 18 February 1999 He also ended a policy of deporting Burmese refugees, especially ethnic [[Karen people|Karens]], back to Burma. "He's been a friend to us," said Pastor Robert Htway of the Karen Refugee Committee. During his term, Thai soldiers took part in the [[United Nations Peace Keeping Force]], assisting UN-PKF efforts in [[East Timor]]. To stop drug and drug cartels into Thailand, Surayud, in March 2002, ordered one of Thailand's largest military operations in recent times, when Thai troops moved deep into [[Myanmar]] territory to destroy drug labs and military bases controlled by the United [[Wa State]] Army.Asia Times, [https://web.archive.org/web/20061130030805/http://www.atimes.com/atimes/Southeast_Asia/HK14Ae02.html Unplugging Thailand, Myanmar energy deals], 14 November 2006 In 2003, after over four years as Army Commander, Surayud was promoted to the position of supreme commander, a loftier, but less influential, post, during the government of [[Thaksin Shinawatra]]. He was replaced as army commander by [[Somthad Attanan]]. His promotion was rumoured to be the result of a conflict with the prime minister, possibly over foreign policy towards Myanmar and the crackdown on drugs. == Privy councilor == On 14 November 2003, King [[Bhumibol Adulyadej]] appointed Surayud to his [[Privy Council (Thailand)|Privy Council]] of personal advisors. Several months later he asked the king for permission to ordain as a monk for a brief period at a forest temple in northeastern Thailand. Surayud and Privy Council President [[Prem Tinsulanonda]] had been perceived to have a key role in the promotion of General [[Sonthi Boonratklin]] to the position of army commander.''The Statesman'', [https://www.thestatesman.net/page.news.php?clid=8&theme=&usrsess=1&id=130648 Sonthi: The man who made it happen] {{dead link|date=January 2017|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}, 20 September 2006''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/09/28/headlines/headlines_30014841.php Warning from Surayud: Thaksin's return 'a threat'] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061012234806/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/09/28/headlines/headlines_30014841.php |date=12 October 2006 }}, 28 September 2006 Facing an escalating [[South Thailand insurgency|insurgency in the south of Thailand]], Surayud urged the media to paint a more positive picture of the violence. "Truthful words that may not be beneficial nor do any good to the public should be avoided", noted Surayud to the Press Council of Thailand. He was contradicted by Deputy Prime Minister Chaturon Chaisang, who noted that he couldn't think of any news about the conflict in the South that could or should not be reported by the media.''The Nation'', [http://www.komchadluek.net/breaking/read.php?lang=en&newsid=68470 Media criticised over 'unhelpful news'] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312214316/http://www.komchadluek.net/breaking/read.php?lang=en&newsid=68470 |date=12 March 2007 }}, 4 July 2005 In response to numerous claims made by anti-Thaksin activist [[Sondhi Limthongkul]] that his [[People's Alliance for Democracy]] was "fighting for the King", Surayud responded by saying that, "Recent references to the monarchy were inappropriate. The institution should not be involved in politics. Political disputes should be solved in a political way."DPA, [http://news.monstersandcritics.com/asiapacific/article_1207115.php/New_Prime_Minister_a_respected_former_army_commander New Prime Minister a respected former army commander] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070323205251/http://news.monstersandcritics.com/asiapacific/article_1207115.php/New_Prime_Minister_a_respected_former_army_commander |date=23 March 2007 }}, 1 October 2006 In January 2008, not long after Surayud ended his term as prime minister, he was again reappointed to King Bhumibol Adulyadej's Privy Council. In 2020 Surayud stood in for Vajiralongkorn in the [[Rice#Culture|Royal Ploughing Ceremony of rice]], directing the planting of [[Dok Mali 105]], [[Pathum Than 1]], [[Kor Khor 43]], [[Kor Khor 6]], and [[Kor Khor 79]].{{cite web | title=Privy Councilor Gen Surayud presides over Royal Ploughing Ceremony | website=[[Thai Public Broadcasting Service]] World | date=2020-05-11 | url=http://www.thaipbsworld.com/privy-councilor-gen-surayud-presides-over-royal-ploughing-ceremony/ | access-date=2021-12-07 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518145500/http://www.thaipbsworld.com/privy-councilor-gen-surayud-presides-over-royal-ploughing-ceremony/ | archive-date=2021-05-18}} == Environmental protection == Surayud was chairman of the [[Khao Yai National Park]] Protection Foundation.''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.warthai.org/content/education/elephants.htm#35 New Highway Planned to Let Herds Mingle] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070214001358/http://www.warthai.org/content/education/elephants.htm#35 |date=14 February 2007 }}, 26 April 2004 However, after becoming premier in 2006, he was accused of breaching the Forestry Act and the National Forest Reserves Act by illegally owning forest land in Yaithiang Mountain of [[Nakhon Ratchasima Province]]. He vowed to resign and return the land (which he did not deny owning) if found guilty.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30022862 Activists call on Surayud to resign for alleged forest encroachment] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070102172825/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30022862 |date=2 January 2007 }}, 29 December 2006 In February 2010 after demonstrations by "Red Shirts" at Khao Yaithiang Mountain, Surayud, who by then had already left politics, returned the land to the Royal Forestry Department when it was found that the land was within forest reserve land under the ministry's decades old code. The plot of land is now under Royal Forestry Department's care. However, up until now no legal action has been taken by Thai authorities against him or other landowners of similar case around the country. Some opposition pressed him to resign from his post as privy councillor only as to understand later that Surayud "had no ill intention" and that it was highly inappropriate to ask for resignation of the post on such unreasonable ground.{{Citation needed|date=August 2020}} == Prime Minister of Thailand (2006–2008) == {{main|Thailand 2006 interim civilian government}} {{see also|Policies of the Surayud government}} [[File:Surayud with Bush.jpg|thumb|Surayud (right) with U.S. President [[George W. Bush]] at the National Conference Center in Hanoi]] Surayud was already considered a strong candidate for appointment as civilian prime minister premiership immediately after General Sonthi overthrew the government of Thaksin Shinawatra. Indeed, Surayud's appointment to the Premiership was confirmed by junta leader [[Sonthi Boonyaratglin]] on the morning of Sunday 1 October 2006. After a couple imploring asks for Surayud to take the temporary premiership, Sonthi had a formal audience with King [[Bhumibol Adulyadej]] at 4 pm that day to nominate Surayud's name to the monarch.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30015095 Sonthi to be granted an audience to nominate interim PM at 4 pm] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061017091543/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30015095 |date=17 October 2006 }}, 1 October 2006''The Nation'', [http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=113281 Sonthi: Surayud to be PM] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070313201014/http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=113281 |date=13 March 2007 }}, 1 October 2006 "Security and social unity" were cited by Sonthi as the key reasons for appointing Surayud.''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/News/02Oct2006_news02.php Surayud's military past posed worry], 2 October 2006 Surayud announced that as premier, he would "Focus on self-sufficiency, more than focusing on the GDP numbers. I will focus on the happiness of the people, more than the GDP."''CNN'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20061026023039/http://edition.cnn.com/2006/WORLD/asiapcf/10/01/thailand.coup.ap/ Former Thai army chief sworn in as interim PM], 1 October 2006 He also claimed that he would be "Friendly to every party, trying to receive information from every side and meeting people as much as possible. I will lead a government based on justice." Due to influences from junta and those behind the scene, the policies and positions of several ministers in Surayud's cabinet changed very frequently, sometimes on a daily basis. Notable flip-flops included Thailand's refusal to share [[avian flu]] samples with the [[WHO]], capital controls against foreign investment, shareholding limits for foreign investors in telecommunications firms, the identity of bombers in the 2006 New Year's Eve bombings, and the role of the Malaysian government in mediating the South Thailand insurgency.{{Citation needed|date=August 2020}} While he was prime minister, Surayud's wife, Colonel [[Khunying]] Chitrawadee, was awarded the Dame Grand Commander (Second Class) of the Most Illustrious [[Order of Chulachomklao]], allowing her to use the prefix [[Than Phu Ying]].''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/x1h6k5o0b0rtx PM's wife elevated to 'thanpuying'], 6 May 2007 === Popularity === [[File:Vladimir Putin at APEC Summit in Australia 7-9 September 2007-4.jpg|thumb|right|Surayud (4th from left) at [[APEC Summit]] in Australia]] The Surayud government's initial nationwide approval rating in October 2006 stood at 60%, with 8% disapproving. By early-November, this fell to 55% approving and 15% disapproving.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30018746 Thai public support for post-coup government falls: poll] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070112123208/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30018746 |date=12 January 2007 }}, 14 November 2006 For comparison, a nationwide poll in July 2006 found that 49% of respondents would have voted for Thaksin Shinawatra in the cancelled October elections.{{cite news |title=Embattled TRT Still Holds Edge Over Opposition: Poll |url=http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/07/31/headlines/headlines_30009984.php |newspaper=[[The Nation (Thailand)|The Nation]] |date=31 July 2006 |access-date=20 September 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930031651/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/07/31/headlines/headlines_30009984.php |archive-date=30 September 2007 |df=dmy-all }} The [[2006 Bangkok New Year's Eve bombings]] caused Surayud's popularity to drop to 48.5% according to [[Assumption University, Thailand|Assumption University]]'s polling arm—and just 11% said they had "full confidence" the government can handle the crisis.''Bangkok Post'', [http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=115767 Poll: Public skeptical of govt claims] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071006090221/http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=115767 |date=6 October 2007 }}, 5 January 2007 The 2007 Chinese New Year Bombings, which saw [[South Thailand insurgency#Escalating violence|38 bombing attacks, 26 cases of arson, and seven ambushes]] within a single day, caused Surayud's popularity to drop even further: 53.7% of respondents living in Bangkok and other major cities in felt the government and the CNS could not put an end to problems in the country. Only 24.6% thought that the situation would improve in six months.[http://pages.citebite.com/n1p1v4n4t2oek Poll: Thais lose trust in govt, CNS], 22 February 2007 By 24 February 2007, his popularity among Bangkokians had further dropped to 34.8%, although he was still more popular than Thaksin Shinawatra, whom 28.8% of Bangkokians favoured.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/02/25/headlines/headlines_30027834.php Surayud's popularity further drops] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070227111011/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/02/25/headlines/headlines_30027834.php |date=27 February 2007}}, 25 February 2007 By 4 March 2007, only 31.3% of people in Bangkok supported the government's political stance. This fell dramatically to 12.5% by 26 March 2007.''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/p1a4c3o6a5hjo Protests did not enjoy wide support in Bangkok], 26 March 2007 Notably the main reason behind the drop was that people wanted to see quick changes in state policies and that actions and judgments for the ousted former prime minister were not forthcoming soon enough. The US government decided to continue holding "[[Cobra Gold]]" joint [[military exercises]] with the Thai government. Immediately after the coup, Washington had halted all military co-operation with, and aid to, the junta. US law forbade assistance to governments of a country where an elected leader has been deposed in a coup.''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/c1i1f1x5q6tma Cobra Gold war games get green light], 19 February 2007 In early-May 2007, activists from the Assembly of Isaan People met with junta chief Sonthi Boonyaratglin in order to appeal for him to remove Surayud Chulanont. Sonthi personally met the anti-Surayud activists at army headquarters and promised he would consider their request. This was the first time that Sonthi met people calling for the removal of Surayud.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/05/09/headlines/headlines_30033754.php Activists plead for Sonthi to remove PM] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070510052857/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/05/09/headlines/headlines_30033754.php |date=10 May 2007 }}, 9 May 2007 Sonthi later claimed that he was "tricked" into meeting the activists.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/05/10/national/national_30033849.php Gen Sonthi 'tricked' into meeting anti-PM group] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070512210939/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/05/10/national/national_30033849.php |date=12 May 2007 }}, 10 May 2007 Surayud launched a weekly talk show called "Poed Baan Phitsanulok" ("Opening Up Baan Pitsanulok"; Baan Pitsanulok is the informal name for Government House) so as to share views and progress of interim government's aim (towards peaceful, internationally recognised general election). The show aired on state-run Channel 11 every Saturday between 08:30 and 09:15. Calling the weekly radio show that was hosted by Thaksin Shinawatra when he was premier "propaganda", he denied any similarity between the two shows.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/05/12/politics/politics_30034034.php Surayud goes for talk-show format] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929153901/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/05/12/politics/politics_30034034.php |date=29 September 2007 }}, 12 May 2007 The military junta's popularity continued to decline. By late-June 2007, an ABAC Poll found that only 13.6% supported the government, with 69.8 of respondents disappointed with the political situation.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/06/25/politics/politics_30037733.php Voters want election as govt support drops] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070627014438/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/06/25/politics/politics_30037733.php |date=27 June 2007 }}, 25 June 2007 The government's popularity continued to decline into July, when survey respondents in Bangkok and outlying areas gave the government an average score of 4.32 out of 10. The average score had been 4.53 in March 2007 and 5.27 in January 2007. Fewer than 15% of respondents in the survey felt that the nation's overall situation had improved during the government's nine-month tenure, while 31.6% said the situation remained unchanged and the majority, 34.9% said it had worsened.''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/v1f9o4o0g5ybl Thai government's popularity declines], 8 July 2007 === Drafting of a permanent constitution and elections === The junta's [[2006 Interim Constitution of Thailand|2006 Interim Constitution]] authorised the junta to appoint a 2,000 person National Assembly which would select members to become candidates for a Constitution Drafting Assembly. From the onset of his appointment as premier, Surayud Chulanont was urged by academics to override the junta's control of the constitution drafting process. Somchai Siripreechakul, Dean of Law at [[Chiang Mai University]], urged Surayud to call a general election as soon as possible and hand the task of drafting a charter to an elected parliament.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/02/politics/politics_30015137.php Poll should precede new charter: law experts] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930031238/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/02/politics/politics_30015137.php |date=30 September 2007 }}, 2 October 2006 [[Banjerd Singkhaneti]] of [[Thammasat University]] noted of the constitution drafting process, "I think it will be a mess and the next constitution will be just that."''Bangkok Post'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/News/28Sep2006_news10.php Draft charter loopholes can 'resurrect Thaksin regime'], 28 September 2006 After the coup, the military junta had originally promised to draft a permanent charter within eight months and to hold elections in October 2007. However, Prime Minister's Office Minister Thirapat Serirangsan later announced that elections might not occur until one year and five months.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/18/politics/politics_30016453.php Drafting new charter 'may take 17 mths'] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930004950/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/18/politics/politics_30016453.php |date=30 September 2007 }}, 18 October 2006 After a constitutional referendum on 19 August, Surayud promised that elections would “definitely” be held in late December.''The Economist'', [http://www.economist.com/world/asia/displaystory.cfm?story_id=9687312 Not a Vote for the Generals], 23 August 2007 === Cabinet appointments === Some believed that [[Prem Tinsulanonda]], President of the King's [[Privy Council (Thailand)|Privy Council]], played a significant role in picking the members of Surayud's cabinet. It was, however, Surayud who made the final decision. General Boonrawd Somtas, a former CDRMA classmate and longtime friend of Surayud, was appointed defense minister.Associated Press, [http://www9.sbs.com.au/theworldnews/region.php?id=131834®ion=2 THAI KING TO SWEAR-IN CABINET]{{dead link|date=March 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, 9 October 2006 former Interior Permanent Secretary Aree Wong-araya was appointed interior minister, former Energy Policy and Planning Office director Piyasvasti Amranand became energy minister, central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula became finance minister, and Bangkok Bank Chairman [[Kosit Panpiemras]] became industry minister. Michael Nelson of [[Chulalongkorn University]] noted that the cabinet was dominated by bureaucrats and that "It's very strongly guided by military ideas combined with some technocrats, some people in economic areas and some former bureaucrats."{{cite news |title=Thailand's post-coup cabinet unveiled |date=9 October 2006 |work=The Australian |url=http://www.theaustralian.news.com.au/story/0,20867,20550793-23109,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070312041044/http://www.theaustralian.news.com.au/story/0,20867,20550793-23109,00.html |archive-date=12 March 2007 }} Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Pridiyathorn resigned on 28 February 2007. His resignation shocked the political world as well as the business community.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/business/business_30028169.php Concern over stability of govt] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070303001103/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/01/business/business_30028169.php |date=3 March 2007 }}, 1 March 2007 His cited reasons for resignation included, * Surayud's decision to appoint Pridiyathorn's rival, former Thaksin-government Finance Minister [[Somkid Jatusripitak]], as a [[self-sufficiency economy]] special envoy. Somkid resigned from his position after less than a week. * Prime Minister's Office Minister [[Thirapat Serirangsan]]'s alleged preference to certain private media interests.''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/y1e1s8e9b3afb Pridiyathorn resigns as deputy prime minister and finance minister], 28 February 2007 Several analysts speculated that he was referring to the preferential treatment the junta gave to leading anti-Thaksin critic [[Sondhi Limthongkul]], who was also a long-time critic of Pridiyathorn.''International Herald Tribune'', [http://pages.citebite.com/p1m1l9u8i3tph Thai minister resigns amid cabinet disarray], 28 February 2007''The Nation'', [http://www.bangkokpost.com/topstories/topstories.php?id=117117 Pridiyathorn resigns as deputy PM, finance minister], 28 February 2007 Pridiyathorn was replaced by [[Chalongphob Sussangkarn]], an academic who led the [[Thailand Development Research Institute]]. Chalongphob had previously criticised the junta's capital controls policy.''The Nation'', [http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/09/opinion/opinion_30028868.php Chalongphob a pro-market academic for a reeling economy] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070311214837/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/09/opinion/opinion_30028868.php |date=11 March 2007 }}, 9 March 2007 === Policies === ==== Telecommunications ==== * The planned merger of state-telecom companies [[TOT (Thailand)|TOT]] and [[CAT Telecom|CAT]].''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20070312142440/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/16/business/business_30016254.php Call for end to policy corruption], 16 October 2006 * The cancellation of plans to list [[TOT (Thailand)|TOT]], [[CAT Telecom|CAT]], and Thai Post on the [[Stock Exchange of Thailand]].''The Nation'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20061104174034/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/10/28/business/business_30017353.php Sweeping changes in state telecom boards], 28 October 2006 * The cancellation of the Thaksin government's telecom excise tax policy. The Thaksin government imposed an excise tax on privately offered fixed and cellular services, and then allowed telecom companies to deduct the amount they paid in excise tax from concession fees they had to pay to state concession owners TOT or CAT Telecom. The total amount paid by the private telecom firms did not change. The Surayud government's excise tax cancellation meant that [[TOT (Thailand)|TOT]] and [[CAT Telecom|CAT]] would receive their full concession payments. However, TOT and CAT were then forced to increase their dividends to the Ministry of Finance to account for their increased income.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/24/headlines/headlines_30024946.php Telecom excise tax revoked] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071025095747/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/24/headlines/headlines_30024946.php |date=25 October 2007 }}, 24 January 2007 * Changing the publicly listed state-enterprise media company [[MCOT]]'s policy from focusing on monetary benefits to social benefits. MCOT's stock prices dropped 5.13% to an 11-month low as a result.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/11/04/business/business_30018020.php MCOT plunges on policy reversal] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061124152251/http://nationmultimedia.com/2006/11/04/business/business_30018020.php |date=24 November 2006 }}, 4 November 2006 * Surayud reversed policies many times regarding the fate of the [[iTV (Thailand)|iTV]] TV station. Surayud first announced that it intended to take over the station and promised that the station would not be taken off the air no matter what happened regarding its concession controversy. However, in early-March 2007, PM's Office Minister Dhipawadee Meksawan announced that the station would be taken off the air on midnight on 6 March 2007, following the cabinet's revocation of iTV's concession. Thai embassies were ordered not to facilitate his travels. Traditionally, all former prime ministers and foreign ministers of Thailand were permitted to hold on to their diplomatic passports for life.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/10/headlines/headlines_30023787.php FM cancel ousted premier and wife's diplomatic passports] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070116151951/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/10/headlines/headlines_30023787.php |date=16 January 2007 }}, 10 January 2007 Thaksin later publicly announced that he was quitting politics. Surayud's Defense Minister later announced that the junta would refuse Thaksin's reconciliation offer, claiming that Thailand was being threatened by "ill-intentioned people" and capitalism.''Bangkok Post'', [http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=116526 General scorns Thaksin reconciliation] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081207110436/http://bangkokpost.net/breaking_news/breakingnews.php?id=116526 |date=7 December 2008 }}, 3 February 2007 Surayud's government completely purged all senior military officers perceived as loyal to the Thaksin government, replacing them with officers trusted by the new regime.''Bangkok Post'', [http://pages.citebite.com/w1s4v0j1u1jku Sonthi loyalists put in key military positions], 22 March 2007 In April 2007, during an interview where reporters asked Surayud what he would say to Thaksin if he could meet him in person, Surayud responded, "I would say please don't ever come back."''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/26/headlines/headlines_30032797.php I want to tell Thaksin "don't ever come back," : PM] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070428102422/http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/26/headlines/headlines_30032797.php |date=28 April 2007 }}, 26 April 2007 ===Council for National Security=== The Surayud government allowed the [[Council for National Security]] to interfere with many government responsibilities, including the transfer of civil servants. The CNS was allowed to control a nationwide reshuffle of the civil service in April 2007 in order to weed out officials "clinging" to the deposed "Thaksin-regime".''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30023690 Non-cooperative civil servants face axe by CNS] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070112135405/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30023690 |date=12 January 2007 }}, 9 January 2007 Surayud also authorised the removal of police chief [[Kowit Wattana]] from his position in early February 2007. Kowit had also been police chief under the ousted government of [[Thaksin Shinawatra]]. In March, junta leader Sonthi asked Surayud to declare emergency rule in Bangkok in response to the protests by the founders of [[PTV (Thailand)|PTV]]. In an interview, Sonthi noted that the protests, attended by approximately 1,500-3,000 people, had so far been peaceful but that he was afraid the movement could lead to "mutiny and chaos in the country."''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/28/headlines/headlines_30030459.php Thai junta chief calls for emergency rule in Bangkok] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070513115003/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/03/28/headlines/headlines_30030459.php |date=13 May 2007 }}, 28 March 2007 CNS Spokesman Sansern Kaewkamnerd asked, "What will we do if the numbers of protesters go beyond 100,000? It will greatly damage the country's image." Emergency powers allowed the government to ban public gatherings, impose curfews and censor local news reports.IHT, [http://www.iht.com/articles/ap/2007/03/28/asia/AS-GEN-Thailand-Emergency-Rule.php Thai coup leaders urge government to impose emergency rule], 28 March 2007 On 3 April 2007, Surayud approved a 15% pay rise (on top of an earlier 15% pay rise) for members of the CNS, as a "special reward" for their "honesty, tolerance and dedication on weekdays and weekends."''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/05/politics/politics_30031147.php Junta at risk of a backlash over lucrative benefits] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070422193454/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/05/politics/politics_30031147.php |date=22 April 2007 }}, 5 April 2007 Despite this, relations between Surayud and the CNS deteriorated. Rumours swirled in mid-April 2007 that the CNS would overthrow the government. However, in a meeting with the CNS President, Surayud declared, "Don't ever think of launching another coup. If you utter only one word, then I am ready to resign."''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/13/opinion/opinion_30031803.php Surayud survives barrage and hangs onto job by a thread] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070427184340/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/04/13/opinion/opinion_30031803.php |date=27 April 2007 }}, 13 April 2007 ==Criticism== Besides being heavily criticised for gaining power through the 2006 coup and his subsequent actions as premier, Surayud has been accused of forest encroachment and corruption. ===Forest encroachment=== Surayud was accused of breaching the Forestry Act and the National Forest Reserves Act by illegally owning forest reserve land in Yaithiang Mountain of [[Nakhon Ratchasima]] province. When Surayud was Commander of the 2nd Army Region, he was sold the plot of land for 50,000 baht. He later transferred ownership of the plot to his wife. Surayud vowed to resign and return the land (which he did not deny owning) if found guilty. He was defended by Interior Minister [[Aree Wongarya]], who claimed, "Gen Surayud purchased the land from someone else so the question has to be posed to the first owner whether the land is reserved." National Human Rights Commissioner and Thaksin sympathiser Jaran Ditthapichai noted, "I cannot agree to have someone call himself a man of morality and sufficiency if he built a fancy house in a forest reserve."''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/15/headlines/headlines_30024142.php Thumbs down for the next charter] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070117095033/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/15/headlines/headlines_30024142.php |date=17 January 2007 }}, 15 January 2007 However, the National Counter Corruption Commission (NCCC) refused to investigate the land encroachment charges, claiming that the statute of limitations on the case had run out. NCCC member Klanarong Chantik noted that Surayud retired from military service in 2003 whereas the charges were made 4 years after his retirement, and that the NCCC could not legally investigate an officer for alleged wrongdoing beyond two years after retirement.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30037479 NCCC rules against probe into Surayud's land] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929122012/http://nationmultimedia.com/breakingnews/read.php?newsid=30037479 |date=29 September 2007 }}, 22 June 2007 In February 2010 after demonstrations by the "Red Shirts" at Khao Yaithiang Mountain, Surayud returned the land to the Royal Forestry Department, without any removals of structures or plants, weeks before a formal notice from the department was issued. The plot of land is now under the care of the Royal Forestry Department after Surayud moved out. However, up until now no legal action has been taken by Thai authorities against Surayud or other landowners of similar type all over Thailand. ===Corruption=== Surayud, an avid collector of model trains, was accused of illegally acquiring four train compartments for his resort home in Kho Yaithiang mountain, [[Nakhon Ratchasima]]. Surayud claimed that he had more than 4 compartments, but they were all in his residence in Bangkok and were all models driven by household class electricity of 220V.''The Nation'', [http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/12/26/politics/politics_30022525.php Surayud denies train carriages allegation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070922035603/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2006/12/26/politics/politics_30022525.php |date=22 September 2007 }}, 28 December 2006 However, Thai-language newspaper [[Khaosod]] published a photo on the front page of its edition of 26 December 2006 which showed a building resembling a railway carriage near Surayud's resort home. The National Counter Corruption Committee was petitioned to scrutinise the land at Surayud's retreat residence, but refused to take action (see above). Before the end of his tenure as prime minister, Surayud invited dozens of reporters from various fields to visit and have a lunch at his disputed Kho Yaithiang home, where they realised that what seemed to be train carriages were only a resort building of his friend nearby viewed from a particular angle. {{Citation needed|date=January 2014}} While Surayud was frequently accused of corruption, many in the business community believed otherwise. A poll conducted in January 2007 found that 66% of business people thought that local corruption would increase, with only 10.5% thinking that it would decrease. However, only about 14% believed that leading figures in Surayud's administration were corrupt.''The Nation'', [http://nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/29/headlines/headlines_30025362.php Business leaders see corruption increasing] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070202233152/http://www.nationmultimedia.com/2007/01/29/headlines/headlines_30025362.php |date=2 February 2007 }}, 29 January 2007 ==Royal decorations== Surayud has received the following royal decorations in the [[Thai Honours Order of Precedence|Honours System]] of Thailand: * 2018 – [[File:Order of Chula Chom Klao - 1st Class (Thailand) ribbon.svg|80x80px]] Knight Grand Cross of the Most Illustrious [[Order of Chula Chom Klao]] * 1995 – [[File:Order of the White Elephant - Special Class (Thailand) ribbon.svg|80px]] Knight Grand Cordon (Special Class) of the Most Exalted [[Order of the White Elephant]] * 1992 – [[File:Order of the Crown of Thailand - Special Class (Thailand) ribbon.svg|80px]] Knight Grand Cordon (Special Class) of The Most Noble [[Order of the Crown of Thailand]] * 2019 – [[File:King Rama X Royal Cypher Medal (Thailand) ribbon.svg|80x80px]] [[Vajiralongkorn|King Rama X]] Royal Cypher Medal, Third Class * 1990 – [[File:Order of Rama 6th Class ribbon.svg|80px]] Rama Mala Medal of the Honourable [[Order of Rama]] * 1974 – [[File:Freeman Safeguarding Medal - 1st Class (Thailand)
