Accessed 3 May 2007. {{in lang|ru}} In mid-1985, the [[Soviet Union]] and [[Democratic Republic of Afghanistan|Kabul]] launched [[psychological warfare]] against Pakistan in an attempt to morally destabilize society. As part of this strategy, the [[KGB]] and KhAD deployed hundreds of young girls of Central Asian, and Russian origin to corrupt Pakistani society. This influx initially targeted the major urban centers such as [[Islamabad]], [[Lahore]], [[Karachi]], [[Faisalabad]], [[Multan]], and [[Quetta]].{{Cite news |date=September 1992 |title=The Herald |pages=23–28}} These groups of prostitutes strategically selected affluent areas in these cities and operated within a well-organized structure. Many of these prostitutes had connections to [[KGB]] and KhAD agents, with high-ranking government officials and [[Pakistan Army|Pakistan army]] officers being their primary targets.{{Cite news |date=July 1985 |title=Asia Week |pages=9–11}} On 28 June 1985, two Afghan [[Mil Mi-24]] helicopters with five crewmen defected to Pakistan, landing at Miramshah,[https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/national/1985/07/14/afghan-air-crews-defect-with-2-soviet-helicopters/067573ba-0ca3-4ee9-8b6e-304955e5f76f/ Afghan Air Crews Defect With 2 Soviet Helicopters] the aircraft belonged to the 377th Independent Helicopter Regiment, piloted by Mohammad Ishak and Mohammad Omar. The helicopters were later transferred to the United States for evaluation, they were later returned and one of them is now at display in Khalid Aviation Base Quetta (Pakistan). On 19 August 1985, 4 Afghan aircraft bombed the village of Kewas inside [[Pakistan]], killing eight and wounding twelve, and five houses were also destroyed.{{Cite web |title=Afghan planes bomb Pakistani border village - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/08/19/Afghan-planes-bomb-Pakistani-border-village/2771493272000/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} Around 1985, Pakistani police in the city of [[Karachi]] were becoming alarmed by an increased number of killings. While the murders took place in different areas of the city, an investigation found these murders were done in the same manner; a single blow to the head with a hathora (the word for "hammer" in [[Urdu]]). Some Pakistanis newspapers alluded that the Hathora group was actually made up of members of the Soviet intelligence agency, the [[KGB]], and KHAD, who were striking back due to the Pakistani government backing the [[Afghan mujahidin|Afghan mujahideen]] against the [[Democratic Republic of Afghanistan]].{{Cite web |last=Paracha |first=Nadeem F. |date=2015-04-26 |title=Hathora Group: Karachi's first terror |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1177771 |access-date=2023-09-05 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en}} In late 1985, Pakistani government sent 3,000 Frontier Corps personnel to capture Wali Khan Kukikhel, leader of a faction from the [[Afridi]] clan believed to be working with the DRA and to subdue the Afridi and Shinwari tribesmen under his influence and dismantle their smuggling networks. 50 people were killed and 150 were injured in Pakistan in 1986, in a Soviet-Afghan cross border sabotage campaign across the border.{{Cite web| title=AFGHANISTAN-PAKISTAN: Air Attacks | url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP86T01017R000302510001-9.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250224044953/https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP86T01017R000302510001-9.pdf | archive-date=2025-02-24}} ===1986=== {{See also|Second Battle of Zhawar}} On 7 January, a roadside landmine planted by KHAD killed 15 Afghan refugees in [[Kurram Agency]]. On 23 January, KHAD targeted the [[Pakistan International Airlines|PIA]] building in Peshawar with a bomb blast, killing five and injuring 25 Pakistanis.{{Cite web| title=Pakistan: Trouble Along the Afghan Border | url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP06T00412R000606330001-2.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240816204647/https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP06T00412R000606330001-2.pdf | archive-date=2024-08-16}} On 28 January, 4 Afghan [[Mi-24]] helicopters violated Pakistani airspace and bombed [[Parachinar]], killing one person and injuring 13.{{Cite web |title=Foreign News Briefs - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/01/28/Foreign-News-Briefs/5889507272400/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 31 January 2 Afghan helicopters violated Pakistani airspace 3 times near [[Parachinar]], dropping bombs which injured 3 women.{{Cite web |title=Two Afghan helicopter gunships violated Pakistan's air space three... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/01/31/Two-Afghan-helicopter-gunships-violated-Pakistans-air-space-three/6143507531600/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 2 February, KHAD saboteurs disrupted the electric supply in [[Mardan]] by bombing an electrical grid station. The No. 15 squadron intercepted a couple of Soviet [[Mig-21]]s in February 1986 but were ordered not to engage them.{{cite journal|journal=Defence Journal|author=Air Commodore A HAMEED QADRI|title=PAKISTAN'S AFGHAN WAR AIR STRATEGY AND OPERATIONS|archive-date=28 January 1999|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990128150750/http://www.defencejournal.com/aug98/pakafghanwar1.htm |url=http://www.defencejournal.com/aug98/pakafghanwar1.htm}} On 15 March, 16 Afghan refugees and three Pakistanis were killed and 11 Afghan refugees were wounded in a KHAD landmine blast in [[Parachinar]]. On 22 March, five Afghan refugees were killed and 19 were wounded in an Afghan Army artillery strike on Mata Sangar refugee camp in Kurram Agency. On 27 March, three Afghan refugees and one Pakistani were killed and 17 Pakistanis were wounded in a bomb blast targeting a restaurant in Peshawar, by KHAD. In the area of operations of the [[15th Independent Special Forces Brigade|15th Spetsnaz Brigade]], commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Babushkin, repeated mujahideen attacks inflicted heavy losses on [[Spetsnaz]] troops. The Mujahideen, using [[Krer]] as a supply base, conducted major attacks including the destruction of an entire company in February 1985, leaving only two survivors and an ambush on a ~50 man recon team in August 1985. However, all combat within five miles of the [[Durand line|Pakistan-Afghanistan border]] was prohibited to avoid an international incident. During a mission, the [[spetsnaz]] captured an Afghan mujahid who provided Intel about the Krer camp and the spetsnaz fomented a plan to destroy it. Krer camp was situated along the route to [[Bajaur]], a major mujahideen supply hub in Pakistan. It was garrisoned by Asma bin Zaid's regiment of the [[Abdul Rab Rasul Sayyaf]] faction with a strength of 400 personnel and commanded by Commander Asadullah. Although usually understaffed, it was heavily equipped with small arms and heavy weaponry. The Soviet order of battle included the 15th Spetsnaz Brigade's 334th and 154th battalions with direct support from the [[66th Mechanized Brigade (Ukraine)|66th Motorized Rifle Brigade]] and figments of the DRA Army, Sarandoy and KhAD. Their main mission was to intercept the supplies from Pakistan. Firstly, a recon raid was conducted against Krer's defenses. Two [[reconnaissance]] companies of the 334th Battalion were dispatched. After climbing the canyon, they saw two forward positions. A simultaneous assault was planned and the force was divided into 2 assault and one support group, but due to terrain, the plan was changed. Firstly, one group attacked and overran the accessible position, following which the other position's defenders arose to observe and were also overrun. Mujahideen Maps and plans were recovered, weapons were seized and destroyed. The attack force then withdrew with fire support from the support contingent. The main attack was planned using this information with the date being set for 30 March 1986 with the 334th advancing from [[Asadabad, Afghanistan|Asadabad]] using APCs, crossing the river and climbing via the same route as the recon force under cover from the APCs. The 154th Battalion using its own APCs advanced from [[Jalalabad]] accompanied by artillery with only the personnel crossing the river linking with the first force on Spina ridge in the morning, destroying the camp and withdrawing at night. However, due to a hepatitis outbreak, the 154th could only supply ~150 personnel for the mission. On the day of the offensive in the afternoon, Commander Asadullah observed a column of Soviet/DRA forces heading to attack. Heavy fighting broke out following the offloading of troops by the APCs and night fell. The 334th got lost in the darkness and climbed the wrong ridge, while the main ridge was heavily attacked by mujahideen. The Spetsnaz were able to flank and take mujahideen positions out using grenades but both sides suffered high losses. The 334th also engaged with a 16-man mujahideen group, not part of the Krer regiment, returning from Pakistan to Pech valley. They were warned of the Soviet presence by a [[ferry]] operator while attempting to cross the river, and they decided to return to Pakistan, forming a defensive perimeter for the night. At 10 PM, they observed Spetsnaz soldiers and initiated fire with Spetsnaz returning fire. Mujahideen withdrew 300m up the hill and struck their old position with Spetsnaz in it and systematically continued repeating this strategy inflicting losses. The 154th meanwhile arrived at the riverbank on 30 March in the morning, crossing the river in 4 hours. By nightfall, they started climbing up the mountains but the DRA forces faced difficulty in doing so, due to a lack of fitness and insubordination but were forced to climb under the threat of abandonment. The 154th reached Spina ridge by the morning, undetected. The planning of 154th's company and brigade commanders was interrupted by Azan of [[Fajr]], following which its 3rd company attacked a mujahideen forward assault position and the rest of the battalion moved down the crest seizing many more positions and raining fire on mujahideen down the crest. The 1st company detonated approaches from Pakistan, infiltrated Pakistani territory and dug 700m inside Pakistan with the area being under full spetsnaz control. The 16-man group which had engaged the 334th was still conducting a systematic retreat into Pakistan, observed the signal rockets of the 154th and immediately retreated into Pakistani territory. After sunrise, ~40 mujahideen attacked the 1st company's positions inside Pakistan but were repelled, resulting in 15 dead. Around 40 minutes later, a mujahideen relief force, traveling on several trucks from Bajaur, charged at the 1st company's positions after being informed of the situation by Commander Asadullah. The Spetsnaz called for artillery strikes which slowed down but could not halt the mujahideen advance. Ultimately, the spetsnaz called artillery strikes on their own positions, inflicting casualties on mujahideen while being battered themselves. The surviving spetsnaz withdrew and the mujahideen occupied the heights, now firing directly at the 154th battalion's command post. By 10:45, the 1st and 2nd companies were rendered combat ineffective and the 3rd was under high stress. The 334th battalion was at a lower position and was faced with a large Mujahideen assault, prompting the brigade commander to call in a [[medevac]] helicopter, making his covert unauthorized operation known to the high command. The helicopter, however, was unable to land due to heavy combat. The 1st Company had been completely overrun by a few mujahideen and the main mujahideen force had infiltrated into Krer, occupying heights and raining fire on Spetsnaz. Commander Asadullah's six-personnel team killed the Soviet officer in the 1st company's command center. Ultimately, Soviet gunship helicopters arrived at the scene, being guided by wounded troops inside an adobe, who were besieged by mujahideen forces. Targets were given but the gunships did not fire as the Battle was on Pakistani soil. After about half an hour, a gunship agreed to strike. The building's roof was cleared by the gunships and the few surviving spetsnaz were able to evacuate. Two companies of the 334th carried the dead and wounded of the 154th. The nearest helicopter landing site was at Hill 1917, 10 km away, controlled by the mujahideen. The Spetsnaz company pushed forward as artillery and air strikes continued. On 1 April, the 66th Motorized Rifle Brigade's personnel landed via helicopters and, along with the 154th battalion, found MIAs, KIAs and WIAs, but two Spetsnaz were left behind. Two patrol parties of the 334th entered Pakistan and briefly captured an abandoned post. The two Spetsnaz who were left behind hid in a cave and were killed by mujahideen after a prolonged fight.{{Cite book |last=Games |first=Ambush Alley Ambush Alley |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Fqq6CwAAQBAJ&q=spetsnaz+Pakistan |title=Classified: Special Operations Missions 1940–2010 |date=20 February 2013 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-84908-774-2 |language=en}}{{Cite book |last=Dimitrakis |first=Panagiotis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hJ-LDwAAQBAJ&q=spetsnaz+Pakistan |title=The Secret War in Afghanistan: The Soviet Union, China and Anglo-American Intelligence in the Afghan War |date=30 June 2013 |publisher=Bloomsbury |isbn=978-0-85773-377-1 }}{{Cite journal |last1=Grau |first1=Lester W. |last2=and Ahmad Jalali |first2=Ali |date=1 December 2005 |title=Forbidden Cross-border Vendetta: Spetsnaz Strike into Pakistan during the Soviet-afghan War |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/13518040500354943 |journal=The Journal of Slavic Military Studies |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=661–672 |doi=10.1080/13518040500354943 |issn=1351-8046|url-access=subscription }}{{Cite web |title=Forbidden Cross-border Vendetta: Spetsnaz Strike into Pakistan during the Soviet-afghan War |url=https://community.apan.org/wg/tradoc-g2/fmso/m/fmso-monographs/241811#:~:text=2005-12-01%20Forbidden%20Cross,Grau%20and%20Ali%20Ahmad%20Jalali |website=Apan}}{{Cite book |last=Coll |first=Steve |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZCS3aIepU0sC&q=spetsnaz+Pakistan |title=The Bin Ladens: Oil, Money, Terrorism and the Secret Saudi World |date=5 March 2009 |publisher=Penguin Books Limited |isbn=978-0-14-191778-8 |language=en}} The Pakistan Army [[Special Service Group]] was alleged to be involved in the battle, but the Russians dismissed the claim.Lester W. Grau & Ali Ahmed Jalali, [http://fmso.leavenworth.army.mil/documents/Krer-SOF.pdf Forbidden Cross-Border Vendetta: Spetsnaz Strike into Pakistan during the Soviet-Afghan War] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304110537/http://fmso.leavenworth.army.mil/documents/Krer-SOF.pdf |date=4 March 2016 }}, [[Journal of Slavic Military Studies]], December 2005, p.1-2 Referenced copy was obtained via the [[Foreign Military Studies Office]] website On 2 April 1986, an incident took place during the [[Second Battle of Zhawar]] when, instead of [[Zhawar]], the 38th Commando Brigade of the [[Democratic Republic of Afghanistan]] arrived near [[Miram Shah]] in Pakistan with a force of 120 soldiers and eight helicopters. After arrival, the commandos did not observe any signs of combat amidst the darkness of the night. Thinking the force had lost its way, they asked the command post for signals in the form of flares. At 3 A.M, Afghan artillery fired a flare on Dawri Gar, which the assault group commander reported to be about 15 kilometers from their location. A second flare was launched five kilometers south and the distance was reported to be ten kilometers. Command post relayed that the air assault group had accidentally crossed the border and landed near [[Miranshah]], 5 kilometers inside Pakistan and immediate withdrawal preparations were initiated. Following the failure of the air assault, the Soviet Air Forces bombed Mujahideen positions, following which the Mujahideen attacked the landing sites. A single group of Afghan commandos held out for three days facing constant mujahideen assaults, but was finally overrun. All six Mi-8 helicopters and all 120 commandos were surrounded and captured. Following this, hundreds of Pakistani SSG personnel were deployed to Zhawar, army officers were dispatched to Zhawar and attempted to take down Afghan and Soviet aircraft using English [[Blowpipe (missile)|blowpipe]]s but were not successful in doing so; a Pakistani officer and an NCO were injured as a result of Soviet airstrikes. Pakistani forces fired a total of 14 surface-to-air missiles on Soviet aircraft.{{Cite book |last=Riedel |first=Bruce |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hb8xAwAAQBAJ&q=second+battle+of+Zhawar&pg=PP1 |title=What We Won: America's Secret War in Afghanistan, 1979?89 |date=28 July 2014 |publisher=Brookings Institution Press |isbn=978-0-8157-2585-5 |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Bock |first=Jon |date=15 September 2023 |title=How This Subterranean Logistics Base in Afghanistan Bedeviled Soviet Invaders |url=https://www.historynet.com/soviet-afghanistan-zhawar-battle/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=HistoryNet |language=en-US}}{{Cite book |last1=Jalali |first1=Ali Ahmad |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XILyYPv_3a0C&dq=Pakistan+and+second+battle+of+Zhawar&pg=PA324 |title=The Other Side of the Mountain: Mujahideen Tactics in the Soviet-Afghan War |last2=Grau |first2=Lester W. |date=1999 |publisher=U.S. Marine Corps, Studies and Analysis Division |language=en}}{{Cite web |title= Access Denied|url=https://community.apan.org/cfs-file/__key/docpreview-s/00-00-09-39-44/2001_2D00_09_2D00_01-The-Campaign-for-the-Caves-_2800_Grau-and-Jalali_2900_.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240901184810/https://community.apan.org/cfs-file/__key/docpreview-s/00-00-09-39-44/2001_2D00_09_2D00_01-The-Campaign-for-the-Caves-_2800_Grau-and-Jalali_2900_.pdf |archive-date=1 September 2024 |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=community.apan.org |url-status=live }}{{Cite book |last=Ali |first=S. Mahmud |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kbp-AgAAQBAJ&dq=Zhawar+battle+Pakistan&pg=PA185 |title=US-China Cold War Collaboration: 1971-1989 |date=11 April 2007 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-24581-9 |language=en}}{{Cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=Thomas H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TdgnEAAAQBAJ&dq=Zhawar+battle+Pakistan&pg=PA532 |title=Historical Dictionary of Afghanistan |last2=Adamec |first2=Ludwig W. |date=15 May 2021 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing PLC |isbn=978-1-5381-4929-4 |language=en}}{{Cite journal |last=GRAU |first=LESTER W. |date=1 March 2004 |title=The Soviet–Afghan War: A Superpower Mired in the Mountains |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/13518040490440692 |journal=The Journal of Slavic Military Studies |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=129–151 |doi=10.1080/13518040490440692 |issn=1351-8046|url-access=subscription }} On 16 April, DRAAF bombed Saidgi, killing four Pakistani civilians and wounding eight others. On 20 April, a Pakistani was injured in a terrorist attack on the British Airways office in Peshawar. In late April 1986, four people were killed and 14 were wounded in a bomb explosion in the Landi Kotal bazaar, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Pakistan blamed the Afghan secret police for planting the bomb.{{Cite news |agency=Reuters |date=5 January 1986 |title=BOMB KILLS 4 AT KHYBER PASS |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/01/05/world/bomb-kills-4-at-khyber-pass.html |access-date=17 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} On 3 May, Afghan artillery strikes in Kurram Agency, killed three Afghan refugees and 11 Pakistanis while 22 Pakistanis were injured. On 5 May, DRAAF struck Parachinar killing 12 Pakistanis and wounding 14, followed by more airstrikes in Kurram Agency, killing two Afghan refugees and one Pakistani, while three Afghan refugees were wounded. On 6 May, DRAAF struck a tribal paramilitary post in Teri Mangal. On 8 May, nine Afghan refugees were killed in a DRAAF strike on refugee camps in Kurram Agency. On 9 May, DRAAF destroyed a Kotri militia post in Kurram Agency. On 13 May, 13 Afghan refugees and one Pakistani were killed while 22 Afghan refugees and eight Pakistanis were injured in cross-border artillery strikes by Afghan forces in Kurram Agency. On 14 May, DRAAF hit militia posiitions in Kurram Agency and wounded 20 Afghan refugees. On 17 May 1986, [[Pakistan Air Force|PAF]] with 2[[F-16]]s intercepted one Afghan [[Su-22|Su-22M3K]] which had violated Pakistani airspace near [[Parachinar]]. Squadron Leader Hameed Qadri shot down one [[Su-22]] as it was retreating towards the Afghan border by firing AIM-9L missiles within the range of six miles. In a PAF account, he shot down another Su-22 while it was retreating towards the Afghan border, after the execution of a high yo-yo maneuver for gaining the offensive position and fired a three-second burst which resulted in the interception of the second Su-22, although the Afghan government accepted the loss of one aircraft only. Qadri confronted [[List of Mikoyan and MiG aircraft|Mig]] fighters one month later but no engagements were made.{{Cite web |last=Insight |first=Global Defense |date=13 December 2021 |title=The Pakistan's Successful Encounters During the Afghan War |url=https://defensetalks.com/the-pakistans-successful-encounters-during-the-afghan-war/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=Global Defense Insight |language=en-US}} [[New York Times]], however reported that one [[Mig-21]] was destroyed and another aircraft was damaged while two others managed to flee back to Afghanistan.{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=18 May 1986 |title=PAKISTANIS SHOOT DOWN AN AFGHAN MIG |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/05/18/world/pakistanis-shoot-down-an-afghan-mig.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} On 19 May, Afghan army artillery fire killed four Pakistanis and injured two in Kurram Agency. On 21 May, multiple militia positions in Kurram were attacked by DRAAF. On 26 May, Pakistan claimed that Afghanistan shelled 4 posts by 80-100 bombs in the [[Mohmand]] area, near the place where the [[Mig 21]] was shot down. The posts were damaged but no casualties were inflicted on Pakistani forces.{{Cite news |agency=Reuters |date=26 May 1986 |title=AROUND THE WORLD; Pakistan Says 4 Outposts Were Shelled by Afghans |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/05/26/world/around-the-world-pakistan-says-4-outposts-were-shelled-by-afghans.html |access-date=17 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} On 27 May, the main post office in Parachinar was targeted in a bomb blast by KHAD. On 4 June, five Afghan refugees were killed and two were injured in a roadside landmine blast by KHAD. On 5 June, DRAAF struck a refugee camp in Parachinar, killing five Afghan refugees while one Pakistani and five Afghan refugees were injured in the airstrike. On 7 June, three Pakistanis and two Afghan refugees were killed while 40 Pakistanis were injured in a bomb blast by KHAD, targeting a market in Peshawar. On 17 June, power supply to Quetta was damaged as Karik power station was hit by Afghan artillery strikes. On 22 June, a police station in Peshawar was targeted by KHAD in a bomb blast and 21 Pakistanis were injured. On 11 July, an Afghan refugee hotel in Teri Mangal was bombed by KHAD, killing 10 refugees and wounding five while eight more were killed and 12 were injured in a bombing near an Afghan refugee camp in Kurram. On 25 July, Afghan artillery strikes in [[Chaman]] killed seven Pakistanis while a DRAAF strike in Domandai, killed 16 refugees, the next day. On 27 July, another KHAD landmine blast in Kurram Agency, killed six Afghan refugees and wounded six more. On 16 August, the office of the supervisory medical officer for Kurram Agency was bombed by KHAD. On 26 August DRAAF strikes on refugee camps in Domandai killed 16 Afghan refugees. On 13 September, three UNHCR ambulances were destroyed in a KHAD bomb blast. On 16 September, militia posts in Shadal were hit by DRAAF, killing six Afghan refugees and injuring 10. On 19 September, Afghan artillery strikes killed two Pakistanis and wounded 12 in Chaman. On 22 September, [[KHAD]] killed one Pakistani and wounded nine in a bomb blast in [[Hangu]]. On 30 September, a major blast occurred in Peshawar. On 16 October, a hospital in Peshawar was bombed by KHAD wounding 15 Pakistanis, followed two days later by a bomb blast on a train in Peshawar wounding two. On 23 October 1986, an Afghan [[Mig 21]], piloted by Lt. Mohammed Daoud defected to Pakistan, landing at Kohat Air Base.[https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-10-24-mn-7205-story.html Afghan Air Force Pilot Flies MIG-21 to Pakistani Base and Asks for Asylum] On 25 October, Afghan artillery strikes in Bajaur Agency killed one Pakistani and wounded another. On 28 October, a bombing on a bazar by KHAD killed six Pakistanis and wounded 20 in Peshawar. On 1 November, a KHAD bombing on a bus killed five Pakistanis and wounded 13. In December 1986, KhAD attempted a car bombing on the [[US consulate|US Consulate]] in [[Peshawar]], which ended up killing over 30 people as the bomb was being dragged away by police.{{Cite web |title=TERRORISM REVIEW FOR 13 JANUARY 1987 {{!}} CIA FOIA (foia.cia.gov) |url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/document/0000258615 |access-date=10 September 2023 |website=www.cia.gov}}{{Cite web| title=The Soviet Role in Afghan Terrorism in Pakistan | url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP90T00114R000800340002-2.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250223112543/https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP90T00114R000800340002-2.pdf | archive-date=2025-02-23}} ===1987=== {{See also|1987 Karachi car bombing}} On 27 February, Afghanistan bombed the villages of Saigai and Ghulam Mohammad with eight aircraft, destroying 150 shops, killing 35 people and leaving more than 200 wounded.{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=27 February 1987 |title=AFGHAN PLANES SAID TO KILL 35 IN PAKISTAN RAIDS |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/02/27/world/afghan-planes-said-to-kill-35-in-pakistan-raids.html |access-date=16 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite web |title=Afghan bombing raids renewed as Pakistan protests incursion - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/02/27/Afghan-bombing-raids-renewed-as-Pakistan-protests-incursion/5762541400400/ |access-date=16 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 3 March, Afghan jets bombed refugee camps at the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, killing 2 people.{{Cite web |title=More bombs dropped on Afghan refugee camps - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/03/03/More-bombs-dropped-on-Afghan-refugee-camps/3378541746000/ |access-date=18 July 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 23 March 1987, an Afghan raid at [[Tari Mangal]] aimed at destroying gun shops selling arms to the Mujahideen, killed 80 people.{{Cite magazine |last=Desmond |first=Edward W. |date=22 June 1987 |title=Diplomacy Flying into a Tight Corner |url=https://time.com/archive/6709558/diplomacy-flying-into-a-tight-corner/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |magazine=TIME |language=en}} On 31 March, an Afghan [[Antonov An-26]] was shot down near [[Parachinar]] by a Pakistani [[F-16]] using [[air to air missile]]s,{{Cite news |last1=Crossette |first1=Barbara |last2=Times |first2=Special To the New York |date=31 March 1987 |title=PAKISTAN DOWNS AN AFGHAN INTRUDER |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/03/31/world/pakistan-downs-an-afghan-intruder.html |access-date=16 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} killing all 39 personnel on board. On 16 April 1987, Squadron Leader Badar Islam from the Tail Choppers Squadron shot down an Afghan [[Su-22]] with an [[AIM-9L]] Sidewinder, with its pilot Lt. Col. Abdul Jameel ejecting and being captured by Pakistani forces.[https://nationalinterest.org/blog/buzz/how-pakistans-f-16s-fought-russian-jets-and-shot-down-future-vp-russia-51407 How Pakistan’s F-16s Fought Russian Jets (And Shot Down the Future VP of Russia)] On 1 May, the Afghan government claimed to have shot down one Pakistani F-16 near [[Khost]] after warning fire; Pakistan accepted the loss of the aircraft,{{Cite news |last1=Weisman |first1=Steven R. |last2=Times |first2=Special To the New York |date=2 May 1987 |title=AFGHANS DOWN A PAKISTANI F-16, SAYING FIGHTER JET CROSSED BORDER |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/05/02/world/afghans-down-a-pakistani-f-16-saying-fighter-jet-crossed-border.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} attributing it to friendly fire.{{Cite web |title=Exclusive Friendly fire downs Pakistani F-16; U.S. in a coverup - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/07/18/Exclusive-Friendly-fire-downs-Pakistani-F-16-US-in-a-coverup/8251553579200/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 3 May, Pakistan claimed that 7 Afghan aircraft bombed Arandu, wounding five people. On 4 May, Afghan aircraft conducted a targeted strike on Ghulam Khan Killi, who was killed along with two children, and four were injured.{{Cite web |title=Pakistan protests Afghan border bombings - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/05/12/Pakistan-protests-Afghan-border-bombings/1328547790400/ |access-date=16 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} In mid-June, the US Agency for International Development office in Quetta was unsuccessfully targeted by a briefcase bomb. On 13 July, the US Consulate in Peshawar was slightly damaged in a bomb blast. On 14 July, two vehicles loaded with [[RDX]] drove into the Bohri Bazar in [[Karachi]] and parked. The cars detonated at intervals of 30 minutes from one another. The [[1987 Karachi car bombing]] resulted in 67 people being killed and left 300 injured.{{cite news |title=Bombs Kill 72 and Wound 250 in Pakistani City |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/07/15/world/bombs-kill-72-and-wound-250-in-pakistani-city.html |access-date=27 January 2022 |agency=Reuters |date=15 July 1987 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210826021053/https://www.nytimes.com/1987/07/15/world/bombs-kill-72-and-wound-250-in-pakistani-city.html |archive-date=26 August 2021 |url-status=dead}}{{cite news |title=BOMB BLASTS IN PAKISTAN FATAL TO 72 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1987/07/15/bomb-blasts-in-pakistan-fatal-to-72/c6954ab7-f7bd-4e30-a063-8e267734cf16/ |access-date=27 January 2022 |agency=Washington post |date=15 July 1987}}{{cite news |title=Zia accuses 'enemies of Pakistan' of bombing |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/07/15/Zia-accuses-enemies-of-Pakistan-of-bombing/7543553320000/ |access-date=27 January 2022 |work=UPI |date=15 July 1987}} On 4 August 1987, Squadron Leader Athar Bukhari from the [[No. 14 Squadron (Pakistan Air Force)|No. 14 Squadron]] shot down a Soviet [[Su-25]] near [[Miranshah]], piloted by the Soviet pilot, [[Alexander Rutskoy|Colonel Alexander Rutskoy]]. Rutskoy was ejected safely, but was captured by local people and was briefly held as a [[Prisoner of war|POW]] in [[Islamabad]].{{cite book |date=June 2007|title= PAF Over the Years |url=https://www.abebooks.com/PAF-Over-Years-Hussaini-M-Directorate/30089221503/bd|publisher= Directorate of Media Affairs, Pakistan Air Force |page=107 |edition=Revised|chapter=F-16 vs. Su-25}}{{Cite web|url=http://www.aviastar.org/air/russia/su-25.php|title = Sukhoi Su-25 - attack}} The [[Central Intelligence Agency|U.S. Central Intelligence Agency]] intervened to save him to avoid interfering with the [[Geneva Accords (1988)|Geneva Accords]] and the [[Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan]].{{Cite book|last=Coll|first=Steve|title=Ghost wars : the secret history of the CIA, Afghanistan, and bin Laden, from the Soviet invasion to September 10, 2001|date=2004|publisher=Penguin Press|isbn=1-59420-007-6|location=New York|oclc=52814066}} He was later handed back to the Soviets on 16 August 1988; this was his third time being downed as he had managed to eject and escape the earlier two times.{{cite book |author= |date=June 2007|title= PAF Over the Years |url=https://www.abebooks.com/PAF-Over-Years-Hussaini-M-Directorate/30089221503/bd|publisher= Directorate of Media Affairs, Pakistan Air Force |page=107 |edition=Revised|chapter=F-16 vs. Su-25}} On 3 October 1987, two Afghan [[Mil Mi-4]] helicopters defected to Pakistan, landing in [[Chitral]]. Although the helicopters were returned to Afghanistan, the crews were granted political asylum.{{Cite web |title=Avganistan kupuje borbene avione - Page |url=https://www.paluba.info/smf/index.php?topic=7485.10;imode&fbclid=PAQ0xDSwK7eHdleHRuA2FlbQIxMAABp1AN0_nk4vMq5UkIjSTcLDOpK_j2rUVR4fkvJcBoSSNcAz3sfYzAGwixfAXy_aem__nygOjcNz6sHzwZzjuOa2Q |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=www.paluba.info}} According to a report by the US Defense Department, approximately 90% of the estimated 777 acts of international terrorism committed worldwide in 1987 took place in Pakistan.{{Cite news |first= |date=December 1987 |title=International Herald Tribune |pages=3}} ===1988=== {{See also|Ojhri Camp disaster|Operation Magistral|Battle for Hill 3234}} Pakistan Army Special Service Group reportedly engaged in armed battles with the [[Russian Airborne Troops|Soviet paratroopers]] during [[Operation Magistral]], although the reports remained unconfirmed.[http://www.rsva.ru/biblio/prose_af/afgan-soldiers/5.shtml "Клятва тридцати девяти".] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303230758/http://www.rsva.ru/biblio/prose_af/afgan-soldiers/5.shtml |date=3 March 2016}} A. Oliynik. ''[[Krasnaya Zvezda]]'', 29 October 1988. {{in lang|ru}} When the [[Battle for Hill 3234]] concluded on 8 January 1988, the [[Russian Airborne Troops|Soviet paratroopers]] found that the [[Afghan mujahideen]] actually wore the black uniforms with rectangular black-yellow-red stripes, and suspected to be Army Special Service Group personnel; Pakistan's government officially denied their involvement. The American author, [[Aukai Collins]], identified the elements as "Black Storks" who crossed the border to join the Afghan mujahideen–a claim also backed by American author, David Campbell. {{rp|60–61}}{{cite book |last1=Campbell |first1=David |title=Soviet Paratrooper vs Mujahideen Fighter: Afghanistan 1979–89 |date=2017 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |location=New York, US |isbn=9781472817655 |pages=80 |edition=1st |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MKE2DwAAQBAJ&dq=Special+Service+Group+Black+storks&pg=PA64 |access-date=28 January 2019 |language=en-us |chapter-format=google books |chapter=Battlefield Environment |archive-date=14 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230214201823/https://books.google.com/books?id=MKE2DwAAQBAJ&dq=Special+Service+Group+Black+storks&pg=PA64 |url-status=live }} On 27 February, the Afghan Air Force struck Matasanga and Khardand camps, 180 miles west of [[Islamabad]], killing 31 and injuring 49 more.{{Cite web |last=Archives |first=L. A. Times |date=28 February 1987 |title=Afghan Bombers Strike Pakistan Again; 31 Die |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1987-02-28-mn-6505-story.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}} The [[Ojhri Camp disaster]] on 8 April 1988, caused by the explosion of an ammunition depot, resulted in the death of 93 people. [[Zia-ul-Haq]] dissolved the parliament after the incident. The [[United States]] alleged that the Soviet Union and the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan were involved in the incident.{{Cite book |last=Nawaz |first=Shuja |title=Crossed Swords: Pakistan, Its Army, and the Wars Within |date=11 October 2009 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0195476972 |edition=1st |pages=393 |language=English}}{{Cite book |last=Blood |first=Peter R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DRMTO7mn7hIC&pg=PA280 |title=Pakistan: A Country Study |date=1996 |publisher=DIANE Publishing |isbn=978-0-7881-3631-3 |pages=225 |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Faruqui |first=Salman |date=24 March 2024 |title=THE RISE AND FALL OF JUNEJO |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1823424 |access-date=12 May 2024 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en}}{{Cite book |last=Talbot |first=Ian |title=Pakistan: A Modern History |date=15 January 2010 |publisher=[[Palgrave Macmillan]] |isbn=978-0230623040 |edition=2nd |pages=284–286 |language=English}} In early September 1988, DRAAF/Soviets conducted three airstrikes on Pakistani villages killing five and inwounding 17.{{Cite web | title=INTERNAL SITUATION IN PAKISTAN {{!}} CIA FOIA (foia.cia.gov) | url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/document/cia-rdp90m00005r000400040012-6 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224083800/https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/document/cia-rdp90m00005r000400040012-6 | access-date=2026-07-19 | archive-date=2021-02-24}} On 7 September, PAF shot down an Afghan [[Mig 25]] which had conducted a bombing raid, killing one and injuring two people.{{Cite web |title=Pakistani jets downs Afghan warplane - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1988/09/07/Pakistani-jets-downs-Afghan-warplane/9462589608000/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 12 September 1988, [[Flight Lieutenant]] Khalid shot down two [[Mig-23]]. On 3 November 1988, Flight Lieutenant Khalid Mehmood shot down an Afghan [[Su-22]].{{cite web| url=http://www.allworldwars.com/The-Bear-vs-Mujahideen-in-Afghanistan-by-Edward-Westermann.html| title=THE LIMITS OF SOVIET AIRPOWER: THE BEAR VERSUS THE MUJAHIDEEN IN AFGHANISTAN, 1979-1989|first=Edward|last=B.Westermann}}{{cite web |url=http://www.pakdef.info/pakmilitary/airforce/war/indexafghanwar.html |title=Pakistan border battles |date= |publisher=PakDef.info |access-date=23 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081216114250/http://www.pakdef.info/pakmilitary/airforce/war/indexafghanwar.html |archive-date=16 December 2008}} On 26 September 1988, Major V. Astakhov from the [[120th Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment]] downed a Pakistani helicopter during an engagement as it was intruding into Afghan airspace.{{Cite magazine |last=Pavlov |first=Anton |date=2011 |title="Жемчужина Забайкалья": Репортаж с авиабазы "Домна" |trans-title=Pearl of Transbaikalia: Reporting from Domna air base |url=http://www.take-off.ru/pdf/06_2011.pdf |magazine=Vzlyot |volume=6 |language=ru |issue=78 |pages=30–35 |issn=1819-1754}} On 3 November, Khalid Mahmood shot down an Afghan Su-22 by firing two [[AIM-9L]] missiles.{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=4 November 1988 |title=Pakistan Downs an Afghan Plane |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/11/04/world/pakistan-downs-an-afghan-plane.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite web |last=Ranter |first=Harro |title=Accident Sukhoi Su-22 , Thursday 3 November 1988 |url=https://asn.flightsafety.org/wikibase/94849 |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=asn.flightsafety.org}} On 7 November, an Afghan aircraft bombed a refugee camp inside Pakistan, killing two people in Kotri village.{{Cite web |title=Afghan jets strafe Pakistan border town, killing two refugees - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1988/11/07/Afghan-jets-strafe-Pakistan-border-town-killing-two-refugees/8004594882000/ |access-date=18 July 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 19 November, Pakistan shot down an Afghan cargo plane that had lost direction and flown to [[Jalalabad]]. Thirty people were killed on board.{{Cite news |agency=Reuters |date=22 November 1988 |title=Afghanistan Reports 30 Dead On Plane Downed by Pakistan |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/11/22/world/afghanistan-reports-30-dead-on-plane-downed-by-pakistan.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite web |title=Pakistan shoots down Afghan military plane - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1988/11/19/Pakistan-shoots-down-Afghan-military-plane/6507595918800/ |access-date=16 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} Between May 1986 and November 1988,{{cite web |url=http://www.pafwallpapers.com/PAF_afghan_war-1.htm |title=PAF F-16 squadron pilots & crew during Soviet/Afghan War 1979–1988 |access-date=14 January 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120106005100/http://www.pafwallpapers.com/PAF_afghan_war-1.htm |archive-date=6 January 2012 |url-status=live }} the PAF's newly acquired F-16s had shot down at least eight intruding aircraft from [[Democratic Republic of Afghanistan|Afghanistan]]. The first three of these (one [[Su-22]], one probable Su-22, and one [[Antonov An-26|An-26]]) were shot down by two pilots from No. 9 Squadron. Pilots of No. 14 Squadron destroyed the remaining five intruders (two Su-22s, two [[Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23|MiG-23s]], and one [[Sukhoi Su-25|Su-25]]).[http://www.pafwallpapers.com/kill_illustrations.htm] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115121441/http://www.pafwallpapers.com/kill_illustrations.htm|date=15 January 2012}}. Most of these kills were by the [[AIM-9 Sidewinder]], but at least one (a Su-22) was destroyed by cannon fire. Pakistani Flight Lieutenant Khalid Mahmoud is credited with three of these kills.[http://www.f-16.net/f-16_users_article14.html F-16 Air Forces – Pakistan] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090723130433/http://www.f-16.net/f-16_users_article14.html |date=23 July 2009 }}. F-16.net. Retrieved 8 September 2010.{{Cite web | url=https://www.indiatoday.in/magazine/defence/story/19870731-doubts-crop-up-about-f-16-fighting-falcons-capabilities-after-paf-mishap-799104-1987-07-31 | title=Doubts crop up about F-16 Fighting Falcon's capabilities after PAF mishap | date=31 July 1987 | access-date=2 June 2019 | archive-date=2 June 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190602175645/https://www.indiatoday.in/magazine/defence/story/19870731-doubts-crop-up-about-f-16-fighting-falcons-capabilities-after-paf-mishap-799104-1987-07-31 | url-status=live }} By 1988, [[KGB]] and KhAD agents were able to penetrate deep inside Pakistan and carry out attacks on mujahideen sanctuaries and guerrilla bases.{{Cite web |date=28 February 1987 |title=Prime Minister Mohammad Khan Junejo warned today Pakistan would... |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1987/02/28/Prime-Minister-Mohammad-Khan-Junejo-warned-today-Pakistan-would/9072541486800/}} ==Disinformation== The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan faced criticism from the global community, for which the [[KGB]] launched ''Operation Torkham'' to neutralise the negative view of the Soviets and to distract attention from the war in Afghanistan, which involved disinformation. Vasiliy Mitrokhin stated that [[Yuri Andropov]], the chairman of the [[KGB]] approved a plan which included information warfare against the Pakistani military and its involvement in Afghanistan, impeding relations between [[India]] and [[Pakistan]]. According to a KGB resident in Delhi, Soviets saw conflict between India and Pakistan as beneficial as it could lead to decreased Pakistani support for the Mujahideen, therefore weakening Afghanistan's defenses.{{Cite web |title='Torkham' - USSR's Machination To Dismember India And Instigate An Indo-pak War |url=https://www.spansen.com/2025/02/torkham-ussrs-machination-to-dismember.html |access-date=7 September 2025 |language=en-GB}} Through the [[UN]], the message was to be conveyed to the Iranian representatives that Pakistan was willing to grant the [[United States]] bases in [[Baluchistan]], which was close to [[Iran]]. The Chukhrov working group proposed plans to create an independent Azad Kashmir separate from India and Pakistan and to set up a government in exile for [[Balochistan]]; however, the plan was postponed due to complexities.{{Cite web |date=10 May 2012 |title=KGB activities in India, Pakistan and Afghanistan |url=https://canarytrap.in/history/kgb-activities-in-india-pakistan-and-afghanistan/ |access-date=7 September 2025 |website=Canary Trap |language=en-US}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Notes== {{Notelist}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Spillover of the Soviet-Afghan War in Pakistan}} [[Category:1979 in Afghanistan]] [[Category:1979 in Pakistan]] [[Category:1979 in the Soviet Union]] [[Category:1980s conflicts]] [[Category:1980s in Afghanistan]] [[Category:1980s in Pakistan]] [[Category:1980s in the Soviet Union]] [[Category:Aerial operations and battles involving Pakistan]] [[Category:Afghan conflict]] [[Category:Afghanistan–Pakistan border]] [[Category:Anti-communism in Pakistan]] [[Category:Battles involving Pakistan]] [[Category:Battles of the Soviet–Afghan War]] [[Category:Cold War conflicts]] [[Category:Cold War military history of the Soviet Union]] [[Category:1979 conflicts]] [[Category:General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon]] [[Category:Inter-Services Intelligence operations]] [[Category:Operations involving special forces of Pakistan]] [[Category:Pakistan–Soviet Union relations]] [[Category:Proxy wars]] [[Category:Soviet–Afghan War]] [[Category:Terrorism in Pakistan]] [[Category:Wars involving Afghanistan]] [[Category:Wars involving Pakistan]] [[Category:Wars involving the Soviet Union]] [[Category:Spillover of wars]]

17 Aircraft Captured/Defected{{efn|one [[Mil Mi-8]] hijacked and defected on 26 April 1981, a [[Mig-17]] crashed during a defection attempt in October 1982, an unspecified helicopter in late October 1982, one [[Su-7]] defected on 20 November 1983, one [[Mil Mi-25]] defected on 16 July 1984, an [[An-26]] defected on 22 September 1984, two [[Mil Mi-24]]s defected on 28 June 1985, six [[Mil Mi-8]] captured on 2 April 1986,{{Cite web|url=https://community.apan.org/cfs-file/__key/docpreview-s/00-00-09-39-44/2001_2D00_09_2D00_01-The-Campaign-for-the-Caves-_2800_Grau-and-Jalali_2900_.pdf|title=Campaign for the caves of Zhawar}} a [[Mig-21]] defected on 23 October 1986, two [[Mil Mi-4]] defected on 3 October 1987}}
'''Per Pakistan:''' 10 Aircraft shot down{{efn|including two [[Su-22]]s on 17 May 1986, an [[An-26]] on 31 March 1987, a [[Su-22]] on 16 April 1987, a [[Su-25]] on 4 August 1987, a [[Mig-25]] on 7 September 1988, two [[Mig-23]]s on 12 September 1988, a [[Su-22]] on 3 November 1988 and an unspecified cargo aircraft on 19 Movement 1988}}
'''Per Soviet Union:''' 5 Aircraft shot down{{efn|including three [[Su-22]]s, a [[Su-25]] and an [[An-26]]}}{{cite web|url=https://nationalinterest.org/blog/buzz/pakistan%E2%80%99s-f-16s-battled-soviet-jets%E2%80%94and-shot-down-future-vice-president-russia-47717|title=Pakistan's F-16s Battled Soviet Jets – and Shot Down the Future Vice President of Russia|date=16 March 2019|work=National Interest|last=Roblin|first=Sebastian|access-date=20 December 2019}} | casualties2 = {{flagicon image|Flag of the Afghan interim government-in-exile (1988–1992).svg}}/{{flagdeco|Pakistan}} '''[[Pakistan]]:'''{{bulletedlist|5,775 killed{{Cite book |last=Andrews |first=Dr Sudhir |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PXzlEAAAQBAJ&dq=soviet%E2%80%93afghan+war+pakistan+5%2C775&pg=PA118 |title=BACKLASH TO TODAY |date=25 November 2023 |publisher=Blue Rose Publishers |pages=118 |language=en}}|6,804 wounded |1 [[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon|F-16]] fighter aircraft lost/shot down{{efn|lost to friendly fire, according to Pakistan and shot down, according to Afghan authorities}}Markovskiy, Victor (1997). Due to the Soviet Union's steadfast support for India, which contributed to the loss of Pakistani territory in the years leading up to the Soviet-Afghan War, Pakistani leaders moved to support the [[Afghan mujahideen|mujahideen]] in their fight against the Soviets. Western powers provided financial support to Pakistan in exchange for their involvement. The Pakistani military trained mujahideen and produced volunteers to help Afghan forces. As a result, there were attacks on Pakistan by both the Soviets and communist Afghan groups. During this period, millions of Afghans fled to Pakistan for safety. The consequences of this were great and long-lasting: the [[Inter-Services Intelligence]] (ISI) agency established [[Madrasa|madrasas]] along the Afghan border, which fostered a dual religious and political ideology that contributed to the establishment of the [[Taliban]]. In the decades since the Soviet-Afghan War, there have continued to be disputes over territory and immigration between Pakistan and Afghanistan. ==Background== {{Excerpt|Foreign involvement in the Soviet–Afghan War#Pakistan}} ==Timeline== A table covering the spillover incidents of the Soviet-Afghan War in Pakistan from 1980 to 1988 is as follows:{{Cite journal|url=https://www.humapub.com/admin/alljournals/girr/papers/JWbvQVIcpS.pdf|title=Pakistan – U.S. Relations and its Impact on Afghanistan|author1=Muhammad Imran Ashraf|author2=Iqra Jathol|author3=Mubbshar Ali|year=2020|journal=Global International Relations Review|volume=3|page=6|doi=10.31703/girr.2020(III-I).01 }} {| class="wikitable sortable colleft" style="text-align: centre;" |- | Year{{efn|Data for 1979 and 1989 not included}} ! colspan="2" | Terrorist Blasts ! colspan="2" | Artillery Attacks ! colspan="2" | Air Attacks |- ! ! On 2 December 1981, a helicopter gunship fired by Afghan forces killed seven people in [[Balochistan]]. On 18 December, six Afghan helicopters again attacked a refugee camp, this time in [[South Waziristan]], killing a child and destroying two houses.{{Cite news |agency=Reuters |date=21 December 1981 |title=Pakistan Says Afghans Strafed Refugee Camp |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/12/21/world/pakistan-says-afghans-strafed-refugee-camp.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} ===1982=== In early October 1982, an Afghan defector moving towards Pakistan was killed as his [[Mig-17]] crashed near the border in Chaman, but a helicopter was able to successfully make it across the border, later that month. ===1983=== In May 1983, the [[No. 17 Squadron (Pakistan Air Force)|No. 17 Squadron]] while operating from [[PAF Base Samungli|Samungli Airbase]] along with the [[No. 23 Squadron (Pakistan Air Force)|No. 23 Squadron "Talons"]] was put on air defence alert after a surge in aerial intrusions by [[Afghan Air Force|Afghan]] and [[Soviet Air Force|Soviet]] warplanes during the Soviet-Afghan war. It performed 682 [[Combat Air Patrol|CAP]] missions and 238 [[hot scramble]]s. Unfortunately, the record of the aerial interceptions and other events was not maintained. {{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990128150750/http://www.defencejournal.com/aug98/pakafghanwar1.htm|title=PAKISTAN'S AFGHAN WAR AIR STRATEGY AND OPERATIONS|author=Air Commodore A HAMEED QADRI|website=Defence Journal|url=http://www.defencejournal.com/aug98/pakafghanwar1.htm|archive-date=28 January 1999|access-date=15 September 2025|url-status=dead}} On 17 September 1983, Afghan [[MIG-21]]s violated Pakistani airspace with the possible aim of targeting [[Mujahideen]] camps. The aircraft conducted a bombing raid in [[Parachinar]], killing a man. Pakistan condemned the attack and summoned Afghan officials. A protest was held in Parachinar against the attack during the Islamic holy event of [[Eid ul adha]].{{Cite web |title=Pakistan lodged a protest today over the Afghan Air... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/09/19/Pakistan-lodged-a-protest-today-over-the-Afghan-Air/2571432792000/ |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=19 September 1983 |title=PAKISTANI DIES AS AFGHAN JETS ARE REPORTED TO RAID VILLAGE |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/09/19/world/pakistani-dies-as-afghan-jets-are-reported-to-raid-village.html |access-date=17 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} On November 20, 1983, Captain Mohammed Nabi Korinzay defected to Pakistan with his [[Sukhoi Su-7|Su-7BM]] fighter-bomber.[https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/11/20/Afghan-pilot-defects-to-Pakistan/6486438152400/ Afghan pilot defects to Pakistan] The aircraft broke up during a crash landing on the runway at [[Dalbandin]]. ===1984=== On 16 July, an Afghan [[Mi-25]] helicopter defected and landed in [[Miranshah]].{{Cite web |title=Intrusions, Overflights, Shootdowns and Defections During the Cold War and Thereafter |url=https://myplace.frontier.com/~anneled/ColdWar.html?fbclid=PAQ0xDSwK7drRleHRuA2FlbQIxMAABp1AN0_nk4vMq5UkIjSTcLDOpK_j2rUVR4fkvJcBoSSNcAz3sfYzAGwixfAXy_aem__nygOjcNz6sHzwZzjuOa2Q |access-date=15 June 2025 |website=myplace.frontier.com}} On 13 August 1984, DRAAF bombed targets in [[Parachinar]].{{Cite web| title=Pakistan: Trouble Along the Afghan Border | url=https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP06T00412R000606330001-2.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240816204647/https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-RDP06T00412R000606330001-2.pdf | archive-date=2024-08-16}} On 14 August 1984, three Afghan aircraft bombed Kunj Alizai, near the village of Nisti Kot killing one and injuring five women.{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=14 August 1984 |title=AROUND THE WORLD; Afghans Said to Bomb A Pakistani Village |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/08/14/world/around-the-world-afghans-said-to-bomb-a-pakistani-village.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} The next day, on 15 August, two Afghan jets again violated Pakistani airspace dropping two bombs over [[Pewar]] Kotal region, killing 13 people and injuring five.{{Cite web |title=Two Afghan aircraft violated Pakistani air space in the... - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1984/08/15/Two-Afghan-aircraft-violated-Pakistani-air-space-in-the/4329461390400/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 18, 19, and 21 August, Afghan Army conducted artillery strikes in Parachinar, followed by an airstrike on 23 August. On 22 September 1984, Colonel Haji Fakir, flying an [[Antonov An-26|An-26]] of the 373rd Transport Aviation Regiment defected from Afghanistan to [[Miranshah]] Air Base, Pakistan. On 2 October 1984, Afghanistan denied the Pakistani claim of its forces conducting a bombardment campaign in [[Tari Mangal]] which had killed 33 people and injured 48.{{Cite news |last=Ap |date=2 October 1984 |title=Bombing of Pakistan Is Denied by Afghans |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/10/02/world/bombing-of-pakistan-is-denied-by-afghans.html |access-date=15 June 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} ===1985=== {{See also|Badaber uprising}} On 24 January, Pakistani authorities said that 2 Afghan aircraft had violated Pakistani airspace for three days near Arandu and had dropped two bombs, but caused no damage.{{Cite web |title=Foreign News Briefs - UPI Archives |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/01/24/Foreign-News-Briefs/1566475390800/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |website=UPI |language=en}} On 14 April, Pakistan claimed that two Afghan jets violated Pakistani airspace near [[Chitral]] and dropped two bombs, they also accused Afghanistan of further violations near [[Arandu, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa|Arandu]]. The accusations, however, were rejected by Afghanistan.{{Cite web |date=22 April 1985 |title=United Nations |url=https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n85/115/95/pdf/n8511595.pdf#:~:text=On%2014%20April%201985%2C%20one,kilometres%20south%2Deast%20of%20Arandu.&text=two%20bombs%20approximately%207%2F8%20kilometre%26%20north%2Dwest%20of%20Drosh.&text=A%2F40%2F50%2FRev%2C%201.&text=20%20rockets%20approximately%202%20kil. |website=General Assembly Security Council - The United Nations}} A [[prisoner of war|POW]] uprising took place on 26–27 April 1985 in [[Badaber]], when Soviet and Afghan POWs revolted at the fortress of Badaber where they were being held captive. The [[Jamaat-e-Islami]] forces and the Pakistani Army's [[XI Corps (Pakistan)|XI Corps]] suppressed the rebellion.
